In interior point methods (IPMs), an iterative solution formulation is often employed, which occasionally necessitates the resort to Krylov solvers to speed up computation. For various reasons, such as preventing thread interference in parallel computing, it may be beneficial to stop the iteration before reaching an exact solution. Hence, a predetermined tolerance for termination is necessary to limit continued solving. The primary shortcoming with conventional tolerance criteria, which rely on residual norms, is that they do not take into account the inherent characteristics of IPMs, specifically the Newton-Raphson method, which often results in an overestimation of the desired tolerance due to the quadratic convergence. As a result, an excessively large number of iterations may be required to reach an acceptable level of accuracy in low-dimensional systems. We introduce an alternative termination criterion that leverages an estimate of the desired accuracy that is specifically tailored to the quadratic convergence of IPMs, which is also corroborated by numerical experiments in dimensions up to 32,597. Additionally, we provide an easily implementable solution that estimates the desired accuracy without incurring additional computational burdens. The proposed criterion has been successfully used in conjunction with CHIMERA and TAME codes for their extensive numerical trials. The modified termination criterion, when combined with an optimal preconditioner, has also been employed to solve a series of large-scale quadratic programs, which further underscores the efficacy of the proposed approach. A computational method is developed that integrates precise renormalization group techniques with gradient descent algorithms. This hybrid approach incorporates a precise transformation of the ultraviolet degrees of freedom, and their associated actions, into a more relevant form at a desired lower energy scale. We apply this technique to renormalize the Wilson-Yukawa system, an interaction model that includes both quadratic and cubic couplings, initially at strong coupling strength in four dimensions. By repeatedly applying the renormalization protocol, we track the evolution of the system's parameters as the ultraviolet cutoff is gradually introduced, and demonstrate its ability to produce predictable and predictable outcomes. Furthermore, we show that the renormalization group flow can be used to clarify the mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking in this system, specifically in two cases: one with two major components (two flavor symmetry and U(1) gauge symmetry) and another with three components (SU(2) gauge symmetry). Current reference models for business processes are often based on process models that combine flow of information and material, such as BPMN and EPCs. These models do not explicitly address the problem of discrepancies that arise between these specifications and real-world process executions. To address this issue, dynamic monitoring approaches have been developed, but they require process models that can be formally verified. This necessitates process models that are unambiguous and precise, which is typically not the case with current reference models. To bridge this gap, our approach develops a language for dynamic quality management that can handle the validation and monitoring of process models with inherent ambiguities. This allows for the efficient handling of discrepancies during process execution, and our approach is grounded in the automata-theoretic model. By leveraging this model, we can define hybrid process specifications that integrate data and material flows, and provide a generic framework for process management that can be adapted from existing quality management models. Ultimately, our approach provides a robust foundation for processing and managing process-related information during dynamic quality management. (C) 2023. A mathematical equation, specifically a delayed logistic model, has been developed to analyze the dynamics of certain biological systems where the interaction between cells is non-instantaneous. This non-immediate interaction is represented by a constant time lag, denoted as $\tau$. The global stability of this model was theoretically examined using the stable manifold theorem and the Lyapunov-LaSalle theorem. These theorems reveal the boundaries of stable and unstable manifolds, which divide the global plane into distinct regions depending on the lag value. The regions are characterized by the presence of unique equilibrium points, such as the non-stable and unstable internal equilibrium. The analysis shows that a stable internal equilibrium exists and is globally asymptotically stable only when the lag value is within a specific range, while two other internal equilibria exhibit unstable dynamics in this context. The study also presents distinct phase plane patterns for different lag values, influencing the model's overall behavior and the occurrence of bifurcation phenomena. The novel postponed logistic equation provides a useful representation of the saddle-like, star-shaped bifurcation and offers an alternative approach to modeling biological systems where the time lag is constant but not zero. The work presents the first attempt to comprehensively analyze a delayed logistic model with a positive lag value, shedding light on its global dynamics and offering an easily implementable approach to modeling biological cell interactions. The study confirms the model's applicability to real-world scenarios such as population growth and further expands the utility of logistic models in biological research. The proof of global stability and the critical sets identified in this analysis will contribute to the development of delayed nonlinear mathematical equations, while the model's equilibrium points and their associated stability also provide essential tools for effectively utilizing the novel postponed logistic equation in biological modeling. The study presents an easily understandable approach to postponing the logistic equation and identifies critical conditions for the occurrence of bifurcation, providing a versatile tool for modeling biological cell interactions and understanding the global behavior of delayed nonlinear equations. The work also presents an alternative approach to the existing $R$ operation method for studying discrete nonlinear models and contributes to the development of novel mathematical tools for analyzing difference equations. The isometric log-ratio (ILR) transformation has emerged as a highly effective tool for modeling compositional data and applying depth-based analysis methods. However, the majority of research on the ILR transformation has focused on continuous variables following a specific distribution. In contrast, our work extends the concept of statistical depth to point processes via the ILR transformation, encompassing a broader range of random measures and multivariate temporal networks. To achieve this, we develop a new distance metric, referred to as the Wasserstein distance based on the directed kernel, which enables the efficient application of the ILR transformation to measure distributions. Furthermore, we derive an explicit expression for the depth of a point process by employing the repulsive force principle and developing a simple, computationally viable approximation method. By incorporating these advancements, researchers can now efficiently calculate the depth of a point process, such as a network's density, in real-time. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we apply a real-world case study to a temporal network of human face pose, achieving meaningful results. The proposed methodology is further exemplified through a series of simulated experiments. The underlying mathematical concepts are detailed in an appendix, along with the used code is available at https://github.com/jiansi1990/ILR_Depth_Protein Networks. The presented ideas are theoretically grounded and mathematically rigorous, with key proofs provided in the appendix. The isometric log-ratio transformation, statistical depth, and repulsive force principle contribute to the theory, while the efficiency and efficacy are demonstrated through empirical testing. The used techniques for the depth of a point process, such as the efficient approximation method, Wasserstein distance based on the directed kernel, and temporal networks, encompass a range of machine learning and computer science concepts. The underlying ideas for the paper were conceived during a research visit to Princeton University, where the problem was identified through a discussion on applying the isometric log-ratio transformation to face pose sequences. The solution, which utilized a combination of statistical depth and repulsive force principle, was developed through further research on the underlying mathematical concepts. The band depth for a temporal network, such as a face pose sequence, is measured by employing the ILR transformation to convert the sequence into a real-valued function, which is then sliced into equally sized parts to calculate the depth of each function slice. The depth of each slice is efficiency approximated and its distribution is subsequently calculated, allowing the determination of a band depth for the original temporal network, which can be visualized and the efficacy of its depth measured

We introduce an innovative strategy to boost the accuracy of structured text recognition by incorporating a novel training objective that emulates the patterns and conventions found in formatted documents. The new objective, termed Regex-favoring, seeks to optimize model preferences towards specific sequence patterns, akin to how regular expressions are used to extract desired information from text. By integrating the Regex-favoring objective into end-to-end structured text recognition models, we observe a substantial enhancement in accuracy on a range of dataset benchmarks. Furthermore, models trained with the proposed objective exhibit a more transparent and interpretable bias towards structured text patterns. To facilitate widespread adoption, we also propose a simplified approach to prescribing preferences in structured text recognition, dubbed Preference Templates, utilizing similar notation as regular expressions, making it easily applicable to new datasets. Experimental results on various datasets validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, demonstrating substantial gains in accuracy and the facilitation of dataset preferences. Our implementation and additional details can be accessed at: https://github.com/aleksiech/RFRx. In proton-nucleus collisions at high energy, the color of the proton can interact with the color of the nucleus, causing modifications to its internal properties and the characteristics of final state particles.  These effects have been investigated in parton-scattering events involving heavy quarks, particularly top quarks, which are relatively rare but provide a powerful tool for analyzing the interactions between partons and the saturation of the proton.  Since top quarks decay quickly into other particles, their production is challenging to detect directly, but researchers use indirect indicators such as certain types of subatomic particles in proton-proton collisions.  By analyzing these indicators in proton-nucleus collisions at various energies, scientists can better understand how top quarks behave in these collisions and what changes to their production and interaction behavior may occur due to the presence of multiple partons in the nucleus.  Furthermore, measurements of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions can provide valuable insights into our understanding of matrix elements that govern quark production and parton interactions, ultimately helping to refine models of the saturated proton and improve our knowledge of its internal properties.  By analyzing the modifications to parton behavior in top quarks, scientists can gain new understanding of the interactions between partons and the color of the proton, potentially leading to breakthroughs in our knowledge of matrix elements, parton dynamics, and the nature of the proton.  This research is particularly significant as it is the first analysis of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions, providing crucial data to guide the development of new models and precision calculations that will aid future research.  By doing so, scientists can advance our understanding of the saturated proton, parton interactions, and matrix elements, ultimately leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the fundamental building blocks of matter. Developing a machine learning model that can effectively process a wide range of SQL queries presents significant challenges, primarily due to the diverse linguistic patterns in which SQL commands are expressed. To tackle these complexities, researchers divide SQL language into distinct categories, such as update, delete, and insert, and develop separate models for each type of query. However, this approach ignores the common underlying structure of SQL commands within a single domain, as well as the universal linguistic patterns across different domains. To better capture these cross-domain linguistic patterns, we propose a comprehensive end-to-end text-to-SQL analysis system, consisting of a single table generator module for all SQL command types. Our method employs a data-driven auxiliary task to identify the appropriate SQL pattern (update, delete, insert, etc.) and selectively generates the relevant table fields based on this pattern. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our end-to-end table generator model through experimental evaluations on three large datasets, achieving superior performance compared to the current benchmarking methods. The auxiliary task successfully learns to recognize common linguistic patterns across different domains and seamlessly integrates with our end-to-end table generator module to produce exceptional results. The source code for our approach can be found at https://github.com/asharathp/End-to-End-Table-Generator. Additional details are available in the research paper titled "End-to-End Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL Analysis" (SMSI2022), authored by Asharath P. and supervised by Yash Kumar Patewari. Yash Kumar Patewari is a machine learning researcher at IIIT Bhubaneswar, India. This research was supported by the Centre for Machine Learning at IIIT Bhubaneswar, India. We've investigated the galaxy energy spectrum of the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey's first data release across the 35-190 MHz frequency range, using a specially designed, LOFAR-optimal dataset called the 'Galaxy Spectrum'. The Galaxy Spectrum is a weighted average of galaxies identified within a specific UV-excess selected sample and serves as a galaxy energy spectrum. Between 35 and 115 MHz, the Galaxy Spectrum ramps up at a rate of m_Fnu ~ t^(1.0±0.1)_-star. At frequencies above 115 MHz, the spectrum levels off with a rate of m_Fnu ~ t^(0.6±0.1)_star. These findings align with the expectations from synchrotron radiation by compactness. It's evident that galaxies become more abundant at lower frequencies as stellar emission declines, making it harder to detect them. We've discovered that a lower frequency cutoff of around 35 MHz is needed to fully capture the galaxy population. Additionally, our data suggests an upper frequency limit of around 125 MHz to obtain an accurate galaxy representation. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the LOFAR data is susceptible to biasing due to the influence of stellar emission, leading to over-representation of galaxies with high radio luminosity and rapid star-formation at lower frequencies. Conversely, at higher frequencies, the biasing effect favors galaxies with high radio luminosity and slow star-formation. Therefore, any conclusions based on these frequencies should be interpreted cautiously, taking into account the biasing effects. Finally, we've demonstrated that the Galaxy Spectrum can be used for biasing outcome detection, thereby serving as a frequency-biasing indicator. It's thereby capable of identifying regions with varying levels of biasing across different galaxy observations. However, we've also noted that this approach may not always yield accurate results, particularly in cases where biasing effects are masked by varying levels of stellar emission. To further refine our approach, future developments may incorporate more advanced select samples that better represent the galaxy energy spectrum, thereby reducing variations in stellar emission and allowing for more accurate biasing outcomes. Moreover, future upgrades to the LoTSS dataset will provide greater insights into the biasing outcomes, thereby refining the Galaxy Spectrum and helping to obtain more precise results. Ultimately, our approach to detecting biasing outcomes can be applied not only to LoTSS but any large-scale radio survey, thereby providing crucial insights into galaxy development and promoting a deeper understanding of the underlying physical processes. The High-Dimensional Ranking Lasso (HDR Lasso) is an enhanced version of Lasso, specifically designed for feature ranking in high-dimensional data with complex correlations. Unlike conventional Lasso, HDR Lasso handles data of infinite dimensions and incorporates an adaptive-sieving-based algorithm to improve feature selection accuracy. Our adaptively enhanced sieve-likelihood-estimation algorithm refines the HDR Lasso's original marginal-decimation method, yielding superior performance in feature ranking. Additionally, we developed an optimized computational approach, incorporating both active-set strategy and cyclic gradient-descent, to significantly boost the algorithm's efficiency. Our experimental results demonstrate the robustness of the new algorithm in a wide range of applications by outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods such as Lasso, HDR Lasso, and S-Lasso. Furthermore, the computational complexity analysis confirms that our algorithm achieves reduced computational cost. Our algorithmic enhancements and analytical findings indicate that feature selection accuracy improves and computational cost decreases concurrently as the correlation in the data increases. Conversely, the selectivity of HDR Lasso and our adapted approach decreases while the computational cost increases in the presence of anticorrelation. Our proposed algorithm is an effective, high-performance solution for feature ranking in high-dimensional data with various types of correlations. The source code of our algorithm is available at https://github.com/jaechang/HDR-S-Lasso. Additionally, the simulated data used in our study can be accessed via https://dataoffice.usc.edu/ and real data can be obtained from public datasets, such as NCI-60, by contacting Sung Kim at university of southern california. Our findings contribute to the feature ranking literature by providing an in-depth analysis of theoretical results, including the asymptotic behavior and computational complexity of our algorithm, as well as extensive experimental results demonstrating its high performance in feature ranking. Utilizing the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and maximum entropy production principle, we investigate the entropy creation of a system subjected to weak and rapid driving forces. This analysis reveals that in situations involving rapid driving, these two principles converge to outline a single boundary, defining the zone of increased entropy production. Beyond this boundary, within the system's response time frame, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem indicates a reduced entropy creation, whereas the maximum entropy production principle stipulates a increased entropy creation. To further contextualize our findings, we examine this scenario in relation to stochastic thermodynamics, demonstrating that the system's average current may be used to determine whether the maximum entropy production or fluctuation-dissipation theorem boundaries are approached, without necessarily knowing the dissipation ratio or relaxation time. This insight holds potential for evaluating the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in experiments involving rapid entropy changes. Additionally, our analysis reveals that, in some cases, the system may revert to a lower entropy state than its initial state, thereby reframing the concept of entropy production in thermodynamics. This study provides a foundational framework for evaluating the applicability of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in non-equilibrium experiments, potentially extending the theorem's applications to drives exceeding the system's response time. Lastly, our analysis also sheds light on the relationship between the relaxation time and drive velocity, displaying opposition for slow drives but convergence towards a common value for high drive velocities. This behavior can be attributed to the system's inability to fully respond to the drive, resulting in a delayed convergence towards a new equilibrium state. To summarize, our analysis outlines a convex boundary, defining a region of increased entropy production, and reveals a counter-intuitive aspect of entropy analysis due to rapid driving, thereby redefining the concept and potentially evaluating the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in high-velocity experiments. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the utilization of the system's average current to determine the boundary of fluctuation-dissipation theorem, without requiring knowledge of the dissipation ratio or relaxation time, and also explores the relationship between drive velocity and relaxation time, displaying delayed convergence and potential for evaluation in high-velocity experiments. Lastly, our analysis sheds light on the system's behavior following a non-equilibrium drive, and reveals a possible state where the system may revert to a lower entropy state than its initial state, thereby reframing the concept of entropy production in thermodynamics. This study provides a foundational framework for evaluating the applicability of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem in non-equilibrium experiments, and potentially extends the theorem's applications

To assess the effectiveness of control policies in process engineering, authors often employ procedural monitoring, analyzing the impact of interventions on system behavior through feedback. This work advances that research by exploring predictive, prescriptive procedural monitoring - interpreting results from control actions to inform future behaviors in process operations. We devise a protocol to develop predictive, prescriptive processes: define a controlled system, determine a performance metric, and develop predictive models for both the controlled system and the mechanism behind the imposed restrictions. This framework is illustrated with a practical application - predictive, prescriptive modeling of a heating, cooling, and hold strategy for a pharmaceutical batch process. Compared to conventional procedural monitoring, this predictive approach yields predictions in line with actual results, while future actions are optimized to minimize costs, aligning with the prescriptive goal of recommending the best future behaviors. Failing to consider the mechanism behind a control policy may result in recommendations at odds with the operator's intent, leading to suboptimal decisions. Moving forward, we suggest incorporating the mechanism's purpose into future predictive, prescriptive monitoring methodologies. Additionally, the decision-making aspect of the pharmaceutical example can be formalized as a stochastic optimization problem, whose solution provides the recommended actions. However, we encounter challenges in directly linking this decision-making problem to process data, hindering us from fully automating the prescriptive monitoring of process behaviors. We explore potential solutions to streamline the operator's decision-making process, such as utilizing adjustable rate limits within predetermined ranges or adjusting surveillance frequencies based on prior experiences. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of predictive, prescriptive procedural monitoring and paves the way for predictive, prescriptive process control. This research introduces an error management system for a Boussinesq model with adaptive mesh refinement. The Boussinesq model simplifies a complex Navier-Stokes system by assuming nearly incompressible velocity and heat transfer rates. However, this approximation may not always yield satisfactory results, particularly in scenarios where the fluid's thermal expansion significantly impacts its motion. A proposed Boussinesq model extension, the generalized Boussinesq model, incorporates the fluid's thermal momentum relaxation relaxation time and represents a more realistic thermal boundary layer. Associated goal-oriented adaptive algorithms are developed to optimize a variety of simulation goals related to heat and velocity. The study utilizes test cases with marked thermal expansion to verify the effectiveness of the suggested framework. The utilized generalized Boussinesq model is compared to a Boussinesq model under different levels of thermal boundary layer approximation and velocity solution requirements. The investigation validates the hypothesis that the generalized Boussinesq model provides more accurate approximations of the full Navier-Stokes simulation outcomes, particularly in regards to velocity and heat transfer boundary layers. Additionally, the study demonstrates the feasibility of achieving multiple optimization goals with adjustable priorities, yielding substantial gains in computational efficiency and error reduction. The research further explores the impact of adaptive mesh refinement and goal-oriented error management strategies, revealing their complementary utility in achieving optimized performance and error control. The proposed framework presents a versatile framework for managing error and adapting algorithms in fluid dynamics simulations with multiple optimization goals, alongside providing comprehensive documentation and source code for the employed numerical methods and test cases. The code can be accessed via a GitHub repository at https://github.com/pmeqwiki/adaptative_gb_test_cases. The generalized Boussinesq model introduced in this research can serve as a valuable tool for tackling a broad array of thermal expansion-related problems, encompassing both numerical and analytical case studies. The proposed algorithm also offers a practical solution for the goal-oriented adaptive algorithm challenge, showcasing the effectiveness of an error management strategy with adjustable priorities and multiple optimization goals. Furthermore, the study underscores the significance of accurately modeling the fluid's thermal momentum relaxation for realistic thermal boundary layer approximation, thereby validating the proposed generalized Boussinesq model. The theoretical framework presented in this research can be applied to other modeling approaches, such as the Brinkman-Forchheimer model, to develop an adaptive algorithm with multiple error management options and heat and velocity-related goals. To address the issue of stacking, which is a fundamental challenge in creating tall free-standing structures with layered materials, a new algorithm is proposed that significantly reduces the input size while preserving solutions of interest. By applying a series of pre-processing steps, the algorithm obtains various useful configurations of the base layer, thereby enabling efficient solutions to be identified within a much smaller parameter space. This improved approach leads to faster computation, yielding soluble base layers at a rate 100 times faster than the original method and solving the entire problem at a rate 10 times faster than solving it from scratch each time. Furthermore, the algorithm enables solutions to be found in sub-critical path lengths, enabling the evaluation of alternative stacking strategies and demonstrating that highly efficient stacking strategies exhibit similar structure to the greedy approach. Finally, the algorithm facilitates the generation of diverse, effective stacking strategies through simple modifications to the base layer, thereby expanding the algorithm's utility to applications outside of algorithmic evaluation. The algorithm demonstrates tangible results, with 522 new compounds identified, 121 of which exhibit superior stacking scores compared to the previously best-rated compounds in the PDB database, while also rivaling the performance of chemically synthesized materials in terms of superior stacking scores, with solutions at least partially solution-configured accounting for 62\% of all identified compounds. Key features of the algorithm include its compactness, with all relevant information captured within a 7-configuration window, its ability to solve the problem efficiently without resorting to time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations, and its ability to produce solution-configured results, all without supplementing the base layer with additional atoms. In a scenario of global uncertainty, individuals form opinions about social structures, translating this opinion into a level of confidence in their existing beliefs. This level of confidence dictates their willingness to take risks in challenging the established order. As more individuals share the opinion of dispersing the current structure, it may lead to a preference for change, potentially triggering a societal shift. However, if this opinion remains isolated, it may result in persecution, prompting individuals to conceal their sentiments and maintain silence. A mathematical equilibrium exists when no one alters their perspective, and we examine how differing confidence levels and opinion distributions affect this equilibrium in large populations. Our analysis reveals a division within the population between 'extremists' who express confidence in a better future and 'conservatives' who prioritize maintaining the status quo. Numerical data demonstrates that only a narrow range of opinion densities initiates a societal shift, and we examine how altering parameters, such as opinion density and confidence threshold, affects this range. Finally, a related model is explored which considers individuals to be uncertain about the structure of society, developing their own opinions through interaction with neighboring individuals, and a new division within the population is observed. These two groups, known as 'enthusiasts' and'skeptics,' exhibit distinct behavior, and a new range of opinion densities is identified which results in a societal shift, and we examine how altering parameters affects this range in an efficient manner. Furthermore, a considerable difference is discovered in behavior when the structure of society is fixed rather than randomly selected, and it is proven that a threshold exists beyond which only 'enthusiasts' persist in a society. Our work offers a framework that can be applied to various societal shifts through a variety of opinions and confidence mechanisms. It also provides a potential explanation for the widespread support of revolution and the reluctance of most people to engage in radical change. Additionally, it offers a potential explanation for why experts are often willing to engage in radical changes while the general public remains skeptical. Finally, it also offers a potential explanation for the widespread silence and skepticism during the Nazi era in Germany. Our work also discovers a new class of social equilibrium known as'structural opinion equilibrium,' and it also offers a potential method to determine when a structural change in society is beneficial for society. Different proteins' transcriptional activation times influence their cellular levels, 
but the complex relationships between nearly 20,000 genes, their transcription factors, 
and the proteins produced from them make this problem too large for traditional modeling strategies.
A new approach has been developed that allows for the simultaneous modeling of multiple genes' transcriptional dynamics, 
using the interdependent times of RNA production for these genes.
This model's effectiveness is demonstrated by its application to S. cerevisiae, 
where it accurately predicts the cellular levels of over 6,500 proteins with high precision.
Notably, the model identifies patterns such as the early production of core metabolic proteins and delayed production of proteins involved in structural processes like chitin turnover. 
The model further reveals that the times of RNA production for proteins performing similar cellular functions tend to concentrate around a limited number of optimal times, 
suggesting an underlying organizational structure in the genetic code.
The model's reliability is confirmed by its successful prediction of the effects of mutations on protein levels, 
including known and previously unknown examples. 
The tool for generating these results is available at http://dev.yinlab.washington.edu/pathwayx/ and has been confirmed to work on other species with known transcriptional data. 
The code for generating these results is available at https://github.com/yinlabwashington/pax.py. 
The data used in this research is available at NCBI, UniProt, and FlyBase. 
The figures used to illustrate these results are available at https://yinlab.washington.edu/shared/pax_figs/.

The existence of a 0 spin state in 64Ni has been confirmed through an experiment-free assessment that incorporates the most up-to-date nuclear structure calculations. This investigation emphasizes the significant influence of tensor interactions in explaining the structure of this nucleus and related isotones. Calculations indicate that a specific tensor interaction, characterized by a monopole nature, plays a crucial role in stabilizing the 0 spin state in 64Ni through the correlation of protons with neutrons. Chiral gauge theories are considered to be an active field of research because they have unique characteristics such as infrared instabilities and the potential to be dual to scalar field theories through the duality principle. A specific type of chiral gauge theory, composed of left-handed fermions in three dimensions, is particularly interesting because it is expected to have a non-supersymmetric dual based on the holographic principle. Similarities between gauge and gravity theories facilitate the retrieval of the fermionic dual in a more manageable dual frame. A key aspect of this concept is volume factors, which compensate for the differences in fermion determinants between the original and dual frames. Given the success of this duality in three-dimensional chiral theories, researchers are now exploring the possibility of extending it to more intricate cases, such as chiral theories in higher dimensions with multiple left-handed fermions, and theories featuring global symmetries in additional dimensions. Additionally to the supersymmetric duals of four-dimensional chiral theories, non-supersymmetric duals become a plausible possibility. Furthermore, theories with global symmetances in additional dimensions can be addressed with the help of the holographic duality principle. The volume factors in these theories can be understood as the outcome of the duality, while their high-order infrared behavior may be analyzed through the equilibrium limit. The example of a chiral gauge theory in five-dimensional space, featuring an SU(N) global symmetry and fermions in one additional fermion, is examined in more detail. An action that incorporates this theory is provided, along with the hypothesis that its low-energy dual is a smooth scalar field theory with a nilpotent and holomorphic operator, which has a finite set of eigenvalues. The eigenvalues are anticipated to be highly dispersed due to the volume factor, leading to the nilpotent and holomorphic operator having all derivatives in its leading expansion. This, in turn, implies a relationship with a Weyl field in a different representation, thus facilitating the mapping of the original chiral gauge theory onto this new field theory through a precise transformation. The dual theory can then be used to analyze the chiral gauge theory's behavior in different scenarios. A potential application of this duality is the exploration of the low-energy behavior of various chiral gauge theories, which may then be compared to existing theories from the Lagrangian framework to gain new insights and predictions. Current state-of-the-art techniques for presenting complex graphical models in a compact format, such as chordal decomposition and minimal triangulation, often fail for large-scale models even when exact solutions are possible. We introduce a new efficient method that leverages density information to represent complex graphical models in a concise format, facilitating exact solution options through triangulation. We show that for any given graphical model, our density-based representation can quickly determine if a related optimization problem has feasible solutions, leading to new standard forms for such optimization problems. We also extend this approach to develop a more efficient algorithm for computing minimum partition width in multivariate Gaussian models. Our method exhibits improved performance compared to existing strategies, especially for large and moderately complex models. We provide a detailed comparison with other efficient algorithms, demonstrating that our density-based method outperforms them in solution quality for complex models, although performance varies with problem size. We also introduce a new active sampling method that uses density information to identify relevant variables and structure in complex models, potentially aiding variable selection in Bayesian networks. We provide numerical evaluations that confirm the efficacy of our new density-based format for complex models and demonstrate how it enables new efficient algorithmic approaches, such as improved MPE algorithms and better optimization performance, along with better variable selection results compared to alternative methods. We investigate the shear thickening transitions in aqueous nanofluids by analyzing the viscosity ratios of their diluted and highly-diluted states. Our research reveals a widespread pattern of critical power law scaling, both for systems that thin out and those that thickened, and it challenges the current understanding of shear thickening mechanics. Additionally, we provide a thorough review of shear thickening dynamics, emphasizing the significance of space and time co-variance, pressure waves, and shock-like states. Our data encompasses different particle shapes, various polymer types, and a extensive range of particle concentrations to illustrate the universal nature of these phenomena. Furthermore, we connect the observed scaling to the hydrodynamic flow characteristics of the diluted state, and suggest key principles that govern the dynamics of the highly-diluted state, including energy self-organization and shear-localization. Our study presents a unified framework for the widespread occurrence of shear thickening, and highlights the critical need for further investigating the core physics of the phenomenon. Moreover, we emphasize the implications of its widespread nature on the interpretation of experimental data, and the potential for a new perspective on non-Newtonian fluid dynamics. In recent years, advanced statistical models have greatly improved our ability to forecast electricity consumption. This research aims to develop an analytical framework, grounded in stochastic processes, to model hourly electricity usage during periods of high demand. We demonstrate that, in conditions of power crises, the first two moments of hourly electricity consumption are sufficient to fully capture its probability distribution. This insight enables us to develop two simplified models: the Normal and Skew-Normal distribution models. By estimating the mean and standard deviation of these distributions, we can accurately model the electricity usage, thereby generating reliable predictions. This research further highlights the challenges associated with modeling demand during power crises and offers a method to assess the reliability of models under such conditions. Our analysis is supported by an in-depth case study of the Pakistani electricity consumption during a power crisis in 2015. Furthermore, this research investigates the effectiveness of combining the proposed models with time-series analysis to enhance the predictive accuracy of forecasts made prior to the onset of the crisis. Notably, our study reveals that modifying existing models to account for extreme events can result in significantly better forecasts, achieving up to 15% greater accuracy in this specific scenario. This research is a first of its kind to explore modeling electricity consumption during power crises in developing countries. The analytical framework developed in this research can be utilized by practitioners and academics to model demand during similar events in other contexts. Moreover, this study stresses the need for further investigations into modeling requirements during extreme events and extreme periods of high demand. Additionally, this research underscores the significance of integrating theoretical and practical approaches to forecasting, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex underlying processes driving electricity consumption. Finally, this research offers valuable insights and recommendations for practitioners and policymakers tackling power crises through the development of reliable forecasting methods.

The study analyzed how personalized web search impacted public knowledge of a real-world news story, and revealed notable discrepancies between the model's predictions and the survey respondents' answers. Notably, the results showed that a substantial proportion of participants failed to discover crucial information related to the story due to personalized web search, and that non-personalized web search can significantly affect public knowledge, highlighting a potential risk of bias in the information that people obtain through search queries. A novel deep learning approach is introduced in this paper to automatically generate computer programs from flow diagrams. A new graph-based convolutional neural network called GRCNN is presented, which includes two key components: graph construction and program synthesis. Graph construction involves transforming flow diagrams into structured graphs, while program synthesis leverages the synthesized graphs to generate actual computer programs. Through experimental evaluation, GRCNN achieved superior results on three public datasets when compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, GRCNN outperformed other methods by 9.5% and 7.7% on two specific datasets, respectively, by accurately translating flow diagrams into valid computer programs. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis and subsequent experiments validated the efficacy of GRCNN's components and training protocols. Interestingly, even with varying input configurations, multiple viable solutions were generated for each input, which can be attributed to the diverse representations produced during the graph construction phase. Consequently, the best program is typically selected based on the shortest path in the synthesized graph. Moreover, a comparison between GRCNN and a model relying on node feature engineering revealed that the former outperformed the latter by 5.7%, which underscores the importance of structured graphs in deep learning-based program synthesis. Finally, while this study focused on graph-based synthesis, GRCNN's approach can be extended to other deep learning methods, such as sequence-to-sequence models, as well as explored through human-eye graph-based view in the future. Diminution techniques in climate studies minimize certain climate properties over time, often by explicitly rejecting real-world climate observations in favor of artificially generated data. This is typically done to ensure the presence of a solution, typically a unique solution, to a partially ill-posed mathematical problem in climate dynamics. This review summarizes the recent developments in dimension techniques, specifically those involving the cost of transporting mass and other quantities, primarily in the context of climate models that involve partial differential equations. A key focus of this review is the distinction between two types of dimension techniques: those that minimize the cost of transporting mass or other quantities explicitly, and those that do so implicitly. This distinction is crucial because it arises when considering the presence of terms other than those representing transportation cost in a dimension minimization problem. This presence can render a dimension minimization problem that might otherwise be well-posed (i.e. have a unique solution) to be ill-posed (i.e. have no solution), and vice versa. This and other key challenges and issues in dimension technique theory and application are discussed in this review. Finally, we consider how dimension techniques may be applied to problems in climate dynamics beyond those involving partial differential equations. Although dimension techniques have been primarily considered in the context of continuous systems, there is growing interest in applying dimension techniques to discrete systems as well. This includes problems such as minimizing the cost of transporting mass in networks, and we review these results as well. Ultimately, this review is intended to provide a clear and concise introduction to dimension techniques and their applications in climate dynamics for readers without a background in partial differential equation theory. To this end, we have tried to provide a clear and concise overview of the theory and provide many results explicitly to aid in understanding. Furthermore, we have included a detailed reference section to aid readers in further exploring the subject. Additionally, we have included a brief overview of the background in dimension technique theory that would be considered elementary or even well-known, in order to make the review more accessible to a wider range of readers. This review may also provide a useful and concise summary for readers who are already familiar with dimension technique theory. In particular, we have tried to provide a concise review by noting the key results and providing a concise overview, while still providing a comprehensive and detailed review. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive alternative to traditional supernovae for the search of light element synthesis. Observing an event called GW170817 allowed researchers to test heavy element formation by identifying the characteristics of an r-process produced kilonova. Although essential elements were present in the expected amounts, several key features failed to align with theoretical expectations from the r-process model. Various explanations have been offered to clarify the discrepancies between the observed and predicted phenomena; a primary suggestion involves the presence of real-level structure in the transition metals, specifically gold, osmium, and mercury, which lacks proper atomic data for an in-depth analysis. Radiation oncologists rely on computed tomography (CT) scans to create customized treatment plans for patients, but manually tracing vital organs can be a significant obstacle due to its time-consuming nature. Fortunately, deep learning-based automated segmentation tools have emerged as a promising solution to streamline this process. Although traditionally tested on organs such as the brain and liver, these resources have not previously been applied to the gastrointestinal (GI) canal for head and neck cancer patients. In an effort to overcome this limitation, we have conducted a study that evaluates the effectiveness of a pre-trained, automatically optimized deep learning algorithm for segmenting the GI canal in CT scans. Notably, our results indicate that the AI model achieved a segmentation score of 0.854, outperforming a baseline method by 15% and showcasing the potential of these tools for clinical use. By confirming that the AI model performed better with increasing scan quality, we have also identified a threshold for optimal performance, but unfortunately, the results were hindered by a high degree of variation in performance, ultimately concluding that further refinement of the algorithm is required before it can be relied upon in clinical settings. Nonetheless, our study provides valuable insights for which areas of improvement the algorithm needs to focus, namely by paying closer attention to the spatial anatomy relationships between different sections of the GI canal, with potential applications for the development of more robust deep learning algorithms to accurately detect and trace the GI canal in CT scans for radiation oncology purposes. The data and code used for this study have been publicly compiled for the purpose of facilitating further research and replication of our results. Additionally, the study's findings contribute to a growing library of pre-trained, automatically optimized deep learning models that can be utilized for a range of medical imaging applications. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex, part-whole data sets, which are often described by the cofactor matrix. This form of data is prevalent in various fields such as biology, geology, finance, and medicine. We are experimenting with new approaches to compositional data analysis by developing an original mathematical framework. Our method relies on the properties of the cofactor matrix to define a linear operator, which we use to explore compositional data through visualization and interpretation. Our research focuses on understanding how this operator affects a data set's structure and how it can be used to reveal hidden patterns within the data. This mathematical approach enables us to analyze parts of complex data sets independently and understand their contributions to the entire system. By applying our composition analysis, we were able to discover new insights in biological and economic contexts, which we demonstrate in two practical case studies. Our method is now available as an open-source Python package called CompAna that allows users to reproduce our results and apply our approach to their own data. The package includes a user-friendly interface for data analysis, visualization, and example code to analyze compositional data. The idea that massive planets are less likely to form close to their star's habitable zone has led to a theory that planets within this zone have lower masses below a certain threshold.  We examined this theory by analyzing a sample of exoplanets discovered through the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity program and found that our data do not support it.  In contrast to expectations, our results show that planets within the habitable zone are just as likely to have masses above a certain threshold as those found farther out.  Our findings contradict previous generations of planetary formation models.  Based on our analysis, the lack of slower-moving, massive planets close to their star may be the result of these planets losing speed due to interactions with other stars in the system rather than the planets losing angular momentum to the star's gravitational force.  Further study on the properties of exoplanets, particularly their orbital speeds, is needed to fully understand planetary formation and the movement of planets within their star's habitable zone.  Ultimately, our findings could affect the search for life on other planets by changing the way scientists weigh the chances of finding life on planets with varying planetary masses within their star's habitable zone.  Key findings of this paper are also relevant to other programs such as the TESS and PLATO missions as they search for planets within their star's habitable zone.  Our analysis used data from the exoplanet.eu database and is based on the discovery of exoplanets through the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity program.  The sample consisted of 260 planets with known masses and those that orbit within their star's habitable zone or outside of it.  The study looked at how the mass of the planets is related to their distance from their star's habitable zone and found that our data do not support a theory based on this relationship.  The study did find that planets within the habitable zone that were discovered through the program have lower masses below a certain threshold more frequently than those found farther out.  The study attributed the difference to how the planets move through their orbit, with those closer to their star losing less angular momentum due to interactions with other stars in the system.  The movement of the planets through their orbit, rather than their final location, may be the key to understanding planetary formation and the search for life on other planets, with key findings of this paper also relevant to other programs such as the TESS and PLATO missions as they search for planets within their star's habitable zone. We investigate the possibility of compressing dark matter particles into a small, dense area, taking into account their Yukawa interaction with standard model particles.  The formation of this dense area, likely a black hole or neutron star, occurs through the accumulation of dark matter particles near its surface due to radiation-driven gravity, facilitated by the Yukawa interaction.  If the Yukawa interaction plays a significant role, we find that the rate of accumulation could be faster than expected, potentially leading to the disappearance of a star's dark matter-induced heating within a few decades. These methods primarily rely on key, which is typically learned using advanced optimization techniques, to transform raw data into engaging narratives. To address these challenges, we propose TCube, a novel neural model that uses a novel neural transformation for time-series storytelling. TCube employs a neutral key that can be applied across various domains without being specifically tailored to a particular dataset. To further enhance its storytelling capabilities, TCube also incorporates a semantic-aware sampling module, allowing it to generate narratives from data samples in a more controlled manner. Moreover, TCube accommodates different time-series formats, making it a more versatile solution. Through extensive evaluations on multiple domains, we demonstrate the superior performance of TCube over state-of-the-art models. Moreover, we analyze the different components of TCube and provide various visualization and demonstration videos that showcase its performance. The source code of TCube is publicly available for reproduction of our results.

Developers and programmers frequently turn to the Stack Overflow platform for expert advice. Beyond internal knowledge shares, they also exchange links to useful external resources, spanning across various categories of 10, comprising discipline, domain, and programming related specifications. External links, though external to Stack Overflow, play a significant role in augmenting the flow of valuable information, enhancing the potential of a single expert opinion with external validity by providing relevant contextual background. By analyzing 868,271 question-and-answer threads on Stack Overflow, this study reveals a detailed portrait of these shared external links, including their distribution, characteristics, and uses, thus providing actionable insights that can improve the validity of expert opinions offered through Q&A platforms via external knowledge sources. Moreover, this study identifies areas for future research, offering a framework that can be applied to other academic communities for conducting similar analyses. By doing so, this study contributes to the development of a metric that can measure the flow of information across multiple platforms, ultimately fostering collaboration among distinct expert groups.

Medical condition diagnosis is greatly aided by reviewing patients' medical records, yet fully leveraging this information requires manually annotating and translating abundant unstructured clinical data into standardized format - a time-consuming and nearly impractical task. To automate this process, machines can learn to identify key symptoms and events mentioned in medical notes, but current approaches typically train and test on a single hospital or language, severely limiting their practical applications. To overcome these constraints, we've developed a domain generalization method for symptom event extraction that can adapt across diverse domains. Our proposed technique outperforms other conventional methods in multiple domains for extractive and selective symptom event extraction, showing significant improvements in F1 scores of up to 14 and 7 points, respectively. This capability enables more comprehensive clinical data utilization, ultimately enhancing medical diagnosis accuracy. Our detailed approach, including data collection, annotation, and model development, is described in our paper, along with a publicly accessible dataset for reproducibility. Our public repository contains the code for our domain generalization method: https://github.com/ChenChihJaw/Domain-Generalization-on-Symptom-Event-Extraction. We introduce a new class of transformations known as avaricious transformations with a gap, a subcategory of beta transformations. It is demonstrated that intermediate beta shifts are a specific instance of avaricious transformations with a gap. Additionally, it is shown that the sequence of intermediate beta shifts exhibits a unique pattern of interlacing, and the Hausdorff dimension of their attractor can be represented by a specific expression, solving a long-standing problem first posed by Keane and Neumann. This new classification also provides a solution to another question raised by Kerr and Sun, which inquires about the existence of beta shifts with certain irrational transform values greater than one half. The key to these findings involves constructing a specific pattern of cuts in the unit interval that satisfy specific conditions, and a technique for expressing the attractor of intermediate beta shifts using these patterns of cuts. Finally, a new category of transformations, greedy transformations with a gap, is introduced and shown to be equivalent to avaricious transformations through a demonstration of bi-directional convergence. The sequence of intermediate beta shifts can also be re-characterized as a sequence of greedy beta shifts and its relationship to the Apoitu map, a specific zeta transformation, is explored through the application of a theorem that generalizes the Tarski skewness into newtons' iterated function schemes. The proof utilizes many innovative techniques including the construction of a spiral pattern in the complex plane, the derivation of a new equation for the attractor, and the splitting of the unit interval, and yields many new findings including the topological entropy of the attractor, the length of the attractor, and the radius of the largest circle that encompasses the attractor, and also generalizes many of these findings to other beta shifts through the derivation of new expressions. The new theory also yields many new findings that relate to other problems including those of Keane and Neumann, Kerr and Sun, and others. The work presents several new inequalities for the Hausdorff dimension of the attractor that relate to beta values, and also derives several new inequalities for the length and topological entropy of the attractor that relate to gap sizes, and generalizes these findings in a way that relates to new predictions. Federated Learning is an emerging decentralized machine learning technique that keeps data in its earliest stages, by processing it on users' devices and synchronizing the local models with a central server. This process avoids transferring sensitive data but poses security risks as malicious entities could manipulate the update process. Our research introduces a new concept called Federated Training across Trusted Execution Enclaves (TFE), which uses hardware-enabled security to safeguard both the training process and data transmission. This novel approach uses multiple TFEs, one for the user and one for the server, and relies on hardware to isolate and verify the integrity of the training process and data transmission. Our proof-of-concept implementation, Flatee, demonstrates the effectiveness of this concept by successfully completing a Federated Learning training process on a real-world dataset across two distant locations, despite a sophisticated attack attempt to interfere with the process. The results show that Flatee can provide secure and decentralized machine learning solutions, protecting against security threats in the wild. Moreover, Flatee achieves this while maintaining comparable efficiency to regular Federated Learning implementation, thus closing the gap between security and efficiency in Federated Learning. The code for this project is openly available at https://github.com/jesouza100/floe. Learn about our project in this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H5Bj4W1c8mY. This research proposes a method to evaluate and compare embedded system operators in a automated manner. For low-power embedded systems, operators are commonly used to process image data efficiently, especially in resource-constrained settings. Although several operator evaluations are already implemented in accordance with the OpenVX standard, the process of comparing and selecting the most suitable evaluation for a given platform and task is complex and requires manual optimization. To resolve this issue, our approach integrates evaluation models with machine learning techniques to automatically identify the best fit among available evaluations for a specific embedded system configuration and application requirements. The proposed system was demonstrated on a Raspberry Pi 4, which is a general-purpose embedded system, and shows improved performance over manual optimization models by reducing compilation time and achieving better performance-outcome proportions in open-source image processing applications. This paper introduces a randomized management technique that builds on Model Predictive Control (MPC). Unlike traditional MPC, which relies on a specific trajectory optimization, our approach uses multiple random trajectories to create a more reliable control strategy. We demonstrate the calculation method for the randomized strategy and its ability to improve outcomes in uncertain systems, utilizing a simple power plant simulation as an illustrative example. Several key advantages of our approach over traditional MPC are then highlighted, including lower computational demands and enhanced robustness against errors or system uncertainties. Furthermore, we discuss how the randomized method's performance benefits can be leveraged in scenarios involving complex constraints. To showcase the applicability of our method on real-world systems, we extend the power plant example to include start-up costs, highlighting the development of a more general framework that calculates the optimal open-loop policy at any time with minimal computational effort. The proposed method is further compared to related concepts, such as zeroing-out and Lyapunov-based design, in the context of power system stabilization. The results of these analyses demonstrate the superiority of our (Random) Model Predictive Management method over these alternative approaches, showcasing its potential to transform the design of control systems for robustness and performance. The concepts and algorithms introduced in this paper were initially presented at conferences in 2020 and 2021, respectively. The corresponding software package, available under open-source licensing, includes MATLAB implementations that users can modify to apply the proposed method to their specific use cases. The source code can be accessed via GitHub at the following address: <https://github.com/hhu-robert/Random-MPM-py>. A pre-compiled version of the package can also be obtained via conda at the following address: <https://anaconda.org/robert-hhu/Random_MPM>. The proposed method can be utilized for designing robust controllers in transcontinental flight management systems, as well as power system stabilization and other applications. We examine the regionality aspect of quantum double models based on abelian groups, focusing on von Neumann algebras. It's proven that the regionality algebra for these double models consists of partial homomorphisms from a von Neumann algebra related to the group, known as the tensor category of subalgebras. This result is consistent with existing findings for free fermions and free bosons. Building on these insights, a larger collection called the quantum double of subalgebras is introduced. It's shown that it forms a closed factor category, offering a valuable framework for exploring regionality in quantum double models. This approach is expected to broaden the understanding of regionality in non-abelian quantum double models as well. Furthermore, it's proposed that the regionality algebra could serve as a first-order representation of the face and splitting operators responsible for decomposing any region into adjacent trivalent vertices, which would enable efficient computation within the regionality algebra. This concept is dubbed the zero-order representation, with the regionality algebra providing the first-order equivalent. As an additional tool, a diagrammatic technique is developed for calculating partial algebraic expressions directly within the regionality algebra. It's shown that this method, known as diagrammatic multiplication, aligns with the topological multiplication used in topological double models. Finally, a method called deconvergence is introduced, allowing a region's algebra to be reconstructed from a reconfigured version of its topological double model's algebra, which is inherently 2-dimensional. This method is initially demonstrated for specific regions, but its application is contemplated for a broader range of regions. It's speculated that a universal version of deconvergence exists, which would include all possible region algebras as their reconfigured 2-dimensionally extended versions. Such a version could likely be obtained by first extending all quantum double model algebras to 2-dimensionally extended versions of their topological doubles. It's believed that a method for obtaining such a version of deconvergence would also yield a universal version of deconvergence. This approach is expected to yield a homomorphism called the deconvergence homomorphism, which would enable a region's algebra to be reconstructed from its topological double model's algebra by means of a specific region-specific version of deconvergence. It's hypothesized that a similar homomorphism, called the convergence homomorphism, would also exist, which would enable a topological double model's algebra to be obtained from a region's algebra through diagrammatic multiplication

To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we integrate a quantum feedback control system, achieving this entanglement for the first time. A coherent feedback circuit is designed to optimize this entanglement by applying an adaptive control method. This method allows for precise control of the system's evolution, leading to increased entanglement. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of dissipation on the system's entanglement. Our results demonstrate that, with coherent feedback, it's feasible to enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement even in the presence of substantial dissipation. The entanglement scale in this system can be adjusted through the quantum state transfer efficiency. Additionally, the system's tripartite entanglement is found to exhibit Bell's nonlocality phenomenon. Our research provides a novel approach to controlling entanglement, which may contribute to the development of novel quantum technologies. Lastly, the findings mentioned above also apply to other systems, such as optomechanics, if the cavity field is replaced by an optical field. In the United States, public schools operate according to a testing regimen designed to evaluate student performance, teacher effectiveness, and school efficiency. This assessment system, tied to funding allocations, aims to achieve high achievement rates across the board. To attain this goal, a complex mathematical formula determines each school's performance score based on various test results. To facilitate comparison of schools and districts, a standardized metric is calculated by adjusting test outcomes with weighted accountability scores. Nonetheless, critics argue that this formula is susceptible to manipulation and distorts the reality of student performance. In an effort to improve transparency and accuracy, we reexamine the intention behind this assessment system and propose a straightforward approach to evaluating school success. By simplifying the calculation of a well-established accountability metric, we provide a clear alternative to the current performance score, one that reflects the diversity of student populations and is less influenced by high-stakes testing. This revised approach is grounded in statistical methodology developed over the past two decades, which emphasizes the accuracy of school performance reports. By leveraging data from the Texas Assessment of Knowledge and Skills, a high-stakes testing program, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in accurately assessing school performance even in the presence of limited testing data. Furthermore, our approach offers a general solution that can be applied to other assessment systems, and its versatility stems from the use of statistical weights, a widely accepted calculation tool. By simulating various testing scenarios, we show that our method is resilient to changes in testing rates and can provide a stable school performance metric across different student population demographics. Ultimately, our paper aims to improve assessment transparency and accuracy by critiquing the underlying mathematical concepts, providing a clarifying alternative, and offering a versatile solution that can be applied to a wide range of educational performance evaluations. Advanced machine learning (ML) applications now play a crucial role in healthcare, defense, finance, and transportation but have a significant vulnerability exploited by Person-in-the-Middle (PiM) attacks that occur during the data collection process. PiM attacks involve malicious actors intercepting the data transmission process between a user and a system, substituting the original with fabricated data. Our research investigates the efficacy of two artificial intelligence-based malicious fabrication frameworks, specifically adversarial and generative networks, in creating counterfeit data. We analyze the outcomes of these malicious operations on three robust ML models, evaluating the impact of PiM attacks against CNN, ResNet, and Mobilenet models. Our experiments reveal that generative networks produce more credible counterfeit data but are slower and require more computational power, while adversarial networks generate less believable data but are faster and demand less computational power. Our findings suggest that defending against PiM attacks with solely technical solutions, such as relying on input data purification, may be insufficient and that a more comprehensive approach that addresses the underlying problem of PiM attacks is needed. Our code and data are openly available on GitHub for reproducibility purposes. Additionally, we have presented our research at the 15th International Conference on Security, Security 2022. Instrumental variables are a common technique used in econometrics for identifying causal relationships, even in cases where the instrument itself does not have causal effects on the variable of interest. The traditional conditions for this technique include having two characteristics: the instrument must be determined independently of the variable of interest, and the instrument must be determined independently of the other variables involved in the analysis. The technique has been the subject of extensive research, although there have been few studies examining what happens when the conditions for this technique are only partially met. This paper presents a new test for a specific application of this technique, an analysis of the causes and effects of the economic benefits associated with fields of study. The instrument in this case is the field of study itself, with various fields connected to distinct industries, serving as a means to gain employment. The proof for this test's validity is based on an examination of the relationships among fields of study, rather than on the relationships between fields of study and the industries to which they are connected. The result shows that the identified causal relationships are not entirely arbitrary, as there are certain common characteristics in the various industries connected to distinct fields of study. This result is documented through an examination of the labels of the different fields of study listed in a reference book. The technique used in this study, an analysis of the causes and effects, can be employed to determine the causes of the observed connections between fields of study and their associated industries, as well as the effects of these fields of study on their connected industries. The instrument in this analysis is not the entire group of students in a specific college, as one might initially assume, but rather an application-based random assignment of students to various programs offered by the college. This study is a part of a broader investigation into the causes and effects, as well as the returns on investment in higher education, an area that the researcher has been examining through data on students who attended a certain college and pursued programs in arts, music, theater, or dance. The results from this study, as presented, focus on one particular program, as the other programs fall short of meeting the required conditions for this technique, having either direct causal connections to the variable of interest or uncertain relationships with the other variables involved in the analysis. Improving the clarity of historical documents is crucial, as it directly enhances text readability, making it more accessible to humans and machine-based technologies. In this research, we introduce an innovative framework called TextRead, a multi-task adversarial network designed to enhance the legibility of handwritten text within documents. By taking a holistic approach, TextRead is capable of improving the overall quality of degraded documents, regardless of their origin or severity of degradation. Building upon the success of the ADGAN model, TextRead expands on its weaknesses by incorporating the restoration of lines, as well as a text enhancement module, thereby demonstrating superior performance in the restoration of handwritten text. Additionally, TextRead is the first model to achieve state-of-the-art results on the ND-AR dataset, as evaluated by the CIDEr metric. Further analysis confirms that TextRead produces readable output, and significantly surpasses the ADGAN model in terms of the clarity of restored texts. The source code for TextRead is available at https://github.com/amishahri/TextRead. Experimental demonstrations can be found at https://amishahri.github.io/TextRead/.

Ancient astronomical images hold significant historical value and could be preserved by restoring faded colors, a process that currently relies on manual or poorly established techniques. Despite the potential, previous attempts to utilize Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been unsuccessful. We present an innovative approach to reconstructing colored images from black and white originals, leveraging domain-conditional generative adversarial networks (DCGAN). Our method employs pixel-level loss functions to mimic the properties of color astronomical images, yielding promising results and outperforming previous attempts to apply GANs to this domain. The reconstruction of 19th-century astronomical plates from the Collection des Estelles reveals high accuracy, and our solution is compatible with existing manual or traditional restoration techniques. The implementation details, along with the restored images, are made available through an open-source GitHub repository at https://github.com/Bradley-N/Astronomical Picture Colorization. Further visualizations of the restored images can be accessed through the Collection des Estelles website at https://collectiondesestelles.qc.ca/en/explore/ and will be showcased in a future online exhibition. Additionally, the open-source repository could be adapted to restore other faded or grayscale color images. The successful reconstruction of colorful images from historical astronomical plates may also contribute to a broader range of fields involving colorful images, such as artistic or medical photography. The proposed solution has the potential to improve knowledge of these image types by advancing the state-of-the-art in deep learning, a development driven by the unique properties of astronomical images. of its inputs, thereby illuminating the role of back-propagation in this
process. Furthermore, this new perspective enables the development of an
algorithm for training neural networks without relying on gradient information,
resulting in a faster and more efficient training process, especially for smaller
networks. The efficacy of this gradient-free training method is demonstrated on
standard datasets, albeit with varying degrees of success. While it outperforms
the traditional approach on some benchmarks, in other cases, performance suffers
in comparison. Nonetheless, this novel framework for understanding neural networks
has the potential to inform the design of future neural network architectures.
