This design for a metastructure features two interconnected lattices oriented in parallel but shifted relative to each other. One of these lattices is made up of a material with a high dielectric constant, causing it to resonate at radio frequencies. Meanwhile, the second lattice is comprised of a material without significant dielectric properties but with a low dielectric constant, causing it to resonate in the optical range. Our research involves reconstructing and reinterpreting the resonant phenomenon observed in this dual metastructure, but this time replacing radio frequency resonances with optical ones. By doing so, we've created a new generation of metastructures capable of directing electromagnetic waves in the optical spectrum at specific frequencies. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the development of optical devices, enabling innovative applications such as guided light propagation and high-speed processing. Additionally, we've discovered that modifying the dielectric constant of one of the metamaterials can either advance or delay the onset of light waves, providing flexibility in designing optical systems. This research paves the way for novel applications of metastructures in the optical realm. Finally, we propose an innovative approach, 'dualism,' that may facilitate the extension of this technology to other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, potentially leading to the development of devices for infrared and terahertz frequencies. This vision could unlock new functionalities in these areas as well. Lastly, we've explored various forms of dualism that could enable the use of metastructures in direct or indirect illumination of devices, opening up further avenues for innovation. This reimagining of metastructures not only brings them in line with modern device design principles (e.g. direct current, radio frequency, digital computing), but also empowers us to rethink innovative applications at the infrared and terahertz levels. This concept, known as human-robot cooperative learning, necessitates complex, collaborative problem-solving methods that take into account the inherent intricacies of human interdependence. Current cognitive architectures are not well-suited to address this complexity due to their lack of advanced learning capabilities, limited capacity to model multi-agent relationships, and inability to handle dynamic changes easily. In this paper, we introduce a pioneering approach that addresses these critical issues by presenting a unified framework called CoHCoL. This innovative system enables large-scale cooperative learning among diverse groups of human and robot agents through the utilization of intelligent cognitive architectures. To effectively manage the intricacy of human interdependence, CoHCoL employs a distributed architecture that leverages graph theory to model relationships among entities and facilitate communication. This powerful framework can adapt and expand various components, such as the underlying cognitive architectures within the nodes, and even integrate human components. Through a practical demonstration, we showcase a CoHCoL setup that facilitates self-organizing learning among a group of robots working together to achieve a common goal. This exemplary application serves as a model for establishing accessible and accessible systems that can facilitate complex, collaborative tasks. Furthermore, CoHCoL's modular architecture, characterized by its distributivity and flexibility in cognitive architecture choices, can be applied to a broad range of applications beyond human-robot cooperative learning. These applications might involve industrial surveillance, search and rescue operations, or even therapeutic treatments involving multiple humans and robots. This diverse array of potential uses validates our contention that the CoHCoL framework offers substantial social value and presents a tangible opportunity for advancement in the field of cognitive architectures. Moreover, by addressing the fundamental challenge of cooperative learning among numerous robots and human entities, CoHCoL may contribute valuable insights to AI research, further solidifying the framework's social utility and innovative potential. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the average absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing an initial upper bound for the bias via an upper bound on the derivative of the check function, the remaining bias is eliminated through a correction term that is asymptotically negligible.  Developed within the framework of a specific alternative model, this estimator is shown to be uniformly consistent across all local median alternatives.  Mathematical analysis also reveals that the proposed estimator achieves the same rate of convergence as the classical estimator.  A series of simulations were conducted to evaluate the performance of this new estimator under various scenarios, showcasing its improved bias-reducing characteristics while maintaining comparable mean squared error properties.  A comprehensive case study involving real data served to demonstrate the practical applications and benefits of the proposed estimator in modern empirical research.  A corresponding proof of concept is provided in an additional appendix.  The main text has been made accessible through a publicly available archive of supplementary materials. The task of Relation Extraction aims to extract relevant information from a text, pinpointing the relationship between two entities. Traditional approaches to this task rely on mark-up languages to identify entities and their interconnected relationships. To improve accuracy in Relation Extraction, researchers propose an enhanced model that leverages Knowledge Graph Embeddings. By treating entities mentioned in a text as nodes in a graph and applying link prediction techniques, the model generates vector representations of these entities, allowing for the improvement of relation extraction through supplementary information. An alternative model, the EREMP Model, has been developed to achieve this improvement. An evaluation process using the ClassicBank dataset revealed that the EREMP model showed substantial advancements over baseline models and surpassed state-of-the-art models in Multi-Linear Model and Neural Pipeline Model experiments. A deeper examination of the model's efficacy on datasets distinct from Bank dataset, the Semeval 2010 dataset, yielded comparable outcomes, indicating the model's capacity to target diverse relationships beyond the domain of financial transactions. As a consequence, the EREMP model can effectively enhance the accuracy of Relation Extraction by integrating Knowledge Graph Embeddings. To validate the model's efficacy on disambigous entities, a simplified version of the model, the FME Model, was developed. An evaluation process using the ClassicBank dataset and the Semeval 2010 dataset revealed that the FRE Model outperformed baseline models and demonstrated satisfactory performance on datasets requiring fine-grained entity disambiguation. To facilitate the development of methods that can effectively target diverse relationships and fine-grained entity disambiguation, the model's implementation will be made accessible through an open-source platform. Moreover, the model's design will be explained in detail to facilitate its replication in similar applications. Through this work, the challenge of Relation Extraction has been addressed, and a solution has been proposed that can effectively improve this task using Knowledge Graph Embeddings. To demonstrate the model's capabilities on diverse datasets, additional case studies will be presented and made accessible on an open-platform repository for model replication. Furthermore, the model's code will be stored on a data repository for public access. Tb3RuO7 exhibits an unusual combination of internal magnetic fields and spin interactions, resulting in a unique state characterized by the partial disintegration of ordered arrangements. Through nuclear magnetic resonance and magnetic susceptibility analyses, a uniform internal magnetic field was detected in the range of 8-10 T, directed along the b-axis, while 1/T1 data indicated the presence of short-range ferromagnetic correlations between Tb and Ru ions. Additionally, the system displays an unusual transition in the Ru spin susceptibility at 4.5 K, attributed to the partial disintegration of the ordered arrangement. Previous studies have explored the use of autoencoders for this task, but they are prone to causing aliasing effects that distort hand movement patterns. MRABAEs outperform conventional autoencoders and other comparison methods in both training and testing, according to the results of our rigorous evaluation. Furthermore, the synthetic hand tracks generated by MRABAEs demonstrate significant improvements in fidelity, as measured by the Success Rate and Normalized Error Distance metrics. MRABAEs use fewer parameters than other comparison methods, making it more suitable for real-world deployment on hardware with limited processing capabilities. MRABAEs generate more accurate local representations of hand movements that generalize to a wider range of novel environments. The source code for MRABAEs is publicly available, allowing other researchers to replicate our results and build upon our work. We evaluated MRABAEs from multiple perspectives, including data-driven local representation generation, synthesis, and tracking. MRABAEs were found to outperform other comparison methods in multiple evaluations, ultimately providing a more accurate and generalizable representation of hand movements that leads to higher fidelity synthetic tracks. MRABAEs can be used to improve the accuracy of hand movement tracking in games and other interactive applications by generating more precise local representations of hand movements. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to significant improvements in jet substructure analysis, enabling precise identification of key physical properties in hadronic decays. However, deep neural networks operate as black boxes, rendering it challenging to incorporate their output into theoretical particle physics simulations. A proposed solution involves utilizing a layer-wise relevance analysis to pinpoint specific features within the network that contribute to accurate jet classification. By leveraging this approach with an additional regression-based technique, it is feasible to obtain estimates of key physical variables, enhancing the interpretability of the networks and allowing for a more in-depth examination of the relationships between variables. Furthermore, we have developed a novel method for constraining high-energy particle properties, taking into consideration the effects of both statistical and systematic uncertainties. Our proposed method demonstrates considerable effectiveness in extracting relevant information from networks, and the expected outcomes might be valuable for the development of future quantum computing applications in particle physics. Additionally, we have explored the applicability of our layer-wise relevance analysis to the accurate visualization of jet images through the application of network-guided saliency maps. Our results suggest that it is feasible to attain visually acceptable reconstructions of 4-dimensional jet images with diminished losses, and the associated saliency maps effectively capture the transient nature of these objects. Given its robust performance, this approach might be useful in various computer vision applications as well. Lastly, we have investigated the development of compact, interpretable models derived from the exploitation of shallow neural networks trained to replicate the behavior of the deep networks, and the subsequent application of layer-wise relevance analysis to their study. Our approach has several inherent advantages, notably a substantial reduction in computational requirements and the facilitation of deep network interpretability. Furthermore, we have devised and successfully addressed an intricate challenge for developing a binary classification of hadron jet substructures, incorporating uncertainties arising from high-energy particle decays in Monte Carlo simulations. Our results indicate that deep neural networks trained on theoretical particle data can achieve remarkable accuracy in binary classification (0.8855) and that the associated uncertainties can be efficiently tackled (0.2603), paving the way for the development of deep learning applications in high-energy particle decays. We are investigating the use of neural networks that take complex-valued inputs, thereby eliminating the sign constraint that restricts the input data to be solely positive. This sign limitation hinders data augmentation, reducing the size of trainable datasets. Our research focuses on the effects of this sign restriction, comparing it to the simplified constraint of working exclusively with positive data. Interestingly, our findings indicate that relaxing the sign restriction results in more precise predictions, with negligible overfitting. Furthermore, our study suggests that sign restriction's chief drawback is the reduced capacity of trainable datasets, which can be mitigated by incorporating more data points. Thus, our study demonstrates the advantage of training neural networks using the full range of quantum data without sign-related limitations. Additionally, our proposed model, with its flexible input, addresses the long-standing sign dilemma inherent in many wavefunction-based quantum models. We have tested this model on high-energy Hubbard models, examining the variability of neural networks trained with both restricted and unrestricted signs, and observed a significant improvement in predictions without the need for sign restriction. Our innovative model's success in overcoming the sign dilemma in quantum chemistry lies in its ability to handle large datasets and scale effectively, even when dealing with limited training data. Consequently, this model may be beneficial in quantum chemistry's most challenging applications, where precise predictions are required but sign-restricted data is often insufficient. Previous research demonstrated that binary star systems create when a spinning proto-core collapses under its own gravity.  Despite this process's rapid progression from core formation to binary creation, early studies failed to notice any emerging binaries within developing star clusters.  To further investigate this enigma, a new series of numerical simulations was conducted, focusing on the effects of increasing core mass on the binary creation process.  Unlike earlier results, which showed binary creation masses that increased in line with core mass, these new simulations indicated a more dramatic rise in binary creation mass in accordance with core mass.  Consequently, these findings suggest that a stage might exist during core development where binary creation significantly accelerates, thereby resolving the initial observation paradox.  Furthermore, it's hypothesized that this stage could be triggered by a sudden spike in core angular momentum at critical core masses, leading to an influx of binary systems into the stage's duration and thus accounting for the absence of early binaries in developing star clusters.  To validate this theory, additional simulations involving magnetized cores were conducted, revealing that a similar increase in binary creation mass occurs when cores attain a certain level of magnetization.  Hence, it's possible that a similar mechanism to the binary creation spike also exists for magnetized cores, thereby contributing to the paradoxical observations of binary star systems in developing star clusters.  To rectify this discrepancy between theoretical binary creation mass and that of subsequent stellar binary systems in developing star clusters, a binary creation efficiency metric was established.  This new efficiency was found to be low during a core's rapid binary creation phase but increases sharply as the core approaches its critical mass, thereby reversing earlier conclusions and revealing that a rapid binary creation phase does indeed exist for developing star cores.  Consequently, these new simulations yield enhanced predictions for the creation of multiple systems, including tidally destroyed binaries and systems with wide orbital separations.  To further verify these new findings, additional simulations involving developing star cores from various masses were conducted, confirming that a rapid binary creation phase does indeed exist and thereby sheds light on the enigmatic observations of binary star systems in developing star clusters.  Consequently, this new research narrows the predictions for the creation of multiple star systems by adding a more precise efficiency metric to previous conclusions and thereby encompasses a wide range of potential outcomes for developing star cores, including various core mass ranges. The resulting algorithm is compared with existing methods on several benchmark datasets, and its performance is found to be comparable in most cases. However, our method delivers superior results on one dataset, and at least comparable results on another. Additionally, the novel approach is shown to be computationally efficient and capable of handling large datasets with high dimensional complexity. The source code is specifically designed to be versatile and adaptable, allowing it to be applied to a broad range of applications and data types, as demonstrated through the analysis of its performance on various benchmark datasets. The comparative evaluations of our algorithm were conducted on a Linux-based system, utilizing GPU acceleration provided by the authors. The benchmark datasets analyzed include the well-established ARCOS dataset, and a second dataset collected from ophthalmology applications, also known as the 'Ophthalmology dataset'. The analysis of our method's performance on the ARCOS dataset reveals superior results, largely due to the presence of noise in the dataset. The results obtained are specifically in the domain of independent component analysis, a more specialized field within sparse component analysis. The contributions of our approach, or m-ar-K-Rapid ICA, are threefold. Firstly, it is shown to deliver superior or at least comparable results, effectively outperforming existing baseline methods. Secondly, the novel algorithm is demonstrated to be computationally efficient, capable of handling high-dimensional complex data. We investigated a key aspect of CPT and found a detailed explanation for its complexity. Our research showed that any diagram-free formula comparing two input sequences has a straightforward proof in the original CPT system. To establish this, we established a crucial concept in model theory, allowing us to tie diagram-free structures to specific types of algebraic objects. Additionally, we discovered a crucial theorem indicating that certain properties cannot be expressed through polynomial equations alone. Leveraging this result, we obtained a crucial demonstration showing that certain CPT refutations are not achievable, thereby significantly expanding the set of refutations proven unachievable in CPT. Our work also examined a related but weaker theory called polynomial calculus, and by introducing a novel concept, we obtained a comprehensive demonstration showing that certain PC refutations are not achievable. Notably, our results have far-reaching implications for the related P vs NP hypothesis. Furthermore, our study connects the CPT model to a distinct framework for algebraic reasoning, and we anticipate that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of this connection. Lastly, our research sheds new light on the nature of certain types of algebraic objects, thereby expanding the set of knowledge in this domain. We establish a new group of domains known as the $\sigma$-elliptic annuli, 
which fall under the broader category of $\sigma$-elementary domains originally 
defined by Dujardins in 2009. This discovery yields an infinite number of 
non-homeomorphic domains, thereby providing a counterintuitive answer to a 
query posed by that mathematician regarding whether the $\sigma$-elementary 
domains comprise a coherent category. Additionally, our research reveals that 
the topology of the $\sigma$-elementary domain is characterized by a unique 
zero-order non-trivial singularity, thereby establishing a topological 
constant for this domain type. This work leverages a recently developed 
algebro-geometric tool known as the $\sigma$-connexity domain, along with an 
infinite set of $\sigma$-connexity domains that are specifically designed to 
have a hole in the center and are constructed by combining a constant 
multiplication domain with an anular region. This novel design enables the 
extension of the $\sigma$-connexity domain into the $\sigma$-elliptic annuli, 
which are comprised of two constant multiplication domains stacked upon 
separate sides of the real axis. This construction enables the linkage of 
the $\sigma$-connexity domain to the neighborhood of a singular point, 
while allowing the domain to retain its $\sigma$-elementary characteristics. 
This research further generalizes the concept of $\sigma$-elementary domains 
by dividing the domain into separate zones along the real axis, with 
different constant multiplications applied in each zone. This study 
demonstrates that the resulting domain remains $\sigma$-elementary, and 
we propose that the $\sigma$-elliptic annuli may serve as a useful tool for 
expanding our understanding of meromorphic functions within the context of

Verifying the integrity of sensitive data played a crucial role in the development of trustworthy systems, from the earliest days of programming to the present day. Multiple researchers proposed and studied various methods for protecting against malicious activities such as tampering or theft by an untrusted program. One particular line of inquiry involved investigating the various forms integrity verification can take. Recently, a notable advancement was made in this field by Demertzis, et al., who introduced a novel framework for simultaneously verifying the accuracy of multiple assertions at minimal additional cost, provided that the assertions being checked are independent and roughly the same size. Our study demonstrates that Demertzis et al.'s framework can be applied without first determining whether certain conditions are met, thus expanding its potential applications. Additionally, our work shows that Demertzis et al.'s framework can handle multiple overlapping assertions and that an efficient method exists for determining the minimum number of operations required to framework an arbitrary program of a given size. One particularly useful concept that arises from our study is the idea of framework complexity, which could potentially serve as a useful metric in the field of integrity verification to answer questions such as whether framework an $n$-bit program is cheaper than brute forcing it, or whether it makes more sense to framework an program or just brute forcing it if the cost of doing so is more than the cost of just checking it, and so on. Our work also made some interesting connections between framework and other concepts such as entropy and the capacity of a binary symmetric channel. Lastly, our study leaves open several questions and possibilities for further inquiry including but not limited to proving the relationship between framework complexity and entropy of a binary symmetric channel, determining whether there is a maximum amount of information that can be gained from a given number of random bits, and so on. Overall, our work provides a framework, no pun intended, for investigating the trade-offs between various forms of verifying integrity. One particularly notable point from our study is that frameworking an program may only be beneficial if the number of bits affected by the program is less than the program's entropy, which could serve as an additional metric for determining when frameworking an program is cheaper than just brute forcing it. Similarly, we show that frameworking an program is only cheaper than just checking it if the program's entropy is greater than the number of bits that need to be checked. One particularly easy to understand example of this point is that frameworking an program that randomly selects an output is only cheaper than just brute forcing it if the program's entropy is greater than the number of bits

The growing interest in location-based social media data comes with complexities, primarily due to inaccuracies in geocoded locations and inconsistent posting patterns. These issues hinder precise temporal identification and analysis of social media incidents. This paper proposes a method to instantly locate social media incidents spatially and temporally. Firstly, incident detectors are created for each monitored area using data from an accurate temporal filter, which helps minimize false positives. Subsequently, a compromised classifier pilot test establishes the reliability of detectors before authorizing their use. This innovative approach enhances real-time incident detection while reducing false alarms, thus facilitating quicker response times from authorities. Simulation tests confirm the superior performance of this method in accurately locating incidents and minimizing errors. Finally, a practical application is demonstrated through analysis of Beijing traffic incidents, showcasing the efficacy of this approach in identifying incidents dynamically and effectively. Our research offers adaptable solutions for incident detection and is applicable to a wide range of social media-driven events such as protests and traffic incidents across various cities globally. Ultimately, this method is poised to enhance real-world incident monitoring and analysis, ultimately improving public safety. A phenomenon known as the distorting effect has the potential to alter the connection between cosmic microwave background radiation patterns and large-scale structure data through a process involving higher-order statistical analysis.  We have developed a quick method to analyze the distorted effect using the cosmic microwave background radiation's bispectrum, which represents a second-order statistical measure, by utilizing a fast and accurate algorithm based on the Lagrange polynomial interpolation technique.  In order to assess the feasibility of detecting the distorted effect through bispectrum analysis, we have conducted two types of simulations, namely those involving a purely mathematical approach and another based on realistic assumptions about galaxy survey data, utilizing the CAMB and GiggleBUGs codes for cosmic microwave background radiation and galaxy survey simulations, respectively.  We observed that while bispectrum estimates of both types of simulated data exhibit oscillatory patterns, data simulated under realistic assumptions exhibit reduced accuracy relative to purely mathematical simulations, primarily due to statistical noise, limited coverage, and other factors, thereby indicating that detecting the distorted effect through bispectrum analysis of actual galaxy survey data may be challenging. Additionally, we found that the feasibility of validating the distorted effect through a cross-correlation analysis between cosmic microwave background radiation and galaxy surveys appears more promising, albeit under certain conditions.  We envision that our employed algorithm will contribute positively to this area of research, while also emphasizing the need for further investigations on the distorted effect's physical implications through more realistic simulations that incorporate various astrophysical biases.  Lastly, we propose the adoption of the acronym "DREAM" to signify Distorting effect through Rapidly Enduring astrophysical Manifestations.  We envision that the distilled idea captured within DREAM will contribute positively to this area of research, while also emphasizing the need for further investigations on the distorted effect's physical implications through more realistic simulations that incorporate various astrophysical biases. Recent research has demonstrated that machine learning models are susceptible to
adversarial attacks, yet many tests to verify their resilience are limited to
relatively simple scenarios. This study establishes a framework to assess the
adversarial resistance of Bayesian neural networks when dealing with complex
image datasets. Our framework relies on two key components: verifiable adversarial
training and a reliable uncertainty measurement. The former involves training
on verified adversarial examples, while the latter involves developing a metric
that accurately indicates a model's uncertainty without compromising its
accuracy. We propose the Nearest Spin Image metric, which effectively measures
a model's uncertainty without compromising its accuracy. Furthermore, this
study investigates the influence of hyperparameters on a model's robustness and
efficiency across multiple configurations. Through its findings, this study can
guide hyperparameter selection and inform the development of more effective
adversarial resistance techniques. The study's results also demonstrate that our
methodology successfully trains robust Bayesian neural networks that accurately
detect attacks and convey a model's uncertainty with high reliability. The
source code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/
jakeheun/adversarial_bayes. The dataset used for this study is drawn from
CIFAR10 and can be obtained at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~pjs/Imagelab/ExtraData/.

The majority of users who shared conspiracy theories were ordinary social media users, rather than influential figures. Our research also explored the strategies employed to disseminate rumors, revealing that some were propagated through media platforms, while others relied on private messages. The impact of social media on the spread of conspiracy theories cannot be overstated, as even minor accounts contributed to the dissemination of certain rumors. Additionally, we observed that some government officials were implicated in the propagation of conspiracy theories, while news organizations played a significant role, either by promoting or debunking rumors. Our findings can guide efforts to counter the spread of conspiracy theories and rumors in China by targeting specific individuals, media platforms, and geographic areas. The research also yields practical insights for fact-checking organizations, including prioritizing news organizations and influential social media users in their efforts to counter misinformation. The model, in turn, can support the design of targeted interventions by policymakers seeking to mitigate the spread of conspiracy theories and rumors. This study investigates the effects of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral image classification, specifically how different methods affect accuracy and computational efficiency. We evaluated several dimensionality reduction techniques, including principal axis transformation, principal component analysis, discrete wavelet transform, discrete cosine transform, and random forest, alongside an assessment of their complexity. Notably, our analysis shows that using the top two principal components for classification achieves the best results, yielding high accuracy with minimal computational demands due to reduced dimensionality and complex internal optimizations in the employed machine learning algorithm. This effectiveness is attributed to these techniques capturing the image's spectral and geometric characteristics. We found that methods like wavelet transform and discrete cosine transformation are inadequate for hyperspectral image classification, likely due to retaining original 2048 dimensions, resulting in high computational complexity and poor performance. Our findings suggest that incorporating geometric methods can significantly improve the accuracy of hyperspectral image classification, and we provide guidance on best practices for achieving high classification accuracy with minimal computational expense. Additionally, we emphasize the importance of considering the complexity of machine learning algorithms when applying dimensionality reduction techniques to hyperspectral images. Our study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the impacts of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral image classification and guiding the selection of appropriate methods and protocols to achieve successful classification. Furthermore, we include a step-by-step classification procedure, including relevant code, to facilitate the reproduction of our results and enable other researchers to explore the performance of different hyperspectral image classification approaches within the HPC environment of national institutions. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianSeb/HPC_Hyperspectral.git. This repository includes the necessary code for the reproduction of our results, along with additional extensions of random forest that can efficiently handle large datasets on national HPC institutions. We believe that our work will contribute positively to the field of hyperspectral image classification by exploring the performance of dimensionality reduction techniques, such as principal axis transformation, and promoting the use of more efficient algorithms for effective hyperspectral image classification. Our study provides a comprehensive assessment of the impacts of dimensionality reduction and complexity of machine learning algorithms on the performance of hyperspectral image classification. We observed that some dimensionality reduction techniques can lead to poorly accurate results, and we advocate for the use of more effective methods, such as principal component analysis. Previous studies have explored the inherent bias in natural language models and their impact on producing unfair outcomes. In this context, research has been conducted to reduce neural language models' disadvantageous biases. However, little is known about the inherent disadvantageous biases present in neural language models and whether existing methods that reduce advantageous biases can effectively address disadvantageous biases. To investigate this, a new set of tests was created to identify and mitigate disadvantageous biases in neural language models. Initially, a straightforward approach was employed to reduce these biases, resulting in limited success. Consequently, a more effective strategy was developed to address the root cause of disadvantageous biases within the training data. When applied to models with known disadvantageous biases, this approach was able to produce substantial improvements in reducing the biased outcomes. Interestingly, this approach also demonstrated promising results on more nuanced evaluation tests designed to identify subtle disadvantages. Moreover, a comparison was conducted between fine-tuning and self-supervised learning methods in reducing disadvantageous biases, revealing that the latter strategy was able to produce more effective outcomes in some cases. Ultimately, the study contributed to the development of a comprehensive toolkit for addressing both advantageous and disadvantageous biases in neural language models through a combination of strategic data selection and the application of post-hoc bias mitigation techniques. Additionally, the study provided implications for the responsible use of neural language models in real-world applications. In particular, the study highlighted the importance for developers and customers to comprehend the inherent biases present in the models being applied and consider the potential for these models to generate unfair outcomes. Furthermore, the study stressed the need for researchers and developers to address the root cause of biased training data, rather than merely adjusting the models' parameters to remedy disadvantageous biases. Finally, the study underlined the importance of long-term efforts required to comprehensively address the inherent disadvantageous biases present in neural language models. The proposed methods and findings have been made available through an open-source repository, including a detailed code description, data annotations, and the models themselves, in accordance with the principles of transparent research. However, accurate prediction of the protein's three-dimensional structure depends heavily on the quality of the atomic movements within the molecule. Therefore, a proposed method uses quantum mechanical calculations to estimate the chemical shifts of amide protons, thereby validating and refining the predicted protein structures. This approach involves incorporating quantum chemical shifts into a potential function that corrects the protein's conformation to better match experimental data. Preliminary results indicate that the inclusion of quantum chemical shifts significantly improves the match between predicted and actual molecular properties, particularly for larger proteins. Furthermore, the development of an efficient quantum approximation technique using the Toray-Akiba-Mori-Singh (TAMSS) method enables the calculation of chemical shifts for larger systems, enabling the precise refinement of protein structures. This method reaches an accuracy of 10-fold higher than previous estimates for predicting chemical shifts, allowing for the refinement of protein structures with improved accuracy. This approach may enable more effective use of chemical shifts in the analysis of protein structure, particularly for refining the three-dimensional structure of proteins. Overall, the integration of quantum mechanical models for chemical shifts and ensemble-based protein structure prediction represents a groundbreaking development in the field of protein structure, and it has the potential to significantly improve our understanding of protein function and the origins of diseases. Additionally, the quantum mechanical model for chemical shifts presents a novel research area with numerous possible applications, and it could be adapted for use in the study of other complex molecular systems. Finally, the precision of the predicted chemical shifts may enable the detection of fake protein structures derived from incorrect quantum mechanical models or poor initial protein templates. This research has the potential to significantly impact protein structure prediction and could be a crucial element in the validation of protein structures in the future. Lastly, the incorporation of the quantum mechanical model for chemical shifts may eventually supplant X-ray crystallography as the gold standard for determining protein structure. A new approach is presented for simulating complex interactions among electrons in solids by breaking them down into smaller, connected components, using a method known as parquet theory. By projecting the electronic system onto a lower-dimensional space constructed from its density, parquet theory simplifies the description of electron interactions without losing crucial details. However, the overall Hamiltonian driving these interactions remains hidden within the theoretical framework. In this work, we provide a clearer understanding of parquet theory by revealing how it transforms the original Hamiltonian into a more complex form, hidden behind the observed density-based correlations. A graphical representation, known as Feynman diagrams, is used to visualize these complex correlations and their associated fluctuations. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrates that parquet theory generates a self-consistent approximation of the original electronic Hamiltonian. This discovery opens the door for improving the theoretical framework by incorporating corrections based on higher-order diagram types. Furthermore, our analysis presents a unified framework for interpreting various parquet approximations within a single, consistent structure. Importantly, our analysis sheds light on the origin and nature of certain diagram types that have previously been poorly understood. By establishing a deeper connection between the original Hamiltonian and the observed density-based correlations, our work sets the stage for the development of future improvements. Future modifications could incorporate corrections derived from higher-order diagram types, such as those associated with the Anderson-Hubbard and Heisenberg models. These potential advancements are a key focus of our proposed theory. Additionally, our analysis presents a new classification system for approximations within the parquet framework, which we hope will become a standard tool for navigating the complex space of approximations within parquet theory. Lastly, our work lays the foundation for a more general approach to interpreting approximations within the parquet framework, which could be applied beyond the context of solids to the simulation of electron interactions in general. Our research has achieved a breakthrough in modeling liquids composed of excitons using ab initio density functional theory. By converting density functional theory into a more robust form, we can accurately reproduce the properties of normal liquids. Our approach reinforces the idea of exciton liquefaction and reveals its potential for enhanced superconductivity. Applying this method to 1T-TiSe2, we found that the conventional density functional theory fails to capture the high-temperature superconducting properties, but our new model successfully explains the experimentally observed superconducting critical temperature of 4.5 K. Furthermore, we predict that the exciton composition in 1T-TiSe2 at 10 K should be approximately 10%, which may facilitate the exploration of exciton superconductivity. Conversely, we also encountered a situation where our new model suggests that 2H-TiSe2 lacks exciton superconductivity, thereby validating the existing understanding that it does not superconduct. Our study provides a reliable framework for investigating exciton superconductors in a theoretical context. Additionally, we are confident that this pioneering approach can be applied to various other materials and systems. Lastly, although our research reveals that 1T-TiSe2's high-temperature superconductivity can be explained, we acknowledge that our final results may still be susceptible to variations due to the current limitations of the electron-phonon coupling calculation. Nonetheless, our theoretical model exhibits a substantial level of stability, especially when compared to other contemporary research, including the results obtained using the density functional perturbation theory. Moreover, our analysis shows that the exciton radius, which governs the exciton behavior, is primarily influenced by one particular type of interaction and one particular energy level, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our model. Conversely, we disagree with the results presented in a different study, which suggested that the strong electron-phonon coupling in 1T-TiSe2 greatly contributes to its high-temperature superconductivity. Instead, our model reveals that the high-temperature superconductivity of 1T-TiSe2 can be primarily attributed to the exciton superconductivity triggered by the excessive exciton composition at relatively low temperatures. Conversely, we also found that the high-temperature exciton superconductivity in 1T-TiSe2 can also be compromised by excessive exciton composition beyond a certain threshold. These incidents, surrounding events of civilian-dispatcher interactions, are often unrecorded, contradicting the abundant availability of citizen-redactor interactions via texting.  Consequently, valuable knowledge of interaction between citizens and dispatchers is lost.  To rectify this, a novel approach is proposed, employing natural language processing and machine learning to analyze user-dispatcher conversations, extracting concealed insights from their conversations. Through thorough testing, the model's performance is compared with two existing emergency classification models, showing its superiority in limited-data scenarios while matching the performance in extensive-data scenarios.  Additionally, the developed model outperforms a baseline model of automatic summarization in extracting insights from user-dispatcher interactions. We introduce a new research area in Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) applications, specifically in neural network training, by developing the first minimax algorithm for SMPC-based neural network training. Our approach is versatile and allows various primary objectives, such as regression and classification tasks, to be realized. visual tasks, we develop a system that enhances an offline ranking method with
visual cues. Since ground-truth labels for visuospatial actions are costly to
obtain, multiple experts provide diverse training data labeled only as better
or worse. However, this labeled data is also resource-intensive. To solve the
problem of reward learning from noisy, expert-labeled data, we introduce the
Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VICR) method. It utilizes an offline model to
visualize and connect similar training data provided by the experts, making
effortless adjustments for human preference. We implement VICR on cross-domain
state-of-the-art visuospatial reward learning methods and evaluate them on
Google's Datasetum dataset. The results show that VICR effectively improves the
performance of the reward learning models, outperforming a strong baseline
by 88.9% in terms of success rate and reducing the time spent on fine-tuning
by a factor of 3. Additionally, VICR's capabilities extend beyond visuospatial
tasks to general ranking tasks. The code for VICR is available at https://github.com/yangyangyys/VICR.

A novel approach to offline reinforcement learning is presented, which accounts for the fact that training and testing datasets may be tainted with fraudulent information. To address this challenge, a concept of data reliability is introduced, which estimates the likelihood of each dataset being trustworthy. We introduce a metric called the trustworthiness gap, which calculates the difference between the trusted and untrusted performance of an offline reinforcement learning model. We demonstrate that this gap can be minimized through the average trustworthiness of individual policies, leading to the development of a trusted policy ensemble. This ensemble is comprised of multiple policies generated using an offline reinforcement learning algorithm, which iteratively creates new policies through data perturbation. We showcase the effectiveness of our method on a range of simulation tasks, such as navigation in a grid world and control of a dynamical system. Furthermore, we apply our approach to a real-world use case of an autonomous driving system, which accounts for the fact that its training and testing data may contain intentional manipulations. The presentation highlights the significance of validating model robustness against manipulation, which is often overlooked in traditional offline reinforcement learning. The development of our method, which educates a set of policies to mitigate performance degradation due to data manipulation, is a crucial component of a system that generates a range of trustworthy policies. This system can generate a trusted policy ensemble, which is an average of multiple policies, providing robust and reliable performance even in the presence of untrusted data. To further enhance model robustness, we propose DataClean, a data manipulation detection and cleaning algorithm. DataClean utilizes a Q-network to detect and remove fraudulent actions from the training dataset. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through empirical evaluation on a real-world autonomous driving use case, showcasing the ability of our method to provide a range of trustworthy policies, as well as significantly outperform other offline reinforcement learning algorithms by accounting for data manipulation during training. Building on prior research into transducers that synchronize inputs with outputs, we expand this concept to a related category, 'unilateral resynchronizability', where a transducer can match part of an input to produce part of an output, without requiring a complete match. This more liberal definition opens up possibilities for greater flexibility in transducer applications, such as translating partial sentences or facilitating partial understanding in speech recognition. Moreover, the added complexity of unilateral resynchronizability raises new challenges in identifying when a transducer can be transformed into a synchronized one, leading to the introduction of a related concept,'resynchronizability degree'. This degree measures the level of synchronization achievable by a unilateral resynchronizer, effectively quantifying its ability to match inputs with outputs. By exploring the properties of resynchronizability degrees, we are able to prove that verifying their presence in a transducer is a decidable problem, paving the way for the development of an algorithm to determine this degree for any unilateral resynchronizer. Our understanding of Jupiter's T-dwarf sibling, GJ 229B, began in 1995, thanks to the discovery by Oppenheimer et al., which has since led to numerous studies on this enigmatic object.  GJ 229B, which is likely composed primarily of hydrogen and helium, exists in a state of instability, and is thought to be a failed Jupiter, existing beyond the planet's escape velocity.  Owing to its proximity to its host star, and the near-perfect alignment of the two, the system offers a unique opportunity to explore the formation and properties of T-dwarfs, especially their characteristics at birth.  Recent cross-correlation of data from spectrographs gathered at the Keck I telescope, and the APOLLO retrieval code allowed for constraining GJ 229B's chemical composition, and analyzing its atmospheric circulation.  The analysis led to several significant findings including the object's low total abundance, and the decline in absorption by various metal ions, especially tellurium, and iron, which contradicts models suggesting these elements are prevalent in T-dwarfs.  The APOLLO algorithm also detected the presence of the object's planet, GJ 229C, and suggested it is orbiting the host star at a distance of approximately 5.2 astronomical units.  The validation of the code's accuracy, and the success of the analysis, enabled scientists to refine their understanding of the dynamics governing the system, and the instability of the Jovian T-dwarf sequence.  The research has significantly contributed to our knowledge of the astrodynamic regime, and laid the groundwork for future studies on the dynamic systems, and the objects within them.  Additionally, the analysis has paved the way for a deeper understanding of the objects within the system, and their interaction with others in the region including a binary system involving GJ 229A, and the T-dwarf sibling, GJ 722B.  The discovery also sheds light on the object's possible exoplanetary past, and the phenomenon of T-dwarf failure, and failed planets, existing in the region due to their close proximity to their host stars, and the resulting loss of velocity.  The research further indicates that GJ 229B, and other objects like it, are critical in the understanding of the planetary formation sequence, and the objects within the region will continue to offer a wealth of information on the dynamic systems, and the objects within them, as they provide a unique perspective on the astrodynamic regime,

The $\beta^+$ decay properties of $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te were calculated using the shell model, specifically considering interactions derived from JUN45, JUN44, and JUN52 effective models. We determined double-beta decay modes and calculated various theoretical constants, including $f_+(9)$ and $R_A$ for $\beta^+$ and $\beta^-$ decays, respectively. Furthermore, by comparing theoretical $\log ft$ values to experimental data, we estimated $|M_0|/M_A$ for $^{137}$Te $\beta^-$ decay. Our analysis also explored the impact of different effective models on theoretical $\log ft$ values. For $^{135}$Te, we predicted $\log ft$ values for 0$\nu$$\beta$$\beta$ decays to $^{135}$I and $^{135}$Xe, with predicted half-lives of around 1.17$\times$10$^{21}$ and 1.25$\times$10$^{21}$ years, respectively. Additionally, we calculated the $\log ft$ values for $^{137}$Te $\beta^-$ decay to $^{137}$I and $^{137}$Xe, with predicted half-lives of 2.94$\times$10$^{21}$ and 3.17$\times$10$^{21}$ years, respectively. Our study also provides predicted $\log ft$ values for double-beta decay in xenon isotopes. Finally, we calculated the $ft$-values for $^{137}$Xe and $^{135}$Xe through both $\beta^+$ and $\beta^-$ decays. Our estimated $ft$-values for $^{137}$Xe and $^{135}$Xe decay are in agreement with previously published results. Additionally, we calculated the electronic structure constants and compared our results with experimental data, specifically considering the case of $^{137}$Xe. Our study also shows that using JUN45 interaction yields the best agreement with experimental data for $\log ft$ values and constant estimations. Moreover, to validate our shell-model calculations, we performed a self-consistent random-phase approximation to estimate the density distribution and compare our results with experimental data. Our study also illustrates the reliability of shell-model results when employing three effective models in the Te isotopic series. Our estimated $|M_0|/M_A$ for $^{137}$Te $\beta^-$ decay is consistent with experimental data

In this research, we introduce a new kernel learning method to enhance the dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), known for its ability to analyze complex data in various fields such as fluid dynamics and signal processing. Our approach, building on DMD, includes two components: a technique to optimize a kernel for extracting meaningful modes from data, and a method for effectively processing noisy input data. By integrating these two elements, we develop a technique for optimizing a kernel that can disambiguate linear and nonlinear interactions within data. This kernel-optimized DMD framework, referred to as linear and nonlinear disambiguation optimization (LANDO), yields modes that align with linear and nonlinear structures present in the data, as demonstrated using geometric visualization. Our study demonstrates that LANDO outperforms DMD in data analysis and provides a more in-depth understanding of the data's underlying dynamics, as it allows for an accurate breakdown of linear and nonlinear contributions to the data. Our approach can be applied to a broad range of problems and its effectiveness in various applications is yet to be fully explored. An open-source code package for LANDO is available at https://github.com/cdt-guru/lando. A Python implementation of the code is also included in the package for easy integration into the DMD toolkit. Moreover, we provide a sample dataset related to our research that can be accessed through the link https://doi.org/10.17632/ucxkzpy28555002424e7d4d8e4e5. This dataset contains numerical data that were used in the simulations presented in our study. Furthermore, we describe the process of our kernel-optimized DMD method, referred to as the LANDO algorithm, and demonstrate its effectiveness using geometric visualization that highlights its performance. This research shows that LANDO can analyze complex data effectively and provide a more in-depth understanding of its underlying dynamics, as it allows for a precise breakdown of linear and nonlinear contributions to the data. In the future, we aim to apply our approach to real-world problems in various fields, as they become available, and continue to refine our method for effectively analyzing dimensional data that contains nonlinear structures. This research introduces a technique for optimizing a kernel that can disambiguate linear and nonlinear interactions within dimensional data, as well as effectively process such data even in the presence of noise. Our approach can be applied to a broad range of problems and its effectiveness in various applications is yet to be fully explored. An open-source code package for LANDO is available at https://github.com/cdt-g

Chess players utilize a lengthy and complex set of moves known as openings, which are strategically planned to achieve a desired outcome, the quickest checkmate or a favorable position. An opening can be defined as a sequence of moves between the initial positions of the white and black pieces, typically lasting between two and fifteen moves. Understanding the variability within these movements and how they correlate with each other in the chess community can facilitate the development of more effective playing strategies. To explore these dynamics, we analyzed a large dataset from the chess.com platform, examining variations within specific openings and how they differ from one another. Our measurements identified the most distinctive openings and tested their accuracy in classifying chess players' skills. Additionally, we investigated the relationships between openings, discovering clusters of connected openings and revealing similarities and differences, ultimately mapping the chess community's understanding of the most effective openings. Our results demonstrate that analyzing the intricacies within a complex domain like chess can uncover profound insights, potentially leading to improved performances. An interactive visualization of the results is available at https://chesscomplexity.xyz/.

A novel 3D model retrieval method, using freely-drawn 2D line sketches in three-dimensional space, is introduced in this research. The proposed approach inherently considers geometric variations and remembers the drawing process, allowing for the capture of skilled and unskilled input. Additionally, it adapts to different drawing tools and velocities without manual calibration. To evaluate its effectiveness, two virtual reality databases were created, containing 3,000 objects, sourced from ModelNet and Google's 3D Warehouse. Our retrieval framework, comprising a neural network-based component, captures the essence of the sketching process, and a ranking system that utilizes geometric similarity and similarity in drawing sequences to prioritize results. The performance of this model is assessed through a virtual reality interface that allows users to evaluate retrieval accuracy using free-hand 2D line drawings. The found results demonstrate significantly improved retrieval accuracy in 3D space, compared to classical sketch-based 3D retrieval approaches. The average retrieval accuracy of our model surpasses state-of-the-art 3D retrieval accuracy by a considerable margin, and shows promising potential for real-world applications and further development. The proposed technique can potentially be applied across a wide range of domains, extending beyond 3D model retrieval to encompass other tasks, such as image and video retrieval by capturing the underlying dynamics of the viewing or navigating processes. The research also opens up avenues for more in-depth psychological and cognitive analyses of human interaction with these digital environments. The developed database and virtual drawing interface can facilitate the exploration of additional epistemic and semantic aspects of digital scenes, and may further elucidate the underlying semantic and epistemic dimensions of digital scenes, encompassing both semantic and epistemic aspects. The actual drawing videos, models, and codes used in this research are made freely available through an online public repository, and the virtual drawing interface can be accessed through a web-based public demo platform. The demo platform provides users with a seamless and intuitive virtual drawing experience, and the drawing videos demonstrate various drawing styles, ranging from simple to complex, showcasing the versatility of human interaction with 3D digital models. The repository and demo platform offer a comprehensive toolkit for reproducing the results and exploring the developed model, as well as a virtual drawing canvas for creating custom 3D sketches and observing the corresponding 3D model retrievals in real-time. The repository and demo platform can be accessed at: \textcolor{blue}{https://3Ddrawing.sketchretrieve.org/}. The repository and demo platforms serve as a resource for reproducing the results

A key factor in successful motor learning through reinforcement learning involves designing an efficient reward structure, which requires careful analysis of the target outcome to create a meaningful endpoint for the learning process. To facilitate effective motor learning, it's essential to have a clear understanding of the desired outcome, also known as end-effect investigation. In this study, we investigate various methods for conducting end-effect investigations in search of optimal movements using high-dimensional modeling techniques. We utilize two search methods: FASTER-Optimal and FASTER-Mixed, which are inspired by Monte-Carlo planning. The FASTER-Optimal method optimizes the target outcome by converting it into a solvable optimization problem, drawing from ideas in convex geometry. The FASTER-Mixed method incorporates a stabilizing term into the reward structure to prevent oscillating movements. The performance of these methods is demonstrated using a combination of 2D simulation models and a physical robot arm setup, with results showing promising outcomes, especially in scenarios with noisy target data. The code used in this study is publicly available via GitHub. The authors also provide step-by-step instructions on how to conduct end-effect investigations through interactive visualizations, also hosted on GitHub. The major findings of this study are: (i) conducting end-effect investigations leads to efficient motor learning; (ii) a single efficient target outcome can lead to diverse effective movements; (iii) incorporating a stabilizing term into the reward structure can enhance the robustness of the generated movements, particularly when there are discrepancies between the simulated and real-world target movements; and (iv) the proposed method successfully tackles high-dimensional optimization problems by leveraging the efficient conversion of the target outcome into a solvable optimization problem, thereby achieving target movements that closely match the optimal outcomes in both simulation and real-world tests. The researchers acknowledge the influence of prior work, including FELIKS, on the development of the end-effect investigation framework and provide comprehensive comparisons with other robust reinforcement learning algorithms, also identifying potential future research directions in this area. The end-effect investigation framework, in particular the use of a stabilizing term, may have applications in other areas of learning and may be extended in the future to tackle challenges involving multiple simultaneous target outcomes. Furthermore, the novel approach to reward design presents an interesting area of study, also involving the conversion of efficient target outcomes into a solvable optimization problem, and may find applications in other areas of learning and in the development of more robust robot policies. This study introduces a class of hypergraphs that exhibit a specific type of substructure across various scales, analogous to clusters in traditional graph models. We develop a framework for creating random hypergraphs with these dynamics and investigate the resulting large-scale hypergraph properties. Specifically, we track how the substructures evolve and stabilize as the hypergraph size increases and demonstrate that their characteristics converge rapidly. Furthermore, we identify a threshold for the substructure clustering behavior in hypergraphs. Our main findings build upon earlier works (Karahasanovic et al., arXiv 2021) on hypergraphs and extend them by incorporating additional parameters. Additionally, we formulate new asymptotic distributions for the substructure clustering pattern in hypergraphs. To showcase the applicability of our model, we generate synthetic data mimicking a network of human interactions. We use this data to analyze the air transportation network and the COVID-19 virus spread within a US state, both real-world systems that exhibit dynamic substructure patterns. Our method successfully captures these patterns and demonstrates a favorable prediction of the resulting large-scale hypergraph properties. Moreover, we achieve a 70% accurate prediction of the longest flight distance in the air transportation network and a 91% accurate prediction of the non-pharmaceutical interventions effectiveness in controlling COVID-19 outbreaks in a US state. Our hypergraph model thus emerges as a valuable analytical tool for understanding complex systems with a deep underlying structure. Our work also connects hypergraphs to established graph-based models, thereby providing new insights into the hypergraph realm. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/averyyoung dynamichypergraphs.

This study demonstrates that the operator expansion of a stress tensor's source current across two spacetime regions can be utilized to calculate a specific entanglement property known as mutual information. Notably, we find that for mutual information, the leading-order ambiguity is sufficient, thereby isolating a correction term that allows us to quantify entanglement exclusively. Secondly, we are able to evaluate the contribution of the c-barrier term, often considered as a null-set, within the context of operator expansion. Following these advancements, we are able to evaluate mutual information for separate spacetime configurations, notably finding that it adheres to holography's Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen constraint. Our work provides a new framework for understanding the entanglement of general quasi-local operators, opening up further avenues of investigation. The study also raises implications for the holonomic implementation of the Hamiltonian, a concept within the AdS/CFT correspondence, and suggests a crucial role for null sets within this framework. Lastly, we propose a conjecture, stating that any quasi-local operator's entanglement surely resides within the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosey bound, thereby extending a prior hypothesis. The mutual information, as derived from our investigation, exhibits spacetime's intricate non-local properties, suggesting a possible pathway for addressing the long-standing holographic principle paradox. Moreover, it sheds light on the nature of null sets within the AdS/CFT framework, revealing them to be pivotal components. Lastly, we pose several open research questions for further exploration. The goal is to verify the state's extremely dense multipolety nature. To achieve this, researchers conduct an experiment at the TRIUMF laboratory using a high-intensity beam of $\mathrm{^{12}C}$ ions, where the Hoyle state is produced through resonance feeding. The subsequent gamma rays from the decay of the Hoyle state are detected by combining the sensitive detection of the Beta-CP TC in conjunction with the magnetic analysis of the QDC-MU. The resulting data show a decay strength of $1.76(15)_]{-0.23}$ mb, which is in line with current theoretical predictions. The data also reveal the presence of a previously unobserved $2^-$ state at 0.13 MeV below the Hoyle state, enhancing the state's non-compact nature. The findings provide a significant understanding of the Hoyle state's quantum many-body system. The researchers utilize an average-angle analysis to minimize the influence of nuclear reactions and show that the Hoyle state's characteristics can be assessed effectively through the TC's unique capabilities in measuring high-energy reactions over extended time frames. The data are also presented from a complementary measurement of the Hoyle state's gamma-decay strength via a detector that rotates around the target, which is then compared to the strength of the Hoyle state, showing agreement within 10 percent. The Hoyle state's unique structure serves as a test bed for understanding highly clustered states in heavier nuclei, as well as their direct-decay behavior, which has important implications for astrophysical processes such as nuclear burning in stars. A recent SemEval task focused on verifying the accuracy of tabular data found in scientific research papers. This is a crucial area of study because tables in research papers are often relied upon to understand key findings, yet they contain inaccuracies due to typos, omission, or incomplete information. To combat these issues, the SEM-TAB-FACTS team developed a system to automatically detect and correct errors in research tables based on a related dataset's values. Unfortunately, the team encountered technical difficulties during the competition that affected their submissions, but this report will detail their initial approach to addressing the task. We analyzed a related dataset with 1,753 tables to understand the context of the SEM-TAB-FACTS task, and our system achieved notable results on the development set, but its performance on the official test set was hindered by the technical issues. For future work, the team plans to enhance their approach by incorporating more accurate table extraction techniques, utilizing relevant knowledge from domain-specific sources, and integrating the team's related work on data fusion to merge information from multiple datasets. Additionally, the team will explore strategies to address the semantic discrepancies between the labels and the target values, and improve their model's generalizability through data augmentation and ensemble methods. To facilitate research on this topic, the team has made their code and dataset available for public access.

We demonstrate a simplified proof that in these cases, the shortened metric dimension of G has a linear relationship with the number of its vertices. Conversely, we present a separate classification of graphs lacking a hamiltonian cycle, for which the shortened metric dimension of the graph possesses a logarithmic relationship with the number of its vertices. Furthermore, we establish a general upper limit for the shortened metric dimension of any finite graph. Additionally, we explore relationships between the shortened metric dimension and other graph parameters such as the chromatic number and the diameter. We present specific illustrations to support our findings. Firstly, a family of graphs meeting the criterion for being soluble, yet possessing a diameter that grows in proportion to the square root of the number of their vertices, while also exhibiting a shortened metric dimension that proportionally scales with the number of their vertices. This research introduces an innovative process that efficiently removes SOx from flue gas using a low-temperature oxidation technology. A numerical model simulating a 1-m long reactor has been developed to analyze the interaction between ozone, UV light, and SOx in flue gas. The study evaluates the effects of ozone concentration, UV intensity, temperature, and gas flow velocity on the reaction. The results indicate that a minimum ozone concentration of 2000 ppm and 10 W/m^2 UV irradiance are required to remove SOx within a 1-m reactor. A temperature increase from 25 to 75 °C enhances the reaction, but has a limited impact beyond this point. The model also shows that a higher gas velocity can extend the reaction distance, but this can be mitigated by increasing the reactor length. The study recommends using a 250 ppm/h ozone generator and low-pressure UV lamps to develop an energy-efficient SOx elimination system. The results are promising, and this work is expected to inform the design of a new SOx elimination system. Consequently, there is a critical need for a suitable testing environment that can effectively validate the functionality of hybrid computing systems involving software-based neuromorphic simulators and custom hardware accelerators in tandem. To address this challenge, we introduce a new virtual framework based on SystemC that enables the simulation of concurrent operations between software-based neuromorphic simulators and custom hardware accelerators. Additionally, this virtual framework can be adapted to model other hybrid computing architectures with minimal modifications. It is noteworthy that the introduced virtual framework can be viewed as a modular extension to the existing Cosima emulator and can be utilized as a standalone tool for the simulation of hybrid computing systems, or in conjunction with the Cosima emulator for extended simulation duration. Decision theory and probability analysis typically rely on clear definitions, but real-world decisions are frequently influenced by ambiguous, incomplete, or uncertain information. This study explores the concept of decision forests - a type of machine learning model - as a potential solution for navigating complex decision-making problems characterized by multiple interlinking uncertainties. By applying the principles of qualitative decision theory, our innovation involves representing decision-making uncertainties through quantified fuzzy sets, thereby enabling the learning and processing of ambiguous criteria and contextual factors. To achieve this, we present a novel formulation for training decision forests in the presence of ambiguity, along with a corresponding algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate that decision forests can effectively handle and adapt to both certain and uncertain decision-making scenarios, often producing outcomes comparable to optimized methods while forest-fallback solutions providing a safety net for emergency scenarios. PrunedDTW is an example of such a variant that reduces computational complexity while preserving its scalar cost, making it suitable for early discarding in nearest neighbor searches. When combined with an early discarding strategy in a time series retrieval scheme, PrunedDTW achieves significant improvements in processing speed and efficiency, particularly at the cost of slight reductions in accuracy. Our study proposes Enhanced PrunedDTW (EPDTW) that addresses a weakness in PrunedDTW by allowing all data points to be considered in the optimal ground state, resulting in enhanced performance. Galopin et al. recently introduced EPDTW but it introduced a complexity cost proportional to the series length via its reverse warping function. We address this limitation by introducing Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPDTW) which maintains the efficiency of PrunedDTW and the enhanced accuracy of EPDTW while discarding irrelevant data points early in the search. Our implementation of EDPDTW demonstrates superior performance in comparison to the previous best approaches, notably with considerable speedup benefits for datasets with large series data. Our study also includes a time series classification application of EDPDTW which reveals a similar performance profile, achieving enhanced speed and improved accuracy over PrunedDTW and EPDTW by discarding irrelevant data points early in the search. Our implementation of EDPDTW outperforms PrPDTW and EPDTW in two early discarding strategies for the task. Conceptual testing, a special type of software testing, is increasingly being introduced in computer science courses, with the goal of improving students' understanding of software development concepts through challenging and engaging activities.  To evaluate conceptual testing, researchers often use detailed evaluation methods, analyzing students' work in relation to software versions, execution outcomes, and test cases.  However, these methods require substantial resources and can be time-consuming.  In this study, we explored an alternative approach, called inquiry-based evaluation, which assesses the effectiveness of conceptual testing by measuring student performance on key evaluation criteria, and found it to be faster and more efficient.  When compared to detailed evaluation, inquiry-based evaluation revealed similar results and showed promise as a more efficient evaluation method for teaching conceptual testing.  The findings of this study can guide instructors in evaluating conceptual testing, either in whole or in part, based on their specific needs and constraints.  The research presented here is a follow-up to a previous study on teaching testing as a development activity, and further validates the efficacy of this approach.  The empirical investigation reported here is based on a testing experiment involving 99 students from a technical university in Turkey, and an additional 5 instructors from a separate institution, who were invited to evaluate the inquiry-based approach, with one of these instructors having a background in educational research.  The results of the study provide practical suggestions and insights for those interested in teaching testing as a development activity, and offer a useful example of this approach for evaluating software testing training. This research introduces a novel approach to explaining DNNs through ILP by merging analysis of deep neural network internals with a comprehensive concept study. Unlike existing methods that either delve into DNN architecture or perform concept exploration, our framework synergizes these two insights via ILP to furnish thorough, worded explanations. Firstly, an ILP model is created to capture DNN workings by compressing a DNN into an equivalent logical expression. Secondly, a separate ILP model facilitates the identification of crucial concepts within a dataset by linking top-ranked concepts to relevant network workings. Ultimately, the outcomes of these ILP models are harmonized through merging to generate ILP-based explanations for the DNN. Notably, our method does not necessitate modifying DNN architecture, thereby allowing it to expound on network workings that may be obscured by compression or forgotten during the training process. Our system can generate over 3000% more explanations than those based on training data comprehension alone and surpasses a leading DNN comprehension method in an empirical evaluation, demonstrating potential in various applications, such as enhancing human-AI collaboration and empirical studies. The proposed approach is further substantiated by an online demonstration at \url{https://research.aischool.ac.kr/neural-explanation}. A dataset of explanation templates and a human-annotated concept bank are made available at \url{https://research.aischool.ac.kr/concept-bank}.
