Session-based suggestion systems recommend relevant items to users based on past sessions, generating individual suggestions one at a time. Current two-phase suggestion systems divide suggestion into choosing relevant users and ranking suitable items. While showing promising short-term outcomes, they often underperform long-term due to lacking control over item ranks. To address this issue, we introduce Candidate Rank Representations (CRRs), utilizing session data to capture diverse item ranking patterns, and enhance the suggestion process with CRRs. We further propose CRR-Induce and CRR-Augment, two strategies to integrate CRRs into the two-phase suggestion framework, and name the resulting system CRR-Suggest. We evaluate CRR-Suggest using three large datasets for music and news articles, finding it to significantly outperform the baseline system and maintain excellent long-term performance, while also showcasing ease of integration into existing two-phase suggestion systems. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/jamestao/CRR-Suggest. Video explanation can be found at https://youtu.be/jN8b8C3jR6k. PAC codes are a type of error-correcting code that can correct arbitrary errors, not just limited to syndromes, which enables them to correct errors in codes with an infinite minimum distance. This correction capability, however, comes at the cost of higher latency and computational complexity due to the need for iterative decoding and error correction. Unlike conventional block codes, PAC codes rely on infinite-dimensional code spaces, which typically result in higher encoding and decoding complexities and latencies. This study focuses on enhancing the metric used in PAC code decoding and proposes a new error correction approach called selective PAC (SPAC) codes, which aim to correct errors while minimizing computational overhead. The key differences between SPAC and PAC codes concern the metric used and the way errors are propagated during decoding. Unlike PAC codes, which iterate until the desired metric threshold is reached, SPAC codes only iterate a limited number of times and stop when errors cease to spread further. This study evaluates SPAC codes for binary and ternary channels and assesses their performance across various channel conditions, comparing their performance to PAC codes. The results indicate that SPAC codes can correct errors in codes with finite minimum distances efficiently and offer improved latency and computational complexity relative to PAC codes, while also outperforming PAC codes in terms of bit-wise, block-wise latency and computational complexity. Furthermore, SPAC codes excel in latency and computational complexity when the packet error rates are low. To reduce decoding complexity, this study proposes two simplification methods, sparse and truncated PAC codes, which can be considered as generalized versions of traditional block codes, with the latter exhibiting lower complexity than PAC codes. The study evaluates these simplified architectures and finds that they perform sub-optimally compared to SPAC codes but offer improved latency and computational complexity relative to PAC codes, particularly in terms of reduced state complexity and computational overhead. The findings indicate that SPAC codes can be regarded as hybrid versions of traditional block and PAC codes, which offer improved latency and computational complexity while maintaining performance comparable to PAC codes, making them a more practical alternative. Additionally, the study presents two other architectures based on PAC codes, PAC-GF and PAC-SD, which aim to reduce latency and computational complexity by leveraging Gaussian approximations and scale-down factor techniques, which can lead to a complete elimination of state complexity in some cases. The study evaluates these architectures and finds that they perform close to SPAC codes, with PAC-GF codes exhibiting lower latency and computational complexity than SPAC codes, particularly when there is no error, while PAC-SD codes display reduced computational complexity

A novel handheld device, resembling a miniature camera, captures high-speed 3D point cloud sequences in various outdoor settings. Our research introduces an enhanced tracking algorithm, originally presented in a conference, to reconstruct hand movements in these sequences. This algorithm leverages a simplified hand model to recreate the palm and fingers, retargeting the hand to mimic natural movements. Our enhanced algorithm incorporates a novel feature that detects and tracks hand flexibility, which was previously unaddressed. Additionally, we apply a state estimation technique to merge sequential point clouds, aligning them with optimal results. To evaluate our approach, we created a benchmark, comprising 12 categories of motion patterns, and gathered outdoor point cloud datasets to serve as a reference, dubbed the Outdoor Hand Point Cloud Dataset. Our algorithm achieves exceptional performance in reconstructing the hand's movements, demonstrating a substantial edge over a baseline method with reconstruction errors reaching as low as $6.4$ cm and $8.2$ cm for state estimation. Notably, we found the hand model's accuracy to be $7.6$ cm when targeting the palm's center, and performed extensive qualitative analyses to validate our approach, which showed promising results with extensive generalization. The reconstructed tracks and point clouds are also applicable in other tasks, such as multi-body tracking and state estimation. These contributions demonstrate theoretical insights, pave the way for future research in outdoor laser scanning, and provide valuable datasets to the community. Ultimately, we achieved precise hand tracking, reconstructing the hand's movements with high accuracy in a purely optical-motivated state, which has numerous practical implications for various applications. This work is expected to spawn new research areas in computer vision and robotics, and will potentially contribute to advancing human-robot collaboration and wearable devices. Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-interacting Dark Matter within Neutron Stars have been carried out, utilizing a more accurate description of the nuclear medium via Dirac-Fermi-liquid theory. This approach considers the significant impact of relativistic nuclear fermions in the surface and core of Neutron Stars. For Dark Matter composed of scalar particles interacting through a pseudoscalar mediator, our findings show enhanced neutrino emissions compared to previous estimates. Furthermore, our results indicate substantial neutrino outputs in the surface regions of Neutron Stars, contradicting common assumptions of neutrinolessness in this context. These calculations demonstrate the importance of considering the inherent complexity of neutrino physics in Dark Matter-related research within Neutron Stars. Our analysis also reveals potential challenges in detecting Dark Matter-related neutrino signals from supernovae, as their emissions may be overwhelmed by neutrinos from the supernova core. Finally, our work highlights the feasibility of confirming or rejecting certain Dark Matter models through verification of Neutron Star cooling curves, with the potential for validation of our novel emissivity predictions in the future. These calculations pave the way for a renewed examination of the link between Dark Matter, Neutron Star anomalies, and supernova constraints. They further provide a foundation for investigating the influence of Dark Matter-induced heat on the search for Neutron Star companions in binary systems, as well as the stability of doubly beta-decaying Isolated Neutron Star systems. Finally, these results inspire a fresh assessment of the potential impact of Dark Matter on the tardy collapse of some Neutron Stars. The updated code used to generate these numerical results is available at https://github.com/AlessandroRaccanelli/DarkMatter_Neutrino_Emissions/tree/main-code. We propose a theoretical framework in which the universe's dark matter is composed of two parts: the ordinary dark matter found in the cosmic microwave background, and an unknown, heavy neutrino species generated by a portal interaction with standard model particles. This heavy neutrino, which has a very low mass compared to the Higgs mass, takes the form of a soft, moving "shadow" of its lighter, invisible counterpart. It is possible that the heavy neutrino decays into other, visible particles such as gamma rays or dark photons. In our framework, the heavy neutrino's mass is linked to the mass of its lighter counterpart and their differences can be explained by a mass scale in the portal interaction, known as the "axion" scale. This framework has two advantages: it provides a natural explanation for the dark matter's velocity at the moment of electron-positron annihilation, and it suggests that the dark matter's homogeneity and isotropy at large scales might be attributed to the cosmic inflation's caustic effect. Furthermore, this framework predicts that the dark matter's homogeneity and isotropy might be compromised by the post-inflationary perturbation effects, resulting in inhomogeneous and anisotropic dark matter distributions at smaller scales. Finally, this framework offers a solution to the long-standing problem of dark matter's halo virialization by hypothesizing that the dark matter's inhomogeneities are not confined to the halos but rather exist throughout the entire dark matter environment. The proposed framework is a universal, high-energy theory that the standard model is a part of, and it is consistent with the observed dark matter phenomena in various astronomical systems. In particular, it is possible that the heavy neutrino decays into standard model particles such as photons or dark photons in the galaxy centers, and the resulting signatures might be detectable by the Chandra X-ray telescope. Additionally, this framework suggests that the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment might be capable of detecting the heavy neutrino's direct decay into standard model particles. Finally, this framework raises the possibility that the ATLAS and CMS particle collider experiments might be able to detect the heavy neutrino's indirect decay into standard model particles. In particular, if the heavy neutrino's mass is less than one third of the Higgs mass, it is possible that the experimental data might be collected within the first few years of the HL-LHC run. Therefore, it is conceivable that the ongoing and upcoming particle collider experiments might provide concrete evidence for or against this theoretical framework in the near future

In contemporary computing systems, randomness is heavily relied upon by machine learning algorithms and cryptocurrency mining operations, among others. Typically, hardware random number generators are employed to acquire high-quality random numbers; yet, their expense and reliance on external components hinder integration. Consequently, a prevalent solution involves utilizing specialized, power-hungry circuits or utilizing side-channel effects from existing hardware, which often boils down to a costly or impractical solution. This paper introduces TuRaN, a novel method for generating true random numbers by harnessing supply voltage instability affecting nearby SRAM cells. TuRaN operates at ordinary SRAM access speeds, necessitates no additional components, and consumes minimal area, all while requiring merely a single input, namely the SRAM column read address. By leveraging the inherent volatility of SRAM storage, TuRaN can generate up to 16K random bits per second on a typical client device, which is sufficient for low-latency applications and has been validated across various processes, architectures, and usage scenarios. Moreover, TuRaN incurs negligible performance overhead and exhibits significant energy savings capabilities when used in malware-driven attacks on cryptocurrency mining applications. In summary, TuRaN is an efficient and innovative approach to 1) producing genuine random numbers at SRAM speeds, 2) minimizing area usage, and 3) maximizing energy savings while maintaining notable read latency, all while being extremely easy to integrate in existing hardware. Its randomized output can be leveraged in various applications, whereas its underscaled SRAM bootstrap capability holds promising potential for future research in SRAM-based hardware architectures. Conclusion: TuRaN is an efficient and innovative approach to 1) producing genuine random numbers at SRAM speeds, 2) minimizing area usage, and 3) maintaining low latency with notable read latency, all while being easy to integrate in existing hardware. Additionally, its randomized output holds potential for future research in hardware-based random number generation. In this research, a novel approach based on causal physical kernels is proposed to evaluate Feynman integrals. By applying a parameter integral transformation, a general framework is obtained that can be used to define a real function for any Feynman integral. This approach is based on the principle that the parameter integral converges when the momentum goes to infinity. When the parameter is set to one, this framework yields a real function solution to the original Feynman integral. While this new approach is general and applies to any Feynman integral, it is not a direct solution to the original integral as the parameter integral needs to be solved numerically. Despite this limitation, this approach offers several benefits, including the ability to apply Monte-Carlo methods to provide a numerical solution to Feynman integrals. By doing so, this method offers an alternative to traditional methods that rely on expansion series or harmonic polylogarithms. The research provides an in-depth comparison between this new approach and existing methods such as Brent-SignChange and ARIZT, highlighting its benefits while also addressing potential issues including numerical issues with divergent integrals, accuracy concerns, and the computational efficiency. Furthermore, this research introduces a set of metrics, including the accuracy per computation, that can be used to numerically validate the results and provide a level of uncertainty for the solution. The findings, including the results for the four-loop case, demonstrate that this approach is viable and efficient. The numerical results are provided for the ABEL, FEYNHELF, and TIDD integrals, among others. The code used for the numerical evaluation is publicly available under the GNU Public License version 3.0. We investigate various types of phase transitions in matter, including quark, baryon, and deuteronic transitions. Utilizing generalized thermodynamic equations, we analyze the behavior of matter in diverse conditions and evaluate the impact of interquark correlations on gas-like matter in neutron stars. We also explore the potential for the emergence of distinct star types, such as composite stars consisting of quark, baryon, and deuteronic matter and stars undergoing phase transitions between these matter states. This research lays the groundwork for a thorough investigation of star masses and the possibility of detecting these exotic stars through the observation of pulsar light curves. Additionally, we anticipate that our findings will encourage the examination of other aspects of quark, baryon, and deuteron interactions in a more widespread context. We expect our results to have far-reaching implications for the extended RPA description of hadronic matter in this realm and may even pave the way for a unified description of matter and antimatter within this Sigma-Omega-Rho model, supplemented by the MIT bag model and NJL models. Furthermore, we anticipate that our findings will emerge as a substantial component of matter at extremely high densities, whereas for normal nuclear matter, the interactions are primarily governed by the Sigma model. We investigate the behavior of matter in three distinct regimes: low-density (gas-like matter), an intermediate density region, and high-density matter. In the low-density regime, which is far removed from nuclear matter, we notice a significant impact of interactions on matter behavior, whereas in the high-density region, the matter behavior is predominantly governed by quark dynamics. Notably, at an intermediate density region, situated between normal nuclear matter and the quark phase, we notice a diminution in the interquark correlation impact. We identify deuteronic matter as the most susceptible to interactions within this matter state while quark matter remains relatively insensitive to interactions. Furthermore, we observe that baryonic matter exhibits a moderate sensitivity to interactions. Additionally, we predict the occurrence of a transition from baryonic to deuteric matter while supposing that normal nuclear matter transitions into the baryonic phase. Furthermore, we notice a significant impact of interactions on neutron star matter when it undergoes a transition from the quark phase to gas-like matter.

For deep learning models, the issue of complexity control has received relatively little attention, particularly since many studies demonstrate that complex models are often capable of achieving superior outcomes, and straightforward architectures with high geometric complexity are then deemed less effective. For instance, the sequence of operations in neural networks is often comparable to an infimum tree, a type of binary tree, and geometric complexity is defined by the length of the shortest path in this tree, which is typically referred to as the tree dimension. It has been observed that certain architectures are preferred over more complex ones even though they perform poorly in downstream tasks, and it has been hypothesized that parameter sparsity might be a major factor behind this phenomenon. Our experiments demonstrate that a straightforward approach of character-level data augmentation yields accurate AEG results, outperforming non-augmented baselines and achieving comparable results with state-of-the-art methods requiring sophisticated feature engineering and extensive training data. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented in this paper.
Our objective is to develop a practical anonymity solution for a decentralized cryptocurrency, capable of supporting thousands of transactions per block and providing users with secure stealth addressing capabilities.

A critical flaw in some quantum key exchange protocols has been discovered, allowing for the possibility of eavesdropping without being detected. This vulnerability arises when both the main and decoy states used in the transmission process exhibit non-fixated phases. If an eavesdropper intercepts the signal, a phase randomizer within the system may introduce random phases to the phases of the main and decoy states during the transmission process. As a result, the probability distribution of the signal states' phases will shift, enabling an eavesdropper to estimate the key with a certain probability while evading detection. Due to this weakness, an eavesdropper may choose to intercept the signal, ultimately hindering the security of the QKE system. To rectify this issue, we propose two possible solutions, thereby improving the robustness of the QKE system used in conjunction with phase randomization. Specifically, introducing a non-fixated source, thereby breaking the correlation between the phases of the signal states, or utilizing a more complex phase distribution across both the main and decoy states could help eliminate this vulnerability and enhance the reliability of the QKE system. These potential fixes were evaluated through numerical analysis and found to yield positive results in various scenarios. With these potential fixes in place, the probability with which an eavesdropper may intercept the signal without being detected is remarkably low. Recent research has demonstrated the effectiveness of in-context learning with large language models, involving selecting specific training data and task instructions on a case-by-case basis.  Nevertheless, little is known about how varying the source of the initial training data impacts its achievement.  In this study, we used eight distinct training datasets for different natural language tasks and examined their influence on the achievement of in-context learning with a 48Gbps language model.  Our analysis indicates that employing training data sourced from the internet leads to better outcomes across the board, as compared to a more limited, professionally curated dataset, even though both were equally effective in traditional supervised learning scenarios.  Moreover, when leveraging a broader range of diverse training datasets, internet-sourced data yielded significantly superior performance compared to a single large dataset of professionally curated content.  Finally, our findings also reveal that the achievement gains associated with internet-sourced training data are largely resistant to augmentation techniques designed to expand professional datasets.  Notably, our research focuses exclusively on the impact of the initial training dataset, as opposed to subsequent fine-tuning, and our findings highlight the need for more in-depth research into data sourcing in the context of in-context learning.  Our code is publicly accessible via this GitHub repository: https://github.com/HostZero/LargestLM-inContext and the full version of this paper can be viewed at arXiv, document number arXiv:2202.008106.

Discrepancies between theoretical predictions and observed data for certain processes involving the elements b and c are investigated. The analysis focuses on the underlying source of these discrepancies, specifically whether they stem from the effects of CP-violation or imperfect theoretical modeling. The investigation reveals that current data on tree-level processes such as B->D*tau nu and B->D tau nu do suggest the presence of significant CP-violation, especially when taking into account the results from angular observables in these processes. However, the findings also indicate the presence of considerable uncertainties in the theoretical predictions, particularly with respect to radiative corrections and final-state interactions. The study emphasizes the need for further experimental and theoretical research to refine the understanding of these phenomena. The investigation also reveals the presence of discrepancies between theoretical predictions and observed data for processes that are sensitive to radiative corrections, specifically the process B->K star tau nu. The study suggests that these discrepancies could be attributed to the effects of unaccounted-for long-range effects in the final states as well as to challenges inherent in the theoretical modeling of the process. The analysis highlights the potential of these phenomena to provide insights into the broader mechanisms of CP-violation in the Standard Model, specifically the electroweak sector, and the presence of CP-violation in new physics scenarios. We've derived previously unpublished high-loop string scattering amplitudes in a bosonic string theory using a specific duality approach. This approach, based on a residual symmetry of the string, yields a general formula for string scattering amplitudes. This formula is consistent with the Gross conjecture, providing a mathematical explanation for the pattern. Additionally, the derived amplitudes align with the string field theory approach of IZ. The presence of loop-dependent factors in the scattering amplitudes, similar to those in the beta function, implies that the Gelfand-Krylov-Lids majorization could play a crucial role in solving the string spectrum. The duality approach can be applied to other sectors of the superstring theory. However, the direct extension to the fermionic string sector is complicated by the disappearance of the residual symmetry. Nevertheless, the approach may facilitate a re-examination of the fermionic string case. The research indicates that the duality approach is suitable for the sectors IIA and IIB, which can be understood through the dualities AdS/CFT and DSF/DGF. To effectively manage the vast and unpredictable resources within a 5G network, a more automated and decentralized approach is necessary. This study introduces a novel central network management system, which employs an optimization-driven decision making process to manage 5G radio resources in a distributed manner. To achieve this, we develop a management framework consisting of multiple management domains, each managed by a central unit, and utilize a multi-agent optimization algorithm to facilitate communication and resource allocation across these domains. Furthermore, we propose a dynamic resource allocation strategy to address problems of power allocation, user scheduling, and cell selection. Our solution ensures that each cell provides the best possible service to users through a distributed strategy, which is managed by the central unit, resulting in an efficient and sustainable resource allocation. Our findings show that this approach outperforms existing methods in terms of minimizing the loss in users' achievable sum data rate and a metric called SRE, which indicates the reliability of the network's resource allocation. This is achieved while maintaining decentralized and autonomous radio resource management. The details of our method, including its flow and logic, are provided and used to obtain these results. Our study assumes a single cell per management domain for simplicity, which we plan to relax in future studies. The performance of our approach, characterized by its average loss in users' achievable sum data rate and SRE, is quantified for different 5G scenarios. Our study shows that a central network management approach, employed in conjunction with a decentralized 5G radio resource management approach, results in an efficient and sustainable resource allocation. To obtain these results, we propose a management framework consisting of multiple management domains, each managed by a central unit, and utilize a multi-agent optimization algorithm to facilitate communication and resource allocation across these domains. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of applying a central network management approach to enable sustainable radio resource management in 5G networks. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we evaluate its performance, characterized by its average loss in users' achievable sum data rate and a metric called SRE, for different 5G scenarios. A method for voice synthesis without language knowledge, based on auditory units, is introduced. It employs unsupervised transcript data, obtained from human listeners, to generate speech. This approach relies on human perception to group speech into meaningful units, and uses transcripts from these units to train a neural network for voice synthesis. Without access to language-based transcription data, we develop an unsupervised audio segmentation technique to identify these units from a metric that detects similarities within speech. Although it requires a limited amount of labeled data for fine-tuning, the method excels in voice synthesis without language knowledge, and even outperforms a similar model with transcription data in certain aspects. Furthermore, it surpasses state-of-the-art voice synthesis models based on language knowledge in certain metrics, and achieves a comparable performance in others. A demonstration of this approach can be found online at https://perceptual-auditory-units.github.io/. The code and data used for this research are available at https://github.com/perceptual-auditory-units/PAU and https://github.com/perceptual-auditory-units/NAU_100. respectively. A dataset derived from the Perceptual Auditory Units consists of human-transcribed auditory units and associated neologisms, and can be accessed at https://www.couldbelegion.com/PAU/. The team behind the Perceptual Auditory Units project is based out of the University of California, Berkeley. In a test of voice quality, human listeners were presented with speech synthesized by a neural network based on either the Perceptual Auditory Units or a benchmark dataset, and were asked to identify the more natural-sounding example. It was found that the Perceptual Auditory Units-extracted transcripts resulted in a lower error rate in this task, and also that the team's unsupervised audio segmentation technique compared favorably to a method based on language-based transcription in this metric. A novel optimization approach is presented, which comprises multiple complex sub-problems that are easier to solve but still offer accurate predictions through data-driven modeling. By employing a data-driven method to approximate non-linear terms on candidate solutions from the previous stage, this multi-step strategy ensures precise results by correcting approximate values in each iteration. Initially, a planning task is divided into multiple simpler tasks based on spatial or temporal divisions, for solvability and data processing ease. Each task is an optimization problem with its unique set of constraints and variables, some of which are shared with other tasks to increase efficiency. To expedite solution processing, these optimization problems are relaxed, easing constraints on variable relationships while maintaining task-specific requirements. A new data-driven approximation technique is proposed, which estimates non-linear costs using previous solution data and neighboring point information, thereby accounting for non-linearity in a relaxed problem. Once all optimization problems are solved, a final trajectory is generated by implementing a variable sharing policy, which facilitates data reuse and efficient variable management. To test this new approach, a mobile robot motion planning task is simulated over real terrain with varying degrees of terrain smoothness, which influences non-linearity in the motion planning problem. The resulting algorithm is compared with other optimization-based motion planning techniques and shown to offer substantially improved solution processing times with minimal impact on final quality, as measured by a distance metric. Moreover, this new approach is data-efficient, requiring only a single set of data to accurately model non-linear costs for the entire planning problem. By contrast, other optimization-based planning techniques require more frequent data collection for non-linear cost modeling, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. As a result, this new approach is shown to be a superior alternative to other optimization-based planning techniques, with its improved solution processing times and enhanced data efficiency features. The proposed algorithm is now a high-performance tool for mobile robot motion planning, which was developed using a publicly available package for optimization-based planning. The integration of this new approach, which was described through a series of theoretical contributions, is shown to offer improved performance, which can be accessed through its official repository for evaluation. The code repository, which is now freely available, contains the necessary information for reproducing the performance results shown in the accompanying figures, including repository links, code usage instructions, and evaluation metrics. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method in a scenario resembling a decentralized teaching system and find it to be more adaptable and efficient than other approaches. The hydrodynamic model's puller components play a crucial role in reducing initial-state vitality within experiments such as the RHIC's PHENIX and STAR, as well as the LHC's ALICE. This is achieved through the transfer of momentum from the pullers to the fireball, which occurs due to the hydrodynamic flow field. It has been demonstrated that the magnitude of this effect is substantial, accounting for approximately 50% of the total initial-state entropy reduction within the ALICE collisions at a specific impact energy. This process also influences the final particle yields, particularly in smaller systems, where the presence of pullers significantly impacts radial flow and, consequently, particle yields. Our analysis reveals that pullers can collectively explain the observed trends of low-density aerodynamic puller effects, entropy reduction, and radial flow across various energies and system sizes. This analysis also underscores the necessity of incorporating hydrodynamic pullers into initial-state vitality models, even when entropy reduction is primarily driven by other factors. Pullers are essential even in the case of minimum bias events, where the dominant loss of entropy is counteracted by an equal amount of momentum transfer. This gives rise to a significant amount of entropy reduction only above a certain threshold of the initial-state vitality. Our work thus lays the foundation for future research, where the focus will be on thoroughly examining the interplay between hydrodynamic pullers, initial-state vitality, and particle yields within relativistic nuclear collisions. This will help in fully understanding the rapid thermalization process that facilitates the smooth transition from non-equilibrium to hydrodynamic flow. Our analysis also raises important questions about the potential existence of hydrodynamic pullers in free-field simulations, such as VNI, which do not incorporate hydrodynamic flow, and the implications of puller-free simulations for the equilibration process in high-energy nuclear collisions. Furthermore, we propose to extend our research to explore the existence of hydrodynamic pullers in free-field simulations using a finite entropy decrease in small systems as a potential probe. This would enable us to delve into the fundamental aspects of hydrodynamic pullers, initial-state vitality, and particle yields, thereby significantly expanding our understanding of the complex non-equilibrium dynamics involved in the initial-state vitality phase and the equilibration process. Finally, our analysis highlights the need for future relativistic nuclear collision experiments, particularly those focused on smaller system sizes, where the distinct effects of hydrodynamic pullers on radial flow and particle yields can be thoroughly scrutinized and potentially linked to the existence of pullers in non-equilibrium and hydrodynamic flow

We conducted an in-depth analysis of a unique protostellar system, which exhibits unusually powerful jets for an early stage of star formation. Our goal was to determine the potential impact of these jets on the formation of surrounding circumstellar material and the emergence of a lower-velocity outflow. To this end, we created high-resolution models of the interaction between the protostellar jet and the surrounding material. Our calculations revealed that the energy from the protostellar jet is primarily utilized in driving a high-velocity shock wave through the surrounding material. Conversely, the formation of a lower-velocity outflow depends on the interaction with a rotating disk. The results of our simulations indicate that the high-speed jet cannot efficiently drive a low-speed outflow. Rather, a lower-speed outflow can only be generated if it interacts with a rotating structure, supporting the notion that a bound accretion disk is required for efficient low-speed outflow generation. Our findings also suggest that high-speed jets may not be the primary drivers of low-speed outflows in a large portion of star-forming systems. Alternatively, a mechanism such as disk rotation or other processes must be responsible for generating low-speed outflows, especially at speeds below 100 km/s. The solar radiation pressure parameter, which measures the ratio of an object's acceleration to the solar gravitational acceleration, experiences fluctuations due to the changing distance from the Sun that can lead to resonances. These resonances cause irregularities in an object's orbital path that have been observed in near-Earth space, which has sparked research into the behavior of close approaches. Existing theories primarily focus on the first-order mean motion resonance, whereas higher-order resonances remain less understood. This study aims to uncover the behavior of semi-secular resonances resulting from the combination of mean motions and their corresponding frequencies, which arise at specific distances from the Sun. To achieve this, the authors develop an approximate expression based on the characteristics of the solar radiation pressure profile and verify it through comparative modeling of orbital trajectories. Notably, the objects considered in this study are of artificial origin with masses less than 200 kg, which are subject to the effects of gravitational acceleration, atmospheric drag, and other external factors. The results of this investigation can inform the design of spacecraft missions by accurately estimating their orbital paths. Furthermore, the conceptual approach may also be applicable to natural objects under similar environmental influences. We investigate how light-matter interactions behave under transformations that change their state, preserving certain properties. In a theoretical model using tight-binding methods and based on electronic wavefunctions, we find a general condition that ensures light-matter interactions remain the same regardless of the state change. This condition has a straightforward application in simple models with localized orbitals and reduces to a known rule for a specific type of state change. Our findings are validated by applying them to a range of materials, including a 2D graphene sheet, a TMD layer, a silicon crystal, and a silicon phosphide crystal, and we observe that their electronic structures obtained through TB and first-principle calculations match closely. Furthermore, we confirm that the electronic transitions predicted by our TB model align with those obtained through more detailed calculations for the specific materials. In a final step, we demonstrate how our findings can be used to create and visualize electronic states with desired properties using an example. Our work lays the groundwork for developing innovative light-driven technologies. By establishing the underlying theoretical framework to describe light-matter interactions in a consistent and predictable way, we make the underlying mathematical concept of state transparency more approachable for materials scientists. Additionally, we propose a practical method for applying a specific mathematical concept to a broader class of tight-binding models based on localized orbitals. Finally, we identify potential practical applications of our theoretical model, such as controlling and inducing optical phenomena in materials. Our investigation into the preservation of light-matter interactions leads to a fundamental insight into the underlying physics, revealing a deeper connection between the electronic structures of materials and the characteristics of light that interact with them. In a broader context, our work represents a significant contribution to the broader field of contemporary condensed matter research, where researchers continuously seek to develop new theoretical frameworks that describe complex materials in terms of simple mathematical concepts. Our TB model, for example, reduces complex problems associated with light-matter interactions into manageable equations based on orbital interactions, thereby enabling the prediction of electronic states with desired properties and the preservation of light-matter interactions under specific state changes. Our work also represents an important application of the mathematical concept of unitary equivalence, which has far-reaching implications in diverse fields such as mathematics, physics, and computer science to the understanding of light-matter interactions. Lastly, our investigation into the preservation of light-matter interactions also leads to a significant practical application, as our TB model allows us to develop and create innovative light-driven technologies by harnessing the collective properties of electronic states, which have become a crucial factor in the development of next-generation energy technologies

Additionally, two methods are presented to construct classical confidence squares for both parameters, yielding results in the form of lower bounds only. Furthermore, this paper examines the behavior of the proposed methods as the sample size increases, and suggests alternative approaches for larger data sets. The methods are demonstrated using R examples. The complete R code is provided in the supplementary materials. 

The main contributions of this paper are primarily focused on developing methods to construct classical confidence squares for the parameters of a Cauchy distribution, an effort in line with the original work of Stein (1935) Steins (1949). The proposed methods employ a quantitative assessment of the parameter square's coverage area, an approach inspired by the Chandra Pokarabelski theorem. The behavior of the square's boundary as the sample size increases is also systematically analyzed. The proposed methods exhibit desirable asymptotic properties, including smoothness and concentration. The confidence squares proposed in this paper can serve as a useful approach for targeting a range of parameters, including skewness, kurtosis, and other measures of asymmetry or distribution shape, in addition to the location and scale parameters of a Cauchy distribution. The Cauchy distribution's flexible shape has led to its widespread application across numerous disciplines. The location parameter $\gamma_1$ represents a parameter of interest in many fields, while the scale parameter $\gamma_2$ is often a source of additional variability. The proposed methods for constructing confidence squares can be useful in a variety of contexts, including targeting unknown means of independent samples in a normal distribution, or the standard deviations of mixed normal distributions.

In the field of basket trials, where multiple subgroups are studied simultaneously, we examine the issue of determining sample sizes. Our approach incorporates Bayesian principles to mitigate the challenges typically associated with these trials, such as limited knowledge of treatment differences within subgroups, and the interdependence of these subgroups. We propose two Bayesian methods for sample size calculation that allow information to be shared across subgroups. One method uses a Bayesian covariance matrix, while the other employs a sensitivity analysis approach and both methods provide accurate estimates of effect sizes as well as type I and II errors. We compare our approaches to traditional frequency-based methods through simulations and reveal that these techniques yield more conservative results for treatment differences affecting multiple subgroups at once, while producing more accurate results for null hypothesis testing and accuracy in estimating effect sizes. Our approaches also enable a deeper understanding of uncertainties associated with effect size estimates via posterior distribution quantification. Our methodology borrows heavily from the concepts of Steiner design, and we demonstrate how our methods can be applied in a real-world scenario involving a basket trial studying multiple subgroups of patients with solid tumors. This work introduces a cutting-edge motion control strategy based on sequential loop closing that enhances accuracy in high-precision motion systems. Unlike conventional continuous-time linear parameter varying (LPV) controllers, which typically require extensive and challenging linear parameter dependency (LPD) evaluation, our proposed controller leverages the sequential nature of the system to facilitate efficient and realistic parameter updates between movement segments. This allows the system to operate within a predetermined safety margin, ensuring secure and efficient motion. This innovative approach is showcased through successful application to a state-of-the-art aerial imaging system, demonstrating its capability to achieve superior performance while maintaining system safety. Furthermore, our study highlights a heretofore unexplored connection between LPV control and sequential estimation, which is expected to garner more research attention in the future. This research aims to contribute to the pursuit of precise motion systems by addressing challenges in the field and presenting feasible solutions to related problems. As such, key findings are outlined, along with recommendations for further investigation. While registering full volumes is relatively straightforward, partial-to-partial registration presents significant challenges due to missing data, deformation, and part ambiguities. To overcome these issues, a novel, learning-based approach called Partial Registration Network (PRNet) is proposed, designed specifically for partial-to-partial registration tasks. PRNet employs a self-supervised, consistent-based loss function that enables the mapping of unseen partial volumes to a reference reference, thereby capturing local deformations more accurately. Furthermore, PRNet incorporates a cyclic consistency loss to account for arbitrary partial data cropping, eliminating the need for ground-truth cropping and demonstrating superior results compared to existing methods in the medical segmentation and registration community. The evaluation was conducted on three publicly available datasets: ATLAS brain, a cat brain, and a shoulder joint, showcasing PRNet's capabilities and superiority on diverse datasets across various scales and complexities. The source code for PRNet is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/JD-0/PRNet. The dataset can be downloaded from https://cmiccenters.org/brainneuron-Atlas. Visualizations and results can be found at https://jd-0.github.io/PRNet. The empirical results reveal PRNet's state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of registration tasks, surpassing other methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and generalizability. The researchers successfully transferred the PRNet model to a new, unseen dataset, achieving PRNet_MST, a pre-trained model that demonstrates exceptional generalizability and serves as a strong baseline for future comparison. The study's key contributions include the PRNet framework, along with multiple valuable insights, such as the efficacy of self-supervised learning for partial registration tasks, the critical importance of cyclic consistency loss, and the merit of evaluating registration methods using a dataset unrelated to the model's training, which significantly enhances the robustness and reliability of the method. The researchers also pointed out potential weaknesses, such as the over-reliance on the atlas, the difficulty in interpreting the learned partial cropping, and the limited integration of the deformation field in the medical simulation. The work presents a promising approach to addressing these challenges, thereby opening up new areas of research, such as the incorporation of the deformation field in the simulation process, the elimination of the atlas through integration with prior knowledge, and the development of a simulation-based evaluation criterion that reflects the clinicians' actual decision-making processes. A highly efficient method for analyzing time-resolved data is developed, allowing it to be processed either as response surfaces or in high-dimensional trajectories. By treating an algorithmic step as an optimization problem, we ensure its accuracy, thereby addressing the issue of data precision lacking sufficient detail. This approach is inspired by related techniques in machine learning, particularly those with a trajectory framework. It is successful in inverting data from both theoretical and real experiments in diverse fields such as quantum physics and biology. Additionally, we propose an alternative technique that uses an adaptive search strategy to process data, offering a faster and more efficient option. Both methods outperform traditional techniques in handling data imperfections, thereby providing a better understanding of the analyzed systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability of these algorithms to analyze multiple time-resolved data, thereby revealing hidden processes. The efficiency of these algorithms is evaluated by measuring their computational speed and applying a scalable strategy to process data, thereby making them suitable for practical use. The development of a user-friendly software for performing these calculations, named HOSS, is also presented. It is comprised of a modular framework that integrates several advanced algorithms, thereby enhancing their stability and making them accessible to a wider audience. To evaluate the longitudinal and transverse allocations of momentum in mesons, we introduce an concept called allocation amplitude, which allows us to calculate the proportion of momentum allocated to specific directions within a particle. Using this framework, we examine the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons and derive equations to determine allocation amplitudes using Bethe-Salpeter wave functions. By applying this in a specific instantaneous version of the Bethe-Salpeter equation, we are able to derive explicit expressions for allocation amplitudes in the context of massless Bethe-Salpeter wave functions consisting of Dirac strings and loop components. The results we obtain are then compared with corresponding gauge theories. Interestingly, our findings for $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons indicate that a significant portion of a meson's momentum is not in the direction of the momentum exchange during interaction processes. The degree to which a meson's momentum is not in the direction of the momentum exchange varies depending on the mass of the meson and its constituent parts. Notably, our study also reveals that when a $D^*$ meson interacts with a scalar partner through a force, not only does the momentum allocation change but the direction of the allocation also varies with the mass of the exchanged particle. Furthermore, our research indicates that gauge interactions contribute significantly to the allocation of momentum in mesons; however, the overall shape of the allocation function is primarily dictated by the mass of the meson and its constituent parts rather than the interaction mechanism. Lastly, our study also demonstrates that the notion of a meson being composed of one valent particle and a purely virtual particle component does not significantly impact the allocation of momentum in the direction of the momentum exchange; rather, the allocation patterns of momentum in the direction of the momentum exchange and perpendicular to it are predominantly determined by the mass of the meson and its constituent parts. A new method called Instance Division of Unlabeled Modalities (IDUM) leverages a generative adversarial network to segment a diverse dataset into distinct groups, minimizing overlap between them. Unlike previous approaches that segment from labeled data, IDUM deals with the scenario where no labels are available. It can also handle a range of data modalities and ensures each group has a reasonable number of samples, preventing over-segmentation. To achieve this, IDUM combines two key components - a cyclic loss and a special partitioning strategy, resulting in a unique training protocol. The effectiveness of IDUM is validated by applying it to multiple real-world challenges, such as image segmentation and unsupervised cross-domain data partitioning. The technique demonstrates superior performance and more plausible segmentations compared to current techniques in these areas. The authors also provide a deeper understanding of IDUM's performance by visualizing its generative model and analyzing the structure of created groups. The new approach supports a wide range of applications involved in multiple unlabelled data modalities and can be used to analyze various unknown factors in such datasets. Predicting future actions of complex agents is a challenging task in multiple fields.  We address this challenge by developing a novel method which utilizes the capabilities of Recurrent Neural Networks to forecast agent movement.  A key component of our model involves feature extraction through a Radial Basis Function kernelized transformation of RNN encoded features.  In order to accurately forecast movements, we train our model to output a distribution of potential actions rather than a single outcome.  This approach results in our model generating a diverse set of distribution parameters, including location, velocity, and motion direction.  Through testing on a simulated environment, we demonstrate improved movement predictions utilizing sight and sound data from a common video game-like scenario.  Notably, our model achieves enhanced prediction accuracy by incorporating sight information over the use of sound alone.  The main advantages of our model include its flexibility, capability of learning diverse features, and provision of multiple movement possibilities.  While this model may not be suitable for high-speed high-dimensional systems due to computational complexity, it exhibits excellent performance in the tested scenario and provides a valuable contribution to the field of movement forecasting.  Code is publicly available at https://github.com/csujia/Kernelized-RNN.  Evaluation videos are posted at https://youtu.be/4s5jU0GdI1M and https://youtu.be/ajC2V3LTL9Q. We modeled a rare and significant stellar eruption in the UV range using a sophisticated model for cool, starry objects. In 1985, astronomers observed a remarkable increase in the UV emissions from the nearby star AD Leo, reaching near-Earth intensities. Our sophisticated model accounted for the interaction between the stellar photosphere and the surrounding plasma caused by the eruption. The simulation revealed two distinct phases: an initial short-term peak and a prolonged decrease in emissions. The short-term peak may be attributed to the rapid cooling of electrons as they transitioned from the stellar atmosphere to interstellar space, while the prolonged decrease in emissions could result from the absorption of light by the vast number of electrons released in the eruption. Our model's predictions via the UV Optical Electron Counting (UVOECC) method aligned well with actual observations, demonstrating that the eruption injected approximately 1.85 × 10^41 electrons into the interstellar space per second. Furthermore, we estimated that the eruption lasted for approximately 180 seconds or about 3 minutes in total. By incorporating the UVOECC method into our model, we were able to estimate the size and energy released during the eruption, calculating that the order of the disruption was around 41.3 kilometers. The integration of our model and the UVOECC approach provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and analyzing space-related electromagnetic disturbances. The incorporation of our time-dependent model may facilitate real-time electromagnetic storm forecasting, while the UVOECC approach potentially links solar and stellar eruptions to Geodesic Spike and similar phenomena, potentially revealing any underlying patterns or correlations. We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons within the context of nearly G2-manifolds. A nearly G2-manifold can be viewed as a complex vector bundle equipped with a specific Hermitian metric, a connection, and an almost G2-structure that satisfies specific compatibility conditions. Our research focuses on how these components can be modified simultaneously under variation of the nearly G2-structure. In addition, we establish relationships between the deformation spaces of G2-instantons and those of related objects, such as connections and the almost G2-structure itself, within the context of quasi-morphisms of the group algebra of SO(7). A significant deformation anomaly is found, which implies that a specific condition of simplicity cannot be preserved through deformation. However, this anomaly can be resolved by introducing deformed versions of instantons, allowing for the preservation of simplicity. A direct result of this reasoning is the discovery that the space of deformation-analytic G2-instantons on a nearly G2-manifold is isomorphic to the space of connections, weighted by the first Chern class of the associated bundle. Our findings can also be extended to the domain of 7-dimensional nearly hyperholomorphic contact manifolds, which possess a distinct structure related to G2-manifolds. A key connection between these two domains is facilitated through the application of the Fefferman-Graham expansion technique. This technique allows us to gain a deeper understanding of the space of semi-regular points within the deformation theory of G2-instantons, which, in turn, enables the resolution of a long-standing conjecture regarding the space of regular points. This approach also opens up new avenues for research, such as the broadening of instanton theory to encompass a wider range of structures, including deformed and non-deformed versions of G2-manifolds, which would constitute an extension of the realm of hyperkaehler geometry. Furthermore, this research may contribute significantly to the development of a generalized Fefferman-Graham theorem, which would allow the reconstruction of a G2-manifold from its 8-dimensional distribution, armed with essential information regarding its obstructions. In addition, this work may provide a solution to the anomaly, which would enable the preservation of simplicity in the deformed version of G2-instantons, thus establishing a direct relationship between the space of deformation-analytic G2-instantons and the space of connections, weighted by the first Chern class of the associated bundle, for all nearly G2-manifolds.

This paper delves into the study of large $p$-core $p'$-configurations in the context of the partition lattice under the modulus p. Noting a connection between their size growth rates and the p-residue graph walk transitivity, it investigates the p-residue graph more closely. This investigation yields a valuable conclusion: the transitivity of this graph is p-specific. Furthermore, it is shown that for any p, a big p-core p'-configuration can be divided into two distinct parts: a small core and a mixture of p-smaller core partitions. This fundamental finding opens the door for potential future research on the structure of these configurations. Additionally, some intriguing, unsolved questions are posed. One particular query concerns the feasibility of finding a big p-core p'-configuration that consists solely of partitions with a p-trivial hook length. It is proven that such a configuration exists for p = 5. This work may serve as a preliminary exploration into the realm of p-core p-configurations overall. It is hypothesized that a thorough examination of these configurations will reveal a wealth of meaningful and interesting generalizations. Lastly, some promising young mathematician awards are suggested to be established to facilitate the cultivation of outstanding young researchers in the field of combinatorics. Specifically, "The Hook Prize" and "The Partition Prize" are envisioned to be two prestigious awards that will provide essential financial support to exceptional students working on relevant projects, allowing them to present their research at prominent conferences. It is hoped that these scholarships will enhance exhibition opportunities for these students and foster further skill development in this field. Lastly, some relevant conference talks, research papers, and online content are mentioned in a separate section for further exploration. Neural network-based code completion has gained significant traction in recent years, with several frameworks and approaches being developed to tackle point cloud model maintenance. Unlike linear code structures, point clouds are non-linear and require unique handling techniques to ensure accurate model transformation and smoothing. To address this gap, we introduce a novel code completion framework called TPC that utilizes a transformation unique to the context of spatial data. To achieve this, we design a custom method involving a weighted Gaussian filter, which enables seamless integration with code blocks. Our innovative approach, coupled with a unique model architecture and loss function, allows TPC to surpass state-of-the-art models in accuracy while keeping a minimal number of parameters for efficient inference. As such, TPC offers superior generative performance on various evaluation metrics and outperforms competing models in both accuracy and model complexity. Comprehensive ablation studies and human evaluations further demonstrate the efficacy of TPC in supporting developers with code completion, especially when generating point cloud models. The source code of TPC is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/iic-ai/TPC.

We investigate medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, analyzing ALOHA and CSMA methods to optimize throughput and minimize the probability of collisions. Our algorithms utilize radar network performance metrics such as spectral efficiency, user drop rate, and collision probability, which we evaluate through simulations under single-cell and multi-cell scenarios. Our results show that ALOHA offers simple implementation and collision resilience, while CSMA provides near-optimal performance though requiring more complex implementation. To address this, we develop a hybrid algorithm combining ALOHA and CSMA, offering a balance between the two. Our study also identifies areas for future research and presents a possible approach for resolving collision conflicts. Additionally, we apply machine learning techniques to enhance radar network performance, specifically using the Monte Carlo method to train neural networks and an optimization technique to improve performance in single-cell scenarios. Our research demonstrates that FMCW radar networks with ALOHA and CSMA can achieve notable performance, paving the way for further machine learning applications. Finally, we illustrate the feasibility of our study through a real-world application, showing that the derived performance metrics can be utilized in a real-world setting.

Entanglement is a fundamental concept in quantum physics that has been extensively studied through various experiments. One notable area of research involves intertwined photon research, which comprises two types of phenomena: twin-photon absorption and Hong-Ou-Mandel interference. Both phenomena exhibit distinct probability patterns, resulting from the disentanglement of photons when they interact with obstacles in their path. Interestingly, these experiments showcase parallels between these phenomena and reflections of light off physical barriers. This connection inspires a new framework for understanding entangled photon research, drawing from the principles of unentangled photon research, thus providing a fresh perspective on the concept of entanglement and its role in the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiment. Furthermore, this new framework enables the derivation of the probability of finding both photons in their respective outlets, which aligns with the findings of actual Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiments. One notable prediction of this new framework is the occurrence of non-zero probability of both photons reaching the outlet '2' when the beam splitter in the HOM interference experiment is obstructed at a distance shorter than the wavelength of the photons. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
predicting knowledge graph missing facts. Building upon successful
transformer-based models for static graphs, recent developments have
applied similar techniques to temporal knowledge graphs, yielding impressive
results. However, these models have overlooked the inherent properties of
time sequences, reducing their representations to a simple extension of static
graphs. To address this limitation, we propose a new model that integrates the
features of time sequences directly into the representation learning. By
doing so, we enable the model to capture time-dependent correlations, a
key factor in modeling temporal knowledge graphs. To further enhance the model
neutrality, we employ a low-rank constraint on the entity and time features.
Experimental evaluations on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our
model surpasses state-of-the-art temporal KGC methods. Furthermore, our
post-fixing study verifies the effectiveness of our proposed time-extended
representation structure. Notably, our model achieves an impressive 36.4%
higher mean rank compared to the current best approach, achieving a mean rank of
22.0. Additionally, our model outperformed the best model in almost all other
evaluation metrics by a considerable margin on three benchmark datasets. The
code for our model is available at https://github.com/jjyang1989/Time-extension.

The EPR paradox in 1935 proposed an idea of instantaneously quantized connection between two distant events, and the negative consequences of this concept in a closed system were understood as their non-locality implications. In 1964, Bell developed a mathematical test to verify this non-locality, and the violation of this test has since become the standard indicator of non-locality. However, the EPR paradox perfectly illustrates the non-locality of quantum systems through correlation functions, and these functions can establish the validity of Bell's inequality without the need for experimentation. Nevertheless, real-world experiments with imperfect correlations often compromise this validity, rendering the inequality useless in some cases. Nonetheless, the inequality remains a crucial standard in contemporary quantum communication research, and only a single experimental setup in 2020 has successfully claimed its violation without further clarification. We examine a level dynamics approach that incorporates both vertical and horizontal connections between musical levels. This encompasses a broader level dynamics framework that can accommodate nonlocalized, harmonic pitch class distributions as input. Analyzing local frequency spectra in detail, we discover that localized tones typically occupy level bands spanning multiple pitch classes, whereas unlocalized tones occupy a single pitch class. This reveals a distinct pitch class identity for nonlocal tones. Additionally, we explore the applicability of level dynamics principles to the concept of localization, proposing a new criterion - localized sets must form contiguous level bands along the numerical level axis. This leads to an enhanced understanding of the nature of harmonic series, which we find to comprise both localized and harmonic sets. Finally, we investigate the level dynamics representation of percussive sounds, noting that they defy either localized or harmonic categorization, instead existing in a distinct third realm. This fundamental distinction highlights the necessity of a refined definition of localization, one that doesn't rely on the exclusion of unlocalized sounds, but rather recognizes them as a valid entity. Our study introduces a level dynamics based method for classifying sounds into pitch classes, providing a meaningful and structured organization of the spectral domain according to pitch class. This leads to a fresh perspective on the underlying structure of auditory perception, one that we believe will prove valuable in generating music. Furthermore, our work serves as a companion piece to "Revisiting localization criteria," addressing specific concerns raised in that study and offering a more comprehensive understanding of the level dynamics framework and its applications. This study can also be seen as a part of a broader collection of works examining level dynamics, a theoretical framework that seeks to describe musical harmony through the numerical level axis, drawing parallels with chromaticism. We define and study two new concepts: rigidity and charmability, which are topological and dynamical characteristics of certain groups. By demonstrating topological characteristics, such as being non-trivial, compact, simple, finitely-generated, and having a certain structure, we classify which groups exhibit rigidity. Additionally, we define and classify charmable groups under various conditions. Notably, we derive conditions under which rigidity and charmability are equivalent for certain groups. Furthermore, we classify all finitely-generated arithmetic groups that satisfy these conditions, and explore dynamical systems related to these groups. Specifically, for arithmetic groups of rank 1, we show that rigidity is equivalent to charmability, and describe the dynamics of associated action angelic transformations. We also prove that rigidity characterizes (1) hyperbolic groups, (2) finitely-generated commutative groups, (3) finitely-generated groups with a solvable abelian torsion, and (4) certain double-monoid groups. On the other hand, we define and classify charmable groups of arithmetic type under various conditions, and explore dynamical systems related to these groups, such as the action of the integers on certain spaces constructed from them. We also investigate a variant of charmability, which we call susceptibility, and derive conditions under which susceptibility implies rigidity and charmability. Lastly, we classify all finitely-generated arithmetic groups that satisfy these conditions, and explore dynamical systems related to these groups, such as the action of the integers on certain spaces constructed from them. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach centered on influence metrics, leveraging the leading eigenvector of a graph constructed from long-term data trails. This technique is demonstrated on a test case and applied to real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately pinpoint clusters beyond short-term forecasting. Our framework expands the realm of influence-based clustering while providing a transparent, theoretically grounded framework for a wide range of applications. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the derivation of predictive models for each identified cluster, enhancing the practical value of this method. A registered operator, represented as a matrix relative to a given basis, governs the behavior of a finite-dimensional system. However, this operator can be embodied in a more comprehensive, infinitely dimensional system which retains all properties of its original counterpart. This larger system is characterized by an infinitely large, infinite-dimensional space. Infinitely extended dimensional systems can provide insightful alternatives to traditional finite-dimensional systems when seeking solutions. Nonetheless, such systems are often challenged by the issue of defining and evaluating solutions, owing to the vast complexity of their infinite dimensions. Notably, this issue persists even in the context of autonomous systems. In this paper, we address this question: can we define and evaluate solutions for autonomous, infinite-dimensional systems? Moving forward, we highlight practical implications and potential applications of our findings. This study aims to stimulate further discussion and exploration of operator theory in relation to autonomous, infinite-dimensional systems. To contribute to this endeavor, we draw inspiration from the fundamental works of Poincaré, LaSalle, and Kurzweil. Wotzkos and Tao proposed a novel form of freeness denoted as "freeness of type $B$" by Bao, Krishnapur, and Yin. This concept is illustrated by demonstrating the freeness of type $B$ between consecutive Wigner matrices and a matrix featuring iid Gaussian entries above the main diagonal. Additionally, an examination of Wigner matrices reveals the validity of a conditionally independent of type $B$ hypothesis. Consequently, this can be utilized to demonstrate the freeness of type $B$ for specific matrix ensembles, such as e.g., real Wigner matrices, whose spectral distributions converge to the semicircular distribution. Furthermore, an investigation of sums of random matrices, such as the sum of a Wigner matrix and a Wigner matrix with odd symmetry, also yields evidence to support the type $B$ Wigner matrix independence hypothesis. Finally, an independent analysis of sums of orthogonal matrices, such as Haar distributed matrices, reveals the spectral density of these matrices converges to a mixture of two circular laws. These findings align with a broader, unproven conjecture posed by Pazohandi and Bogdanov. Furthermore, an examination of matrices featuring iid entries, rather than Wigner matrices, fails to yield conclusive results but offers an alternative, modified hypothesis of type $B$ Wigner matrix independence. An observation of specific examples demonstrates the necessity for a $B$-Weyl or type $B$ additivity hypothesis in order to further refine the existing type $B$ Wigner matrix independence hypothesis. An independent analysis of e.g., covariance matrices also yields evidence to support the type $B$ Wigner matrix independence hypothesis, particularly in cases where the four moment cumulants of these matrices become negligible as the matrix dimension approaches infinity. This situation typically arises in scenarios such as collapse or black-hole mergers, where a desired starting state may not satisfy all possible constraints. A newly proposed method called Conformal Trajectory Self-consistent (CTSK), designed to create accurate initial conditions for matter under a conformal transformation of the metric, is explored in this study. CTSK's approach is compared to an alternative solution for unspecified modes of the metric, and both approaches are assessed against a known solution for a specific black-hole and two types of matter configurations. Furthermore, the impact of initial conditions on the final outcome of a simulation is investigated in the context of a binary black-hole merger. Our findings indicate that employing CTSK initial conditions yields a more realistic and physically accurate final spacetime, and also improves the stability and accuracy of the gravitational wave signal produced in the simulation. Building upon existing research, we establish uniqueness of solutions under specific conditions and examine uniqueness in the L^2-sense for the case when the parameter vanishes. Our work includes a relabeled version of the results' significance, along with a step-by-step reconstruction method for approximately solving the basis pursuit problem. Furthermore, we provide a series of open research questions and possible approaches for addressing them. Additionally, our unique contribution involves developing a new device, which we call 'excision of tails', that facilitates a direct construction of solutions to the basis pursuit problem through a simplified approach. Lastly, our methods and findings rely on principles from differential geometry and PDEs, as well as techniques from measure-theoretic integration. These techniques may provide new insights and approaches to tackling the basis pursuit problem, as well as broader applications across various mathematical and computational sciences. Finally, our work raises a series of new research questions and possibilities for further exploration and innovation.

The revised CPRK scheme enhances the original CPRK method's ability to effectively handle noisy data in higher dimensional systems, while maintaining its ability to efficiently reduce the issue density. The enhanced CPRK method was tested and validated through various numerical simulations conducted within high-performance computing environments. These simulations include both challenging numerical simulations and a real-world analysis of a turbulent fluid flow. The results of these experiments demonstrate the enhanced CPRK method's ability to consistently outperform the original CPRK method, particularly in multi-dimensional systems. Furthermore, the enhanced CPRK method was found to consistently produce accurate results across a wide range of step sizes, while significantly reducing issue density. The success of the enhanced CPRK method makes it an ideal solution for a broad range of applications, including the simulation of turbulent fluid flows and multi-dimensional interpolation of noisy data.
