Press-molded specimens of simulated Martian and Lunar soil were produced using a compacting pressure of 50 MPa and fired at various temperatures, ranging from 200 to 1200°C, to examine the effect of sintering heat on microstructure and mechanical properties. XRD analysis revealed that firing temperatures significantly affected the crystallization processes in both Mars and Lunar soils. At 200-400°C, a partial crystallization of Martian soil halloysite occurred, yielding strong and flexible walls, whereas Lunar soil feldspar began to crystallize, enhancing its strength. Firing between 400-600°C led to further halloysite crystallization in Martian soil and partial fusion of Lunar soil, resulting in reduced strength. Concurrently, Lunar soil feldspar reached its full crystallization, demonstrating strength increases despite microstructure deterioration, particularly at higher temperatures where Lunar soil feldspar partially melted, resulting in reduced strength in both samples. At 1200°C, both Martian and Lunar soils exhibited similar strengths and microstructures, characterized by significant strength reductions and severe microstructure damage, suggesting extensive melting in both soils. Systematic back-scattered electron imaging confirmed these findings, revealing well- consolidated, strong materials produced at 400-600°C, versus weak, porous materials produced at higher and lower firing temperatures. These results imply that pressing Martian soil requires a higher firing temperature than 400°C to achieve optimal strength, while Lunar soil can achieve optimal strength at 400°C due to its naturally occurring quartz. Additionally, pressing temperatures above 400°C are necessary for optimal Lunar soil strength, suggesting a pressing temperature of 400-600°C for both Martian and Lunar soils. These findings enable targeted 3D printing of both Martian and Lunar soils at 400-600°C to produce strong materials, even on the Moon and Mars. Further research is recommended to establish temperature controls for printing fluids and optimizing 3D-printed sample strength. Given these findings, printing temperatures below the sintering temperature of the materials are necessary for developing strong 3D-printed samples. Therefore, targeting printing temperatures below the sintering temperature of the materials is necessary for developing strong 3D-printed samples. Moreover, further research on the sintering process is suggested to develop functional 3D-printed materials, such as heat-resistant glass, with tailored mechanical and thermal properties on the Moon and Mars. Finally, these findings can contribute to developing structural systems and frameworks on other planets, including the Moon and Mars, with 3D-printed materials,

The Rayleigh-Plateau instability governs the withdrawal of a liquid from a cylindrical tube, leading to wave formation on the liquid surface. These waves can then cause the liquid to break up into droplets as the disturbance progresses. Factors such as liquid slip and gravity contribute to this instability; in the presence of liquid slip, the instability is slowed and its onset only partially affected by gravity due to delayed wave formation. A numerical model has been developed to study this instability in a scenario where a liquid is withdrawn from a tube with a small gap, and the withdrawal velocity varies gradually rather than suddenly. This model reveals that liquid slip significantly alters the instability's dynamics, affecting wave amplitude and the breakup of the liquid into droplets. Consequently, larger droplets form more slowly, and the resulting droplet size distribution is broader, leading to larger average droplet sizes when slip occurs. This effect can be harnessed to improve liquid microdropping technology. Additionally, the model confirms that dynamic slip rather than static slip is responsible for changing the Rayleigh-Plateau instability's characteristics. Finally, the model shows that when a liquid is pulled from a tube at a constant rate, the impact of slip is less pronounced than when the rate changes gradually. This demonstrates that the mechanism of dynamic slip has a more significant effect when the liquid is removed at a continuously varying velocity rather than at a constant velocity. This work, focusing on the dynamics of dynamic slip, bridges the gap between understanding dynamic slip and static slip. Moreover, it reveals that dynamic slip can be minimized by using static slip when designing liquid microdropping technology. Additionally, this work emulates the behavior of dynamic slip, a non-trivial phenomenon, through a numerical model, and such an emulation is valuable for analyzing dynamic slip in other contexts. By comparing star formation rates (SFR) from different methods, the reliability of near-infrared SFR estimates can be assessed. 24 $\mu$m and 22 $\mu$m dust emission are typically used to calculate SFR via infrared radiation, but near-infrared SFR estimates are considered more accurate as they are less sensitive to heavy dust suppression.  Theoretical models predict that the Brackett-$\gamma$ line at 2.166 $\mu$m can be an ideal measure of near-infrared SFR, although previous observations found it to be weak and unreliable.  A new study observed the strong Br$\gamma$ line in   4 nearby galaxies using the Infrared Optical Integral Constellation X-ray (IOCX) telescope, performing kinematic analysis by observing the 1.563 $\mu$m line and discovering a speed variation of up to 125 km/s.  The results from re-running SFR fitting with constraints from Br$\gamma$ were surprising, showing good agreement with other methods, suggesting that Br$\gamma$ can be a reliable method for measuring SFR, although it may need to be used in conjunction with other observations.  A survey of 8 galaxies confirmed the reliability of the Br$\gamma$ method, but an analysis of the SFR-to-metallicity relationship did not support the proposed Br$\gamma$ calibration, instead indicating that the Br$\gamma$ method may need to be adjusted with metallicity as a factor.  Further observation of the Br$\gamma$ line could help establish its utility in calibrating SFR, potentially including in external galaxies.  A novel technique involving spectral fitting with the PROFIT model could also be an effective method for extracting Br$\gamma$ line data from spectroscopy, reducing uncertainty related to the technique.  Future observations with the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope are predicted to provide precise kinematic measurements, potentially increasing the Br$\gamma$-to-Ha line ratio by a factor of 2.5, offering a promising opportunity to improve the estimation of near-infrared SFR.  A proposed observational strategy could help establish this technique, involving rapid spectroscopy of a large number of galaxies, while a model incorporating dust and stellar emission, and constrained by Br$\gamma$ line data and infrared radiation provides accurate predictions of SFR, with an estimated error of 0.1 M$_{\odot}$/yr.  This involves assuming a fixed mass of dust and stellar material in galaxies based on the estimated Br$\gamma$ line flux and infrared radiation

This study presents an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech in various lengths, a strategy that requires no statistical models and is automatically applicable to any speech sample. We identify median periods in speech signals within specified durations as the fundamental unit of speech length, enabling us to extend or reduce speech efficiently. The new method integrates smoothly with existing synthesis techniques that rely on unit selection, including phoneme-based synthesis, and we demonstrate its applicability effectively. A subjective listener test confirms that the modified speech samples preserve its original natural speech characteristics while exhibiting significant changes in duration. Furthermore, we observe that synthetic speeches of varied lengths still embody the distinct features of speech, unlike typical natural speeches with consistent durations. A new application known as Skincare has been developed to interactively classify skin lesions and enhance decision-making in teledermatology. It utilizes an intuitive interface that allows clinicians to confirm a diagnosis by training multiple deep learning models with various clinical inputs, such as images, patient demographics, and medical history. By focusing on the most critical pieces of information and eliminating distractions, Skincare improves efficiency and accuracy. By initiating training with multiple models for different lesion types and critical abnormalities such as melanoma, Skincare enhances diagnostic reliability and accuracy. A pilot study was conducted to assess the feasibility and efficacy of Skincare in an actual teledermatology setting. Results indicate that Skincare can streamline teledermatology processes and enhance clinicians' confidence in their diagnoses. A publicly accessible online demo is available for demonstration purposes. The source code of Skincare, including its interaction framework and deep learning models, has been released for the public to utilize and modify. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By transforming epidemics within hypergraphs into mean-field models of interacting particle systems, we explore the necessary and sufficient conditions for disease extinction and show that these conditions rely on the spectral properties of the hypergraph's adjacency matrix. This framework provides a promising approach to integrating group-based interactions into epidemic spread models, thus potentially yielding more accurate predictions of disease transmission. Furthermore, we derive the extinction conditions for specific types of hypergraphs, demonstrating that the critical transmission rates for these hypergraphs lie within a particular range on the spectrum of their adjacency matrices. By extending this methodology to more complex hypergraphs, we identify various group structures and transmission patterns, ultimately providing guidelines for policymakers to control disease spread within groups, such as schools, workplaces, and public transportation, by targeting high transmission rates. Computations involving the extinction threshold and spectral properties of hypergraphs could be facilitated through numerical methods, such as graph representation and approximation techniques. By bridging the gap between hypergraph models and real-world environments, this framework offers a valuable tool for applying graphical concepts to the analysis of epidemic spread within group-based settings. Lastly, we propose potential avenues for further research, such as integrating individual immunity and the dynamics of multiple disease outbreaks on hypergraphs. By pushing the boundaries of hypergraph-based epidemic modeling, this study contributes to the development of sophisticated models for disease transmission, thus advancing our understanding of epidemic spread within group-based settings. Additionally, we emphasize the versatility of our model, which can be adapted to interact with other mathematical frameworks, such as probabilistic models and optimization techniques, thus presenting a versatile approach for analyzing disease transmission. Lastly, we highlight the practical applications and potential research directions that this study has enabled.

These phenomena, rooted in an intraplanar mechanism, seem to contradict the expectation that these effects would vanish in centro-symmetric materials. To address this discrepancy, we focus on an idealized CrI3 bilayer and examine the origin of its spin profile and Hall effects. Employing a ab-initio realistic tight-binding model and an analytical flux-field approach, we identified the sources of Rashba effect and spin Hall effect, attributing them to an intraplanar mechanism despite the absence of an external spin-polarization. We demonstrate that the spin Hall effect is primarily driven by the intraband contribution of the Rashba effect, with the presence of a finite spin Hall effect even in the absence of a Hall effect. Furthermore, we show that the finite spin Hall effect can be utilized to generate a finite anomalous Hall effect, with the magnitude of the transverse conductivity being significantly lower than the typical Rashba effect prediction. Notably, we observe that the conductivity patterns follow the same trend regardless of the considered scenario, with the conductivity being solely dependent on the chiral charge of the CrI3 bilayer. This novel approach, KDL, does not require manual feature selection, thereby avoiding potential biases. Furthermore, KDL's underlying mechanisms are inherently multi-faceted, making it an attractive deep learning technique. However, prior research on KDL primarily utilized single-modal data, thereby neglecting the potential benefits of integrating multi-modal data. Inspired by the impressive results achieved with multi-modal deep learning models, we have developed a novel KDL framework, dubbed the Shared-Representations Universal K-fan Multimodal deep framework (SKM), which aims to harness the information present in both single-modal and multi-modal feature sets. This breakthrough model leverages the power of shared representations to consolidate the information from multiple feature sets and has demonstrated superior performance on various classification tasks across multiple domains, such as text-based applications and life-science tasks. This remarkable performance stems from the multi-faceted learning mechanisms and the ability of the model to effectively integrate and incorporate information from multiple feature sets. This study aims to enhance our understanding of the impact of these limitations by collecting and analyzing public WhatsApp chats in multiple languages. Our analysis reveals significant reductions in forwarded messages within a week of implementation, but these decreases vary greatly depending on the involved countries. Interestingly, some nations exhibited distinct patterns in forwarded message distribution, with peaks occurring before the limitation introduction. Our research also identifies the most prevalent message types that contributed to the forwarding phenomenon, with these messages often containing misinformation-related content. Furthermore, we observe that certain countries showed an increase in message transmission efficiency after the limitation implementation. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of WhatsApp's countermeasures in reducing the spread of misinformation but also highlight the necessity of further investigations to comprehensively evaluate these measures. This frequency spectrum can be calculated by integrating the joint probability of two allele frequencies within a population, given an ancestral tree structure. In the limit of very low allele frequencies, this frequency spectrum approximates an power-law distribution, specifically $f(x)\propto x^{-p-1}$, where $p=2+\frac{1}{k}$ and $k$ represents the effective mutation rate relative to the selection rate. This frequency spectrum also exhibits a higher order behavior that varies based on the population's branching structure, resulting in either even or odd exponentiation for some classes and odd exponentiation for the others. Spoofing countermeasures in speaker verification aim to prevent impostors from successfully authenticating. Although various countermeasures have been proposed, they are often hindered by a critical issue of occasional false positives that can compromise system accuracy. In this paper, a novel activation function, referred to as the Vigilant ReLU function (VeRU), is introduced. By incorporating an adaptive parameter and position-dependent reactivity, VeRU adjusts its slope in real-time based on the neural network's local and global characteristics, thereby enhancing the spoofing counteraction system's ability to filter out impostors while minimizing false positives. Experimental evaluations were conducted on three speaker verification corpora, namely VCS, SRE18, and VIVISEC, with the system showcasing improved performance in spoofing counteraction and genuine speaker verification tasks. Additionally, the proposed VeRU activation function achieved superior performance compared to standard ReLU and other adaptive activation functions in speaker verification tasks. Furthermore, the study highlights the dynamic behavior of VeRU, which facilitates the selection of an optimal adaptive parameter for peak performance, and demonstrates the flexibility of VeRU to be applied to various neural network architectures with minimal modifications. As a result, the proposed VeRU activation function offers a versatile solution to enhance the accuracy of end-to-end speaker verification systems in the presence of spoofing attacks. We've examined the phenomenon of asymmetry in photon pair correlations generated by spontaneous spontaneous four-wave mixing. By leveraging this process in a chain of discrete atoms, we've identified two distinct mechanisms for asymmetry: a product-type mechanism arising from the detection of two photons of unequal wavelengths, and a subspaces-based mechanism resulting from the distinct natural frequencies of the atoms. Furthermore, we've shown that the product-type mechanism dominates the asymmetry at short distances while the subspace-based mechanism becomes prevalent at longer distances. This understanding deepens our knowledge of asymmetry in photon pair correlations and paves the way for practical applications in quantum communication. Additionally, we've explored the possibility of reversing the asymmetry over a specific distance, an idea inspired by the concept of quantum entanglement swapping. This could be achieved by adjusting the natural frequencies of the atoms or through the implementation of a controlled unitary operation. This displacement of measure leads to an infinite number of distinct Borel sets, thereby solving a problem initially posed by Joseph Riddler. Interestingly, the sets in question are not only measurable but also have the property that their measure is independent of the starting point for the partitioning. Furthermore, this work yields a general method for defining a wide array of new, 1-dimensional continuous measures that are both countable and uncountable. Finally, a related question is explored, concerning the real line's division into non-Borel sets with similar characteristics. It is shown that such a partitioning is indeed possible if, instead of a constant factor in the measure, a sequence or a fractal-like function is used to define the sets' boundaries. Ultimately, this work reveals numerous intricate fractals, each with a zero Lebesgue measure but an infinite new measure defined by the employed function, thereby illustrating a concept known as "fractal geometry". The concepts discussed here can be applied to other dimensions as well, providing a framework for dividing $n$-dimensional spaces into various sets with distinct measures. Lastly, the ideas presented herein may also be connected to the realm of coding theory, thereby indicating a potential link between fractal geometry and error-correcting codes. The decrease in susceptibility is not solely dependent on the already established Kondo screening effect but can also be controlled by the strength of the interaction as well as the band structure of the interface.  To test these predictions, computer simulations of a specific material, consisting of a layer of LaAlO3 and a layer of EuO, were conducted while considering various parameters that influence the magnetic layer's properties and the strength of the interaction between the layers.  The results revealed multiple frequency scales that affect the magnetic layer's susceptibility and predicted the existence of novel phenomena such as giant paramagnetism or negative magnetism at the interface. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming operations, such as disk accesses or network lookups. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less memory to achieve the same false positive rates. A different algorithm, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as a more precise alternative to the Bloom filter. A modification to this earlier work yields the xor filter, which can be implemented with minimal additional memory. Unlike Bloom and cuckoo filters, which utilize hash functions to store elements, xor filters rely on arrays to store values. This modification introduces limitations on the sets these filters can identify. A theoretical analysis of the approximate membership accuracy in xor filters, along with experimental results, is presented. The findings demonstrate that xor filters can be more efficient, consuming both less memory and processing power, than both Bloomier filters and cuckoo filters. A comparison with existing membership testers, such as Bloom and cuckoo filters, is also provided. The experimentally confirmed advantages of xor filters over the currently widely used algorithms highlight their potential to improve the performance of several applications, such as disk access filtering during file compression, network filtering, and data storage on solid-state disks. The implementation of xor filters is now accessible as part of the Java Utilities library at https://www2.math.csudh.edu/~jdarlo/Utilities.html. The source code for this paper's experiments is available at https://github.com/darlo Math Utilities/tree/main/darlo-utils/src/main/java/com/csu/darlo/xorfilter. Additionally, a tool for generating C code for xor filters is at https://www2.math.csudh.edu/~jdarlo/Utilities.html. The performance of xor filters can also be evaluated using the Membership Tester tool at https://www2.math.csudh.edu/~jdarlo/Utilities.html. This tester generates membership filters based on the xor algorithm for any specified set of integers, along with any of three possible approximation levels. The tool is accessible via both web and desktop interfaces. The memory consumption of xor filters can be further minimized through the incorporation of external hashing. A variant of this algorithm, the xormp filter, is discussed in a related study on the optimization of approximate membership algorithms. This methodology produces versatile trends that are resistant to noise, and it's possible to determine the optimal analysis period by measuring indicator stability over differing interval lengths. This work presents FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework that maintains confidentiality. FLVoogd is inspired by the robust learning strategy and utilizes a reliable flux-based model to handle malicious data attacks. We develop a novel method to split training data into two segments and allocate them separately to test our framework's reliability in the presence of adversarial clients. Our framework is then applied to evaluate the performance of convolutional neural networks on two image classification datasets, and the results demonstrate that FLVoogd significantly enhances model robustness and preserves client privacy. Notably, FLVoogd outperforms existing federated learning frameworks by achieving better accuracy and reducing communication costs without sacrificing model confidentiality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework can efficiently handle a diverse number of clients and achieve substantial performance improvements in various dataset scenarios. Our source code is publicly available for review at the URL: https://github.com/IronSnail1/FLVoogd.

Connecting real-world traffic sensing data to simulated training models is a difficult problem.
To bridge this gap, researchers are trying to establish a direct mapping between in-game pixel values and real-world world geometry.
Our approach builds on this idea by using a simplified representation of the real-world environment to translate in-game pixel values into real-world navigation instructions.
We developed an efficient and accurate method for predicting real-world navigation instructions from in-game pixel values, which achieves a 40% reduction in navigation errors compared to existing methods.
Specifically, we improved upon the state-of-the-art Sim2Real navigation model by nearly halving the error rate, and showcasing the feasibility of connecting in-game navigation to real-world traffic routing. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. 
Our approach involves training a model to recognize the correlation between in-game pixel values and real-world navigation instructions.
We then apply this model to predict real-world navigation instructions from in-game pixel values, which achieves a 40% reduction in navigation errors compared to existing methods.
Notably, we found that the predictions made by the model are highly consistent with actual navigation routes in real-world traffic, with predictions made in the Sim2Real traffic dataset exhibiting nearly the same error rate as manually selected routes. 
Our results indicate that the predictions made by the model are also highly consistent with actual navigation instructions in real-world traffic, with predictions made in the KITTI dataset exhibiting a 40% error rate compared to reference values. 
We aim to build upon this finding and improve the accuracy of navigation predictions in real-world traffic, and showcase the feasibility of predicting real-world navigation instructions from in-game pixel values. 
We demonstrate the efficacy of the model on a diverse set of vehicles, including passenger vehicles, trucks, and delivery vehicles, by training the model to recognize vehicle-specific features in in-game pixel values and mapping them to real-world navigation instructions tailored to each vehicle type.

This chapter examines the progress of deepfake research, focusing on both the development of unconstrained media deepfakes and robust deepfake detection techniques. Unconstrained media deepfakes are difficult to create and detect because they can be formed entirely from freely accessible images and videos of individuals without prior knowledge. Conversely, detection techniques are challenging due to the high convolutional nature of deepfake processing. As a result, developing effective detection methods requires considerable amounts of processed data, thereby limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios. To overcome this issue, this chapter introduces an innovative approach leveraging adversarial training to create unconstrained media deepfakes and improves detection accuracy by incorporating pixel-level classification and adversarial training for enhancement. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance in both deepfake creation and detection, achieving an impressive 98\% robustness even after undergoing stringent modifications. The presence of a liquid envelope, especially if it contains water, is a necessary requirement for creating a habitable Earth-sized planet. Detecting such an envelope around small, nearby stars is extremely difficult in infrared thermal measurements but can be identifiable through visible light changes during the process of a planet passing in front of its host star (a transit event). Researchers have proposed a new method to determine if a liquid envelope, specifically containing water, surrounds a certain category of planets (those with masses between that of Earth and Neptune) by measuring how much water is present in the envelope during a transit event. This method relies on the distinct ways in which water and other gases behave under different temperatures, a phenomenon that's visible in spectroscopy data. We provide an alternative framework for understanding how water behaves in a planet's envelope, one that's based on the chemical equilibrium between water and other substances. This approach can result in multiple solutions that explain the same observed phenomena, and we propose future observations, including those enabled by the James Webb Space Telescope, to distinguish between these possibilities. This new framework highlights the need to reconsider how scientists interpret observational data from a planetary science perspective, and encourages flexibility in the interpretation of data as understanding the field evolves. Moreover, our study demonstrates the feasibility of testing compositional models of a planet's interior through transit spectroscopy, a technique with the potential to reveal crucial information about a planet's basic composition, such as the presence of an outer solid layer and a liquid envelope. If these models prove valid, they could provide crucial insights into a planet's formation and evolution, and could serve as a crucial tool in the search for a terrestrial planet with a habitable environment. As such, this study serves as a guide for researchers seeking to understand the composition of exoplanets through various methods and observational campaigns. Inspired by brain neurobiology, spiking neural networks have the potential to revolutionize sequence learning in complex systems, but current implementations using neuromorphic chips struggle with two significant drawbacks: they require extensive artificial slowing down of neurons to operate within the same time frame, and hence operate far away from biological plausibility; and due to their monolithic architecture, are typically only capable of learning a single sequence at a time. This research aims to address these limitations by developing a novel spiking neural network design for sequence learning that not only operates within a biological time frame without the need for artificial slowing, and thus remains biologically feasible, but also enables multiple sequences to be learned simultaneously. We thoroughly evaluate our design by successfully applying it to two distinct real-world datasets, achieving impressive results equivalent to or better than existing methods in both cases. Specifically, we achieve a test accuracy of 99.96% for sequence learning, and 99.97% for learning multiple overlapping sequences in a musical dataset, and a test accuracy of 98.9% for protein structure prediction, significantly outperforming existing methods by over 10%. Our design achieves these outstanding results by employing a novel neuron type that mimics the biological mechanism of temporal summation, and employs a robust spike-based memory mechanism that enables long-term data storage and retrieval. Additionally, we provide a full-scale chip simulation to demonstrate the practicality of our design for real-world applications using neuromorphic chips. Our design serves as a pioneering effort in developing biologically feasible spiking neural networks for sequence learning tasks. Its exceptional performance using actual biological neuron dynamics makes it an excellent example of a neural network that closely resembles a natural learning system, and its state-of-the-art results using actual biological time frames opens up new possibilities for applications in both biological and programming time frames. Moreover, its superior performance over traditional monolithic spiking neural networks demonstrates the immense potential of our design in real-world applications and showcases a fundamental difference between biological and artificial neural networks. Lastly, with successful applications in two distinct real-world domains, our design lays the groundwork for a unified learning mechanism that closely mimics the natural learning process in human brains. A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random solutions to such equations, however, verifying the accuracy of these expansions poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we developed a post-processing method that allows researchers to evaluate the correctness of generalized polynomial chaos expansions in a particular context. This method involves comparing approximate solutions to exact solutions in a designated region, thereby determining the precision of the approximation. By utilizing this method, we were able to provide precise bounds for the errors in approximating random solutions to differential equations, which represents a primary contribution of this study. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we applied it to the study of a Newtonian ball collision, where the outcome was found to be distinct from a previously proposed theoretical model. In contrast to previous work, our analysis reveals that the solution to this problem does not converge uniformly across all dimensions. Rather, we demonstrate the precision of the approximation through the application of our post-processing method, which yields a detailed estimate of the error. Furthermore, our approach reveals that the solution to this problem exhibits singularities in certain high-dimensional scenarios, which were not previously documented in the existing literature. This study represents a pioneering effort to verify the accuracy of generalized polynomial chaos expansions, which holds broad-ranging applications across a variety of fields. By utilizing our post-processing method, researchers can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the precision of approximations derived from generalized polynomial chaos expansions, which includes the derivation of precise error bounds for a range of applications. To facilitate the dissemination of this research, we have released an open-source software package that enables the reproduction of our results, as well as a flexible framework for the implementation of our approach in a diverse array of applications. This software package includes a range of useful tools, including an efficient Monte Carlo method for the evaluation of integrals, which can be applied to the analysis of the precision of approximations in a variety of contexts. Additionally, our approach includes a flexible framework for the representation of complex objects, which can be utilized to study the precision of approximations in a range of applications, including but not limited to Newtonian ball collisions. We anticipate that our research will contribute positively to a range of applications by fostering greater communication and collaboration across a variety of fields, which includes but is not limited to applied mathematics and computer science. We developed a new approach to understanding dwarf galaxies based on their chemical composition and the history of star formation within them. This methodology leverages detailed analysis of chemical data from various elements within galaxies, enabling accurate comparisons with simulations of galaxy evolution. Specifically, we utilized chemical abundance predictions from the numerical simulation ARcheon, applying a machine learning tool to identify the ideal input format that yielded the most accurate matching between simulation and observation. Our analysis focused on two key aspects: the distribution of chemical abundances and the timing of star formation. Regarding chemical abundances, the distribution of metals in dwarf galaxies can be accurately represented by a single parameter, which reflects both the overall metal content and the rate of chemical enrichment. This finding aligns with predictions from simulations, indicating that chemical evolution can be effectively described using parameter space of two variables. Furthermore, we observed a correlation between the average age of stars and the metal content in dwarf galaxies, which can be explained through the mechanism of gas inflow followed by star formation. Specifically, regions with lower metal content tend to have older star populations, which contradicts the standard model suggesting a linear relationship between metal content and star age. Additionally, we analyzed the mass of gas available for star formation in dwarf galaxies, which can be effectively modeled using a dependent relationship on stellar mass. Specifically, the available gas mass decreases steadily with increasing stellar mass, which holds true even at very low stellar masses. Lastly, we noted that although dwarf galaxies generally follow generally uniform evolutionary paths, there are notable exceptions. Specifically, some dwarf galaxies exhibit unique characteristics despite sharing similar properties with others. Furthermore, certain regions within galaxies can be accurately matched to others despite differences in their initial conditions, which suggests that their respective evolutionary paths may have converged. The current study serves as a foundation for a broader research goal, which aims to understand galaxy evolution through detailed analysis of chemical composition, star formation history, and other key astronomical indicators. Furthermore, the methodology developed here can be applied not only to dwarf galaxies but also to various other cosmic objects, which possess abundant chemical data. Ultimately, this research can be further developed into an inverse modeling framework, which utilizes chemical data to constrain simulations of galaxy evolution, thereby providing a mutually beneficial collaboration between observations and simulations. Furthermore, the invariants can be extended to groupoids and linear algebraic groups, providing a clearer understanding of the invariants in these contexts. Additionally, the invariants of a subgroup or groupoid H, given that it satisfies specific solvability conditions, can be computed effectively by identifying a maximal set of subgroups or groupoids that are both closed and open in G. Our research demonstrates that a significant reduction in data labeling costs can be achieved by using low-cost semi-anonymous document annotations obtained through a simple, interactive process. To validate this claim, we introduce the concept of visually rich document semi-anonymization, which involves concealing certain document fields without revealing the layout or structure. Our approach aligns with existing model training methods based on full annotation, and we verify this claim across various models and datasets, including both existing datasets and new creations. Furthermore, we validate the feasibility of semi-anonymous document annotations in multiple domains, confirming the results to be accurate and reliable. Notably, our innovation enables the cost-efficient training of document understanding models for rare document formats or those requiring high extraction precision, opening up new possibilities for visually rich document understanding in various applications. The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using ab-initio calculations, researchers investigated the electronic properties of the EuS/InAs interface, focusing on various bonding configurations resulting from the mismatch between the two materials. It is found that the electronic properties significantly depend on the bonding arrangement and realistic bond configurations enable efficient carrier communication between a magnetic layer and a semiconductor, crucial for the operation of quantum devices. Additionally, the study reveals an increase in the magnetic moment of Eu due to its interaction with InAs, and this effect is observed across all examined bonding configurations. Furthermore, the calculations indicate that the coordination number of S in Eu has a significant influence on the interface's electronic properties. While a significant gap at the interface is observed for configurations matching the 2:3 ratio of InAs lattice constants to Eu sulfur atomic coordinates, a gap reduction is noted when considering multiple atomic layers of InAs due to structural relaxations, indicating that carrier communication is partially disabled at the interface in this scenario. Given the potential for spin-orbit interactions in InAs, the enabled or disabled carrier communication at the interface has implications in terms of magnetic properties and electronic properties, with consequences for quantum device performance. The study's findings contribute to the understanding of magnetic properties at heterostructures and may guide experimental research into magnetic properties and electronic properties of the EuS/InAs system, with the aim of developing materials for quantum device development through magnetic coupling between a magnetic material and a semiconductor. The electronic properties at the interface in ferromagnetic EuS/InAs, influenced by bonding arrangement, may also provide insights into magnetic properties and electronic properties of a system with a magnetic material and a semiconductor, with consequences for quantum device development due to carrier communication disability at the interface in certain configurations. The electronic properties at the interface in antiferromagnetic EuS/InAs, influenced by bonding arrangement, may also provide insights into magnetic properties and electronic properties of a system with a magnetic material and a semiconductor, with consequences for quantum device development due to disabled carrier communication at the interface in certain configurations. By applying this approach, we show how to find an optimal policy by iterating between a dual procedure generating feasible value functions and a primal step using these functions to calculate the optimal action. This method relaxes the requirement for value functions to be strictly convex, allowing us to apply it to a broader class of problems, including those with nonlinear constraints. A new pessimistic approach to Bayesian learning for the "best single-action" dynamic treatment strategy has been developed by constructing a confidence set for the "most favorable" treatment policy at each time, based on historical data and accounting for uncertainty in estimated parameters. Unlike existing set-based methods that rely on model assumptions, this new approach makes no assumptions about the data generating process. Our approach can accommodate complex models with high-dimensional constraints and is adaptable to both small and large datasets, demonstrating improved performance in simulations. Additionally, a theoretical analysis has confirmed that our method's width asymptotically approaches the optimal pessimistic width, previously proposed by Joe and Stein, without requiring any additional assumptions. Furthermore, our approach has successfully applied to real-world data from the Child Health and Disability Outreach (CHADO) program, while making available a publicly accessible R package, named Bayesian Dynamic, that enables users to easily replicate the results. Using this package, we have explored the effects of changing the confidence level on the pessimistic set and how it impacts the strategy's width, revealing an inverse relationship. Moreover, our approach has confirmed the validity of the "try-something-new" rule in a Bayesian context, which can be conveniently implemented using the R package. Ultimately, our new approach has addressed an open question in the field and provided a flexible solution to constructing a pessimistic set, which can be used in various applications, including Bayesian learning for the "most favorable" treatment policy. Additionally, this new approach has confirmed the applicability of pessimism in a Bayesian learning context, providing a new direction for future research and opens up the possibility of further extending pessimism to other types of Bayesian learning approaches. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively employed in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most CT systems utilize low-energy X-ray sources, the resulting images typically exhibit high noise levels at low-frequency ranges. Furthermore, the energy-dependent nature of absorbed X-rays complicates the process of reconstructing images from measured data, especially when multiple materials need to be identified within the scanned subject. To address these challenges, a novel regularized reconstruction framework has been proposed, allowing the simultaneous reduction of high-frequency noise, image filtering, and material decomposition based on the distinct attenuation characteristics of each material. A stabilized iterative scheme, influenced by the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) method, is employed to update the image estimates until convergence is achieved. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in producing accurate double-phase and triple-phase images, even when high levels of artificial noise are introduced into the measured data. Additionally, the reconstructed images appear to be relatively free from artifacts, further illustrating the capability of the proposed framework to decompose bound materials and reduce noise. Several numerical indicators, such as the Phase Shift and Cross Correlation values, are used to quantify the accuracy of the reconstructed images and evaluate their correspondence to reference phase images and noise spectra, respectively. To further validate the capability of the proposed framework in identifying multiple materials, a statistical Energy Weighting Index (EWI) metric is also applied, confirming the excellent performance of the reconstructor in detecting various materials. Our study showcases the outstanding potential of the proposed framework as a versatile tool for enhancing CT image quality through denoising and material decomposition applications. To ensure full transparency, the source code used in this research study is publicly accessible via the linked repository, allowing other researchers to replicate our results and expand the proposed framework at their discretion. Several open-source software packages, including MATLAB and Python, are utilized to implement the reconstructor, providing versatile options for other researchers to engage with and modify the code. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of variational reconstruction frameworks in accurately evaluating internal structures, radiative noise, and material compositions, highlighting their potential applications in various engineering and medical contexts. To achieve accurate predictions for heavy nuclei, our approach combines three established methods: a theoretical framework for nuclear structure, ab initio approximations, and a novel technique for exponential parametrizations. By Exponentially Weighted Gaussian Basis, we can efficiently describe the ground states of nuclei with complex systems, such as nuclear matter and heavy nuclei like $^{56}$Ni and $^{78}$Br, through a finite number of highly localized basis states. This representation facilitates the derivation of important nuclear properties like energy distributions, radii, and $\betawin$. By examining nuclei with different numbers of protons and neutrons, we gain insights into how these properties evolve. Our technique also enables the computation of decay energies and nuclear level spacings, thereby providing fundamental data for astrophysical research, such as neutron star mergers and radioactivity in stars. Furthermore, the technique allows us to quantify the uncertainties associated with these calculations, as illustrated for the case of neutron star mergers in NS-NS systems. Such a fully quantitative approach for nuclear structure, rooted in first-principles physics, paves the way for a precise microscopic description of the matter in neutron stars and other astrophysical events. However, it demands an expansion of the EWGB parametrization to encompass more intricate nuclear configurations, thereby diminishing its practical applicability to the simpler nuclei considered here. To strike a balance between complexity and accuracy, we introduce a second method called Gaussian-basis Sampling, which parametrizes the many-body problem using a fixed, finite number of basis states while incorporating the full complexity of the underlying quantum fluctuations. By employing this technique, we can compute abundant data for nuclei and nuclear interactions without overestimating the uncertainties, as shown for the case of neutron scattering data. Our strategy relies on the utilization of modern ab initio single-nucleon potentials and other fundamental data, thereby facilitating a consistent, predictive framework that can be extended to describe more intricate nuclear configurations and interactions. By combining this approach with experimental data, we can refine the uncertainties inherent in our calculations, thereby exemplifying a fully quantitative strategy for nuclear structure, rooted in a microscopic description of the underlying quantum fluctuations. Nevertheless, our method still benefits from the incorporation of meaningful approximations, as demonstrated by our comparisons with other established theoretical frameworks and experimental evidence. To illustrate the applicability of our strategy, we have computed the interaction between two neutrons at subatomic distances, as well as the distribution of $^{56}$Ni nuclei' energy density and radii at various densities. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly boosts the performance of object-oriented programs, but the performance boost comes at a cost: the high memory allocation costs that are detrimental to GPU performance are exacerbated. To address this issue, we developed DynaSOAr, a novel GPU memory allocator that converges with the host to create a highly efficient memory environment. DynaSOAr is unlike conventional allocators in several key ways: it dynamically adjusts its memory allocation policies in real-time to suit the specific needs of running applications; its memory management is a collaborative effort between the GPU and host, driven by a shared memory pool; its custom-made free memory database ensures speedy memory deallocation. Furthermore, DynaSOAr is an object-oriented allocator that is specifically designed for object-oriented programming, a programming paradigm that is popular but challenging to use on GPUs. In our comprehensive experiments, we found that DynaSOAr delivers speed-ups of up to 31.2% and 11.4% over the current state-of-the-art allocators, and is capable of allocating memory up to 4.2 times faster for some applications. The source code for DynaSOAr is freely available online for other developers to build from. To evaluate DynaSOAr, we developed SOArLang, a new programming language that is specifically designed for object-oriented development on GPUs, featuring a range of innovative features such as automatic memory management, dynamic memory allocation, polymorphism, and shared memory access. In our experiments, SOArLang delivers significant performance improvements, with speed-ups of up to 57.3% and 22.2% over existing object-oriented programming languages for some applications. The source code for SOArLang is freely available online for other developers to evaluate and extend. To further optimize the performance of object-oriented programs, we developed a range of new techniques, including dynamic memory management, polymorphism, and shared memory access, which are now part of SOArLang. In our experiments, these techniques deliver significant performance improvements, with speed-ups of up to 57.3% and 22.2% over existing object-oriented programming languages for some applications. The source code for these techniques is freely available online for other developers to build from. To validate the design of DynaSOAr and SOArLang, we evaluated and analyzed the performance of several existing object-oriented programming paradigms on GPUs, including C++ and OpenCL, and found that DynaSOAr and SOArLang outperform them significantly, with speed-ups of up to 57.3

New $U(1)_X$ standard models have been proposed as a potential alternative to the well-established electroweak gauge theory. These models, however, face challenges in the form of dark matter constraints and difficulty in accurately predicting the $W$ and $Z$ mass values. Recent research efforts have focused on developing a $U(1)_X$ model, here referred to as the $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X}$ model, with $U(1)_X$ derived partially from $SO(10)$, thereby incorporating some of the benefits of from-inside-a-large-dimensional-space standard models. The $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X}$ model demonstrates the capability of resolving the SM gauge hierarchy, with $U(1)_X$ breaking mediated by an optimal combination of scalar fields, and further enables a viable dark matter solution through either gauge fermion or axion-like particle influences. Additionally, the $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X}$ model exhibits its ability to accommodate neutrino properties consistent with existing experimental data, with the possibility of lepton number violation also present. A comprehensive evaluation of the model's consistency, dark matter stability and other relevant characteristics has been provided. Furthermore, predictions for various rare decay processes have been made, with parameters tuned to meet current experimental data requirements. The tuning also ensures that $t$-channel contributions to $Z$ boson decay are sub-dominant, with $\Gamma(Z\rightarrow f\bar{f})$ predictions yielding results very close to the SM model. The $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X}$ model exhibits its potential in addressing issues related to charged current interactions, with future collider experiments such as HL-LHC, HL-lepton, and pp collider having the potential to verify it. A comprehensive analysis of the model's ability to accommodate $X$ boson mass values within one sigma deviation from the SM $Z$ boson mass has also been provided. Lastly, constraints from electroweak precision observables have been analyzed, with the $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X}$ model exhibiting its ability to accommodate these constraints at a 95% confidence level, with the $Z$ pole constraint being the most stringent. Finally, estimates for $\Delta T-T$ and $\Delta S-S$ discrepancies have been provided, with the $\mathcal{M}_{U(1)_X)}$ model exhibiting its ability to accommodate these estimates within one sigma deviation from the SM

To ensure the long-term durability of such systems, like the straw drift tube used in detector systems for proton-proton colliders, it's crucial to understand the longitudinal stress distribution within them, particularly when they are subject to varying pressures and surface stresses. In a numerical simulation, the authors analyzed the mechanical behavior of a straw drift tube equipped with a radiopure epoxy-based thin-walled cone, taking into account surface stresses and internal pressure. The results show a noticeable deformation in the cone's shape, which leads to an uneven stress distribution along the length of the tube. Furthermore, an internal pressure greater than the design specification resulted in a slight decrease in the straw's wall thickness in the cone section, indicating the need for a stricter internal pressure limit. Additionally, the authors report that any surface stress above a certain threshold would cause the straw to crack, and suggest reinforcing the cone with a stress-resistant material to ensure the long-term mechanical integrity of the straw drift tube. The authors also note that further study on the effects of surface stresses of different orientations and magnitude are required, and propose a possible radiation damage scenario for the straw drift tube, and the effect of this damage in the mechanical behavior of the tube, particularly one made from a radionuclide-doped cone. Finally, the authors note that the high resistance of the photoconductor to radiation, combined with the mechanical integrity ensured by this study, makes the straw drift tube an excellent choice for high-power particle detector applications in the future. We analyze two instances of this framework: Bayesian optimization and combinatorial optimization with chance constraints. Our research demonstrates that these optimization problems can be solved using a framework that relies on the representation of probability distributions as probabilistic circuits. Probability constraints on the circuit variables can then be relaxed to yield an upper limit on the total variation between the original and modified distributions. We show that these limits provide valid criteria for determining optimality and feasibility in optimization problems. In contrast to conventional solid systems experiencing oscillations, in superfluids these oscillations have unique characteristics rooted in the application of Bogoliubov's quasiparticle theory, resulting from the interaction of internal energy gradient with the system's Fermi surface. Furthermore, this effect becomes notably amplified in systems nearing a transition to a new quantum state of matter. Additionally, we discuss how this phenomenon can be observed in both spin polarized and ungapped superfluids. Our study also explores the distinct behavior of oscillations in 3D systems, in comparison to 2D superfluids. Finally, we speculate on the feasibility of observing this phenomenon in a specific quantum fluid: superfluid $^{3,4}$He. In particular, we suggest that its intricate internal energy structure could significantly amplify the oscillations and make the phenomenon more visible to measure. Lastly, we anticipate our findings to contribute to the development of novel experimental methods used to measure the internal energy structure of superfluids.

Its distinctive shape reveals either extreme spatial compression or anisotropic mass distribution. We investigated the mass configuration of the CMZ to distinguish between these possibilities. A two-dimensional correlation function was applied to the mean mass density of radial and tangential directions in Parssec units. The outcome showed a significant 1.7 sigma preference for the latter, indicating a more compact configuration in the CMZ along their radial axis. This preference stood out despite data imperfections that could generate up to a 1.3 sigma bias in the results. We considered various alternative methods to explore the anisotropic pattern further; a Gaussian fit also revealed a similar preference with a 1.9 sigma significance. These analyses confirm that the CMZ in the LMC has a more compact shape along the radial axis, likely due to efficient angular momentum removal through outflow. It is interesting to note that this pattern remains evident even after removing data that contains noise, indicating a persistent feature in the data. In fact, removing data along the tangential direction revealed a more pronounced preference (2.1 sigma), while removing data along the radial direction still yielded a moderate preference (1.4 sigma) for the anisotropic mass configuration. These insights provide valuable information on the formation and removal of angular momentum in the CMZ, shaped in a disk. Moreover, the preference remains evident even after the data was rotated by 90 degrees (not provided in the initial submission), suggesting that the anisotropic pattern in the data is robust. Finally, the anisotropic pattern in the mass configuration could be mimicked using a simple analytical model by assuming efficient outflow along the bar axis, leading to a more compact configuration in the middle and far ends. In contrast, the anisotropic pattern in the surface density showed no clear preference for any direction. These insights offer new understanding of the formation and removal of angular momentum in the CMZ shaped in a bar. Moreover, the preferences remain evident even after the data is filtered by different spatial scales (not provided in the initial submission), suggesting a universal feature in the data along the radial axis of the CMZ. The main benefit of this dual perspective is that it enables a straightforward integration of various extensions to Godel modal logics, including those for tension, or according to Fitting and Dummett, in the framework of algebraic and relational modal logic. Specifically, we provide axiomatic definitions and concrete examples of the respective classes of Godel modal algebras and Godel modal frames for these extensions, along with a detailed examination of their respective duality theorems. Our work thus contributes to a more unified understanding of Godel modal logic through the application of algebraic and relational semantics, thereby facilitating a unified treatment of various extensions to the logic via these two semantics. Furthermore, our research reveals an interesting connection between the first-order theory of Godel modal logic and its corresponding modal calculus. Finally, we include a discussion of the decision problems for the theory and the modal calculus, along with a report on the computability of their satisfiability and validity problems. Our approach involves taking the distorted resolvent of the mixed strategy stationarity condition, a concept similar to Fédonné's idea of taking the resolvent of a matrix. This new method can be efficiently computed using linear complementarity problems, and it enables us to obtain rigorous analytical approximations of Nash equilibria by varying a parameter under strict condition. Human minimal clips demonstrate efficient learning and prediction capabilities across various environments, which poses an interesting question: can we attribute these abilities to enhanced sampling in training? To investigate this, we created a controlled environment for training static and dynamic models, then compared their performance to that of a model sampling random clips, all three models trained on a simplified version of minimal clips. Surprisingly, the sampling model achieved similar levels of accuracy as the dynamic model, particularly in complex scenarios. However, the static model struggled in more intricate situations. Our findings suggest that dynamic models can effectively process sequential data, which might be deemed random by the sampling model. This discovery reveals that the sampling model is not merely a theoretical construct but a valuable resource for creating predictive models of dynamic systems. Additionally, our study implies that sequential data can be leveraged for learning predictive models, even if it appears disjointed and unpredictable. Furthermore, we observed that the sampling model excelled in environments requiring rapid adaptation, which may indicate its potential as a versatile model for dynamic systems. Moving forward, we intend to expand our test environment to encompass online learning settings, allowing us to compare the performance of dynamic and sampling models in real-world scenarios. Significant advancements in deep learning have enabled the integration of climate models with predictive capabilities. In comparison to static climate analysis, climate forecasting is more intricate and necessitates the consideration of spatiotemporal interactions. Although existing models excel in their respective domains, they fall short in other areas; for instance, models that excel in climate forecasting often struggle with resolving the interactions between nearby locations, which is crucial for precision in this field. In light of these limitations, this study presents a novel neural network design, referred to as SCLNet, which is an attention-based model that accounts for interactions among neighboring locations in climate forecasting. The proposed model leverages a unique combination of cross-attention mechanisms at the pixel and patch levels, along with a spatial attention module that facilitates the model's comprehension of the forward and backward temporal dynamics in climate sequences. Through extensive testing on the resolution 20 km GSIM dataset, our model has outperformed state-of-the-art baseline models, which includes CNN, CNN-LSTM, CNN-GRU, TransCNN, TransLSTM, and TransGRU, by a considerable margin, with a significant improvement in NSME of 4.64% and a Corr of 0.85. The proposed model's effectiveness in precision is attributed to the incorporation of a spatial attention module that enhances the model's understanding of forward and backward temporal dynamics in climate sequences. The availability of this research paper's code and dataset can be found at the repository https://github.com/tjjeon2022/SCLNet. The proposed model has the potential to be applied in various computer vision applications where spatial information is crucial in precision. Additionally, it can be extended to support high-resolution climate forecasting through downscaling, a feature that is currently missing in existing climate forecasting models, which is another area of improvement for this domain. We develop a concept of completeness for sequences within ultrapowers, utilizing a different approach than previously described by Wagon in his book on Hilbert's paradox. Our methodology focuses on interval coverages, which naturally lead to the introduction of a new category of sequences: infinitely rich sequences. A demonstration of the equivalence between rho-completeness and being infinitely rich is presented, along with an alternate definition of completeness based on interval coverages. Additionally, we establish that infinitely rich sequences are inherently dense in the realm of ultrapowers. Furthermore, under the assumption of choice, we successfully prove that all infinitely rich sequences within certain specific types of arrays are in fact complete. However, through a detailed analysis, we conclude that, without the assumption of choice, not all infinitely rich sequences can be considered complete. Rather, we define a subclass of infinitely rich sequences known as omega-complete sequences, which maintain completeness even in the absence of choice. Lastly, we derive a representation of the addition of two omega-complete sequences. Our work also expands upon Wagon's findings by showing that choice is not required for the existence of complete sequences in certain arrangements. Additionally, we introduce a concept of inner richness, establishing a distinction between inner and infinitely rich sequences, and demonstrate how a specific arrangement of sets impacts the completeness of its ultrapower. Finally, we present an alternative definition of completeness based on internal partitioning, which may provide a pathway for further exploration. The theorems presented here can be applied to clarify a specific arrangement of sets known as fast converging arrays. We also introduce a new concept of compatibility, specifically refining Wagon's definition of compatibility, and derive a categorization of sequences based on compatibility, which may provide a potential approach for clarifying the Arrangement Hierarchy. Lastly, we present an analysis of an arrangement of sets known as fast diverging arrays. Our work also touches upon an arrangement of sets known as AR, which is widely considered to be an important and fundamental arrangement. We derive a precise description of AR in terms of rice's theorem and demonstrate that its arrangements are either omega-complete, infinitely rich but not omega-complete, or neither infinitely rich nor omega-complete. Furthermore, we present an expanded definition of compatibility specifically for the AR arrangement and present a conceptualization of the characteristics of an arrangement of sets, providing a potential approach for further exploration. Additionally, we derive a description of AR in terms of a block structure and show that choosing an arrangement of sets at random is either AR, AR compliant, or AR incompatible.

The effectiveness of modern, hardware-concerned, dataset-aware data processing frameworks heavily depends on how well they profile and respond to varying dataset sizes.  Different datasets due to their distinct characteristics in memory usage, access patterns, and computation requirements, make it impractical to optimize these frameworks with a single, universal approach.  This paper highlights the necessity of tailored solutions, proposing a method that allows for customized, dataset-specific optimization opportunities to be discovered and implemented.  Our approach, involving the use of particularization, enables the efficient evaluation of various optimization strategies, ultimately leading to the development of a switch-based decision network that effectively exploits opportunities specific to each dataset.  Through evaluation on three real-world datasets, we demonstrate that particularization facilitates the discovery of multiple, valuable optimization opportunities previously overlooked by previous, universally-oriented approaches.  Furthermore, particularization allows us to design a more responsive and efficient profile, surpassing the performance of current leading datasets-aware processing frameworks.  Our results reveal improvements in processing time of up to 3.3 times for a single, universal profile compared to the current best, dataset-aware processing frameworks.  The code and datasets used in this study can be accessed via our GitHub repository at https://github.com/jbarragan-udelo/dataset-particular-profiling. By integrating this adaptive kernel width optimization into the existing adaptive graph signal recovery framework, the method achieves enhanced resilience to measurement noise and improved performance with small sample sizes. We provide a new estimate for the initial eigenvalue of a nonlinear elliptic operator subject to a Robin boundary condition. This operator involves a first-order nonlinear boundary condition and a specific homogeneous inhomogeneous boundary condition. Our analysis also yields an upper bound on the first eigenvalue of a related nonlinear Schrödinger operator under a similar Robin boundary condition. These estimates take into account general nonlinearities at the boundary and do not require them to be in a specific symmetry group. We use a variational approach and incorporate energy estimates in our reasoning. 

Next, we consider the same nonlinear operator but switch to a different, more permissive boundary condition. We establish lower and upper bounds for the first eigenvalue in this new scenario. These bounds demonstrate the influence of a constant and a boundary parameter on the estimate, highlighting their relationship through inequalities. We work within the L^2 norm and explain the relevance of choosing this norm. 

Finally, we expand our findings to the first eigenvalue of a related nonlinear Schrödinger operator under a similar boundary condition, yielding an upper bound in this case. These estimates demonstrate the influence of various parameters on the first eigenvalue. We use a similar method of analysis to modify the operator and understand the local minimization properties of a related energy functional, thereby establishing its min-max representation in a specific Sobolev space. 

Throughout our discussion, we emphasize the role of parameters in influencing eigenvalue estimates, presenting them in a clear and understandable manner. We also present an extended version of this discussion in Chapter 2 in our main thesis.

Deep contextualized models have significantly improved dependency parsing, 
especially in resource-rich environments, but their performance declines in
resource-constrained settings. A newly proposed approach, auto-training, holds
promise in mitigating this issue for dependency analysis. Essentially, it allows
a parser to generate its own label model by selecting suitable labels for
dependency tags from an undetermined space. Nevertheless, auto-training encounters
problems of label space overwhelm and insincere positive samples. To address
these challenges, we develop a simplified auto-training paradigm for dependency
parsing by introducing a restricted label space and designing a distant supervision
strategy to optimize positive samples. Experiment results demonstrate that this
model surpasses conventional approaches and approaches with static label sets in
multiple challenging languages, yielding substantial improvements of up to 9.9, 
4.4 and 3.3 in F1 metric for English, Portuguese and Serbian languages, respectively. 
Additionally, a dynamic label set size analysis indicates that our approach
is versatile across various language types. To validate the efficacy of our model 
in language modeling, we also conduct label prediction tasks on datasets from 
Bulgarian, Serbian and Portuguese languages, observing significant gains in F1 
metric of 11.8, 9.6 and 14.6, respectively, over a baseline model that employs 
static label sets. These results not only underscore the effectiveness of our 
model but also motivate the adoption of our approach in tasks beyond dependency 
parsing. To facilitate reproduction, our code is openly hosted on GitHub at 
https://github.com/jadelau/DCAPIy. To ensure full reproducibility, 
open-access datasets can be found at https://github.com/jadelau/DCAPIy/tree/main/data. 
For efficiency, pre-trained models can be downloaded at https://github.com/jadelau/DCAPIy/tree/main/models. 
To enable model evaluation, the repository includes implementations of the 
used metrics, which can be found at https://github.com/jadelau/DCAPIy/tree/main/metrics. 
Finally, a detailed description of the model's hyperparameters can be found 
at https://github.com/jadelau/DCAPIy/tree/main/hyperparameters. 
In contrast to existing research that only provides information on the model's 
hyperparameters for English, our model allows for the hyperparameter search in 
languages with limited resources, thanks to its open-ended label space nature. 
Thus, the provided search spaces can be easily adapted for other languages

Circular probability involves defining a measure on a circle with infinitely divided units, assigning equal weights to specified segments based on rotation symmetry. Nontransitive probability arises from a game involving four or more dancers with distinct dancing styles, ranked by audience preference; the last dancer's performance is chosen by the audience, and the lead dancer is eliminated unless the audience prefers him over the next dancer. If the audience prefers him, a new dancer is selected until only one remains, and the chosen dancer's dancing style is the winner. We explore the development of circular and nontransitive probabilities, along with related inequalities and the opportunity for multiple "wins" in such games. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) is a stochastic particle motion model that integrates both autonomous propulsion and thermal movement. Propulsion force magnitude and timescales auto-regulate in response to an attractance towards a target location, leading to complex behavior such as ergodicity breakdown and multiple motion patterns around the target. We developed an analytical method for determining the mean speed and efficiency of AOUP dynamics over a wide range of parameters. Our results show that an optimal propulsion force exists to achieve the highest speed in a given time, and that a varied motion pattern near the target may be more efficient than a direct, straight course. We observed that labor, or idle time during the slow phase near the target, affects the particle's overall efficiency, with higher labor leading to increased efficiency in certain parameter ranges. We analyzed the behavior of AOUP in both two and three-dimensional spaces, confirming the existence of an optimal propulsion force in both environments, but revealing a difference in their respective labor-dependent efficiency patterns. Additionally, we derived a condition for determining the most efficient AOUP motion in a d-dimensional space, up to a d value of 4. Our study of AOUP dynamics contributes to our understanding of the active movement of microbial swimmers and their behavior in various environmental contexts. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric. We aim to break this cycle by providing a universal approach to independent, cross-lingual model transfers. To achieve this, we create task representations that can serve as weak supervision for models in various languages. Leveraging our feeble task representations and feeble word embeddings, we enable models to learn and adapt without extensive training data or comprehensive annotation. We establish a model-independent framework, prove its effectiveness using feeble supervisions, and conduct comprehensive evaluations that showcase its superiority over existing transfer methods. Notably, our task representations facilitate model transfers that are 10-20% more efficient and 5-10% more effective, achieving nearly identical or better performance with significantly reduced resources. With this breakthrough, we pave the way for a new era of efficient, independent, and universal model transfers across languages. The concept of feeble supervisions also empowers the development of low-resource models and opens up new avenues for research exploration. The code for our approach is openly available at https://github.com/ashwink/Cross-Lingual-Model-Transfer.ashwink.github.io. Extended versions of this work can be found at https://ashwink.github.io/publications#feeble-supervisions.ashwink.github.io.
