The agent training process using model-based reinforcement learning can generate negative results like the formation of inaccurate policy representations or representations that incorporate noise. Our investigation focuses on the the extent to which modular policy structures can aid in learning multiple tasks and the role of representation quality in this process. The results show that using modular policies prevents the degradation of performance in multi-task reinforcement learning, whereas the existing methods fail under such scenarios. Moreover, the experiment results indicate that improving representation quality has a direct and significant impact on enhancing multi-task learning performance. Building upon these findings, we propose a method that leverages a modular structure in both policy and representation to support complex multi-task reinforcement learning. The experiment results confirm that this method produces optimal policy outcomes and achieves better performance compared to existing model-based multi-task reinforcement learning methods. Additionally, the representations generated by our method demonstrate superior quality and remain more consistent even across task variations. Crucially, the representations produced by our method remain highly transferable when applied to similar tasks, often resulting in direct generalization to these tasks without the need for further revision. However, the transfer performance may be impacted by the degree of similarity between the target and source tasks. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the practical effectiveness of our method in a realistic simulation that mimics the characteristics of a real-world factory environment. The proposed method outperformed model-based multi-task reinforcement learning methods in both performance and representation quality. Moreover, the representations generated by our method displayed better policy outcomes and the method achieved higher performance compared to a version of the method that lacked a modular representation. Therefore, the proposed method provides a superior solution for multi-task reinforcement learning applications. We explore the performance of an ideal heat engine, either a classical or quantum system, subjected to restricted control within a finite timeframe. The new parameter we investigate is the 'design time', essentially how much time is allocated for crafting an effective protocol. Considering the realm of classical systems first, we reveal that, regardless of design time, there's a fundamental efficiency limit linked to the maximum entropy of the bath. Moving on to quantum systems, we establish that, given a minimum design time, there are situations in quantum systems - more so than in classical systems - where the assigned efficiency exceeds the classical bound, ultimately achieving temperatures lower than the minimal bath temperature. Furthermore, we provide a measure for identifying these promising scenarios. Lastly, we reflect on the implications of our findings for the optimal operation of real-world heat engines. In a practical context, there will always be a trade-off between the time available for design and the loss in performance, thereby it is vital to identify the best possible balance between these two factors. The model accounts for the interaction between hurricanes and their associated storm surges in relation to the shape and movement of low-pressure systems. To validate this framework, it is applied to historical hurricanes in Florida, and the results show that storm surges can cause more extensive damage in coastal regions, extending further inland than the initial landfall point. The outcomes also indicate that the peak damage periods often differ from the hour of the hurricane's landfall, and the severity of storm surges can amplify total damage beyond initial estimates. The proposed model is comprised of two components: a geometric analysis to define the storm surge-impacted zone, and a temporal estimation based on simulation data. The model's accuracy is confirmed by overlaying the simulated area with actual flood data from storm surges, and the results are further validated by calculating total damage using a probabilistic risk assessment model. The results can also be utilized by policymakers to develop effective strategies for storm resilience in their communities. Furthermore, the research can be utilized by engineers to develop cost-effective and evidence-based measures for enhancing the resilience of individual structures and grid infrastructure. This project presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to create raw audio signals in a pitch-independent manner. To fast-track convergence, QPNet integrates Pitch-sensitive Dilated Convolution Neural Network (PDCNN) as a pitch-dependent feature extraction module. PDCNN's input is processed by two distinct networks: a Multi-Periodic Vocoder (MPV) and a Noise Model (NM) to respectively capture quasi-periodic and transient components, and background noise. All components are modeled autoregressively, and the effectiveness of QPNet is validated through listening tests and PESQ analyses in voice synthesis applications. We observe improvements in subjective and objective metrics when compared to WaveNet, particularly in generating quasi-periodic sections and background noise. These limitations can be mitigated with the deployment of more advanced models, such as Transfer learning-based WaveNet (TL-WNet). pseudofunctorial development, yet their theoretical foundation remains poorly 
understood.  This paper unveils a precise bicategorical interpretation of shadows, 
which bridges the gap between the theoretical framework of shadows and actual 
bicategories.  In contrast to previous results, this finding reveals that shadows 
are inherently linked to tracks rather than paths.  This interpretation yields a 
key corollary: any category with objects giving rise to a monoidal track can be 
reconstructed as a bicategory.  Additionally, this paper systemsizes the concept 
of shadows from a theoretical standpoint, defining various classes of shadows and 
establishing their critical properties.  Furthermore, it introduces the concept 
of stars, which are closely related to shadows but possess more flexibility. 
Lastly, this paper poses several unresolved research questions and hypotheses.  We 
expect that resolving these questions will significantly advance the field of 
higher category theory and shadows.  Specifically, we propose the establishment 
of a theoretical category of shadows and stars and the identification of a 
fundamental track underlying this category.  By addressing these questions, this 
paper contributes to strengthening the foundational framework of the field.  This 
paper also provides a comprehensive overview of the field's current research status

Several image enhancement techniques have been developed to improve visibility in low-light conditions. Although these techniques enhance image visibility, they can also introduce overly bright areas that overwhelm details. A new approach, called universal tone mapping, aims to develop a single algorithm that works across various techniques to produce high-contrast images preserving details. However, existing universal tone mapping methods can't reverse their original versions, lacking a style transfer component. To address this limitation, a novel universal tone mapping framework is presented that incorporates two processes - forward and reverse mapping - to extract a style from image pairs. The forward mapping adapts a single image to match a bright reference, while the reverse mapping transforms a dim reference into a bright image while maintaining the original features. The framework achieves this through a two-stage approach, consisting of a joint style extraction module and a transfer learning block, trained on a diverse image dataset with varied lighting conditions. The novel forward and reverse mapping algorithms enable a style transfer that can be applied across various tone mapping techniques, including HDR, HDR2, and Bonnibrooke. The framework produces a range of images from a single input by adjusting the level of style transfer, preserving original details in low, medium, and high lighting conditions. The framework's effectiveness is validated through a visual comparison with existing universal tone mapping approaches, a user study, and evaluations of the generated images under different lighting conditions, demonstrating its superiority and providing new insights into the design of universal tone mapping algorithms. The code and related information are publicly available on GitHub. Understanding stratified turbulence holds significant importance across various fields. Research on this complex phenomenon is ongoing but still lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework despite its widespread occurrence in environments such as atmospheric conditions during snowfall. In ice formation studies, the existence of preferential attachment sites for ice crystals is a widely acknowledged concept, enabling organizers to initiate crystallization through nucleation. This process exploits localized conditions to control the spatial arrangement of forming structures. Preferential attachment sites in atmospheric turbulence have long been a subject of debate. Unlike ice formation, the emergence of these sites appears to be a result of the complex interaction between turbulence and snowflakes rather than inherent characteristics of the atmosphere. To fill the gap in understanding this phenomenon, a novel approach is presented in this research. A new equation is introduced to describe the development of snowflake clustering in space, accounting for the preferential selection of attachment sites. This equation is based on the principles of preferential attachment and reinforces the importance of unattached snowflakes in the process. In a system dominated by turbulence, the preferential selection process accelerates snowflake clustering, enabling a direct link between turbulence and snowflake arrangement. This process is validated through various simulations and experiments, providing a groundbreaking insight into the role of turbulence in snowflake clustering. As a result, a refined understanding of the atmospheric turbulence mechanism underlying snow accumulation is achieved, paving the way for further applications in atmospheric turbulence research. The proposed equation can also be adapted to describe the emergence of complex structures in various environments through a more generalized approach. Furthermore, this work potentially bridges the gap between traditional condensation microphysics and the newer concept of new-physics atmospheric modeling. By incorporating the preferential attachment principle, a more detailed and accurate representation of atmospheric turbulence is achieved, exemplifying the closer integration of condensed matter physics and geophysical fluid mechanics. Additionally, this work lays the groundwork for a broader applicability of the preferential attachment idea within the context of turbulent systems. Finally, a future research direction is outlined, focusing on the further development and refinement of the preferential attachment equation to describe a wide range of turbulent processes. The challenge of integrating the preferential attachment principle into a larger modeling framework of geophysical fluid mechanics is a notable hurdle that needs to be overcome. Once successfully implemented, this model has the potential to revolutionize the understanding and prediction of atmospheric turbulence, providing novel insights into the complex phenomena within geophysical fluids. Furthermore, the principles developed in this study may be extensively applied to other areas of geophysical fluid dynamics where new-physics modeling is a key component.

In many robotic tasks, generating suitable perceptions necessitates constant interaction between perception and action, necessitating coordinated active sensing. This grounded aspect of perception is often overlooked in existing learning techniques that view sensing as a passive process. To address this gap, we present a new method called Profound Active Inference, an innovative approach that integrates predictive coding principles within a Bayesian framework. This approach treats sensing, prediction, and decision-making as an iterative four-step process, facilitating coordinated sampling and action planning based on the robot's shared predictive insights. By applying this method to a real-world navigation task using a mobile robot equipped with a low-cost RGBD sensor, we demonstrate improved performance over existing passive perception methods in challenging weather conditions. Furthermore, Profound Active Inference enables robots to adapt and evolve through the incorporation of novel sensing modalities, enhancing their robustness and efficiency in unpredictable environments. This approach provides a comprehensive solution for robots to strategically collect informative data, effectively navigating unknown environments and optimizing active sensing, thereby inducing robust and interpretable representations. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/br1tch/Profound-Active-Inference. Additional material is available at https://britch.net/profound-active-inference.

The comprehensive computer code Li6Vx for the experimental study of the 6Li+51V systematic project is presented in detail. This project aims to generate all relevant alpha particle data through 51V(6Li, d)* or 51V(6Li, α) reactions at specific angular distributions for excitations below the threshold of 2.8 MeV. The code Li6Vx incorporates an empirical formula that calculates the cross-section of (6Li, d) reactions as a function of excitation energy, along with a peak normalization constant. Additionally, the code normalizes cross-sections experimentally measured in specific reactions, (6Li, d) on a 39K target for excitations below 7.8 MeV and (6Li, α) on a 35Cl target for excitations below 20 MeV. The results of Li6Vx match well with experimental data; moreover, the theoretical angular distribution of 2.5 MeV li+α particles from a 51V(6Li, α) reaction at an incident energy of 15 MeV corresponds closely to that measured experimentally. The code Li6Vx is suitable for predicting alpha particle production resulting from 6Li+51V collisions at varying incident energies and angular distributions. To estimate the effects of phasing errors in gravitational wave measurements from inspiraling binary compact object coalescences, we develop a formula for the remaining eccentricity of the orbit at the point of merger. This eccentricity is expressed in terms of the gravitational wave frequency at merger, which can be related to the masses of the binary components using post-Newtonian theory. Specifically, our expression for the remaining eccentricity incorporates a term that represents the radial displacement of one compact object within the other's gravitational influence, taking into account higher-order post-Newtonian corrections. Our analysis demonstrates that when binary compact objects' masses are sufficiently symmetric, the radial displacement can be estimated to an accuracy of better than one-tenth of the gravitational wave frequency at merger. In contrast, for highly asymmetric systems, the accuracy of our estimate is comparable to a best-case scenario with the same degree of asymmetry. We validate the accuracy of our expression through comparison with numerical simulations of the binary evolution, observing that for systems with a total mass greater than or equal to six times that of the sun, the residual eccentricity is typically lower than one-thousandth of the gravitational wave frequency at merger. The precision of our expression in this regime is a significant improvement over previous estimates, which yielded errors of up to a few tenths of a thousandth of the gravitational wave frequency. Our analysis concludes with a prediction regarding the effects of phasing errors in gravitational wave measurements, with the expectation that such errors will become negligible relative to other sources for binary compact coalescences with a total mass greater than or equal to sixty times that of the sun. Furthermore, our work refines the understanding of post-Newtonian theory in relation to the gravitational wave frequency at merger, achieving an accuracy of better than one-thousandth of the frequency for which post-Newtonian theory provides a precise, analytic representation. The precision of our result in this precision is a significant advancement over previous estimates, with our conclusion supering a previous upper bound on the precision, with the precision varying from 0.99997 percent for systems with a total mass equal to two times that of the sun to less than 0.99999 percent for systems with a total mass greater than or equal to sixty times that of the sun. Our work in this precision will be a valuable reference for future measurements of binary compact coalescences, with the precision varying from 0.99997 percent for systems with a total mass equal to two times that of the sun to less than 0.99999 percent

This X-ray enhancer achieves high intensities not attainable with conventional FELs, producing a highly focused, transient burst. Our concept involves using a plasma wave to amplify an FELO's short-wavelength laser, generating a high-coherence seed signal. In an equation of state fluid with variable density, we examine how a initially spherical, high-pressure pulse behaves as it collapses. This pulse is bounded by a strengthening shockwave that moves through the fluid, compressing it. Initially, the fluid on the other side of the shockwave is in a low-pressure state, and as the pulse collapses, the difference between the pressure across the shockwave and the background pressure grows, leading to a acceleration of the shockwave. Eventually, the fluid will likely undergo a rapid transformation due to the increased pressure, resolving a long-debated issue about what happens to these pulses in a medium with density fluctuations. Numerical solutions show that the lifetime of these collapse pulses is directly proportional to the square of the initial pressure deviations, and we find specific proportional constants through our analysis. Additionally, we outline the relevant physical parameters that influence these collapse pulses and suggest that they may play a significant role in the formation of supernovae. Finally, we propose that the formation of neutron stars or black holes through collapse may be partially accountable for the observed gamma-ray bursts due to the rapid energy release from the shockwave. If this hypothesis is correct, then the remaining energy from these events, rather than being released as gamma-rays, could instead be stored in the core of the star, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of these bursts. Furthermore, our work also provides a potential explanation for the observed nucleosynthesis in stars, as the high-density fluid on the other side of the shockwave could undergo a rapid and intense nuclear transformation. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is vital to personalize patient care and reduce the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The technological advancements in digital pathology enable a more comprehensive assessment by augmenting the existing histopathological diagnosis. To enhance accuracy in this complex process, extensive training using large datasets is necessary. Current digital pathology datasets, labeled with relevant clinical information, are limited, specifically regarding colorectal polyps and adenoma dysplasia assessments. To address this shortage, a new dataset, UniToPatho, has been developed. This dataset contains 348 annotated images obtained from 66 whole-slide images, showcasing diverse histopathological patterns associated with primary colorectal lesions and metastases. The UniToPatho dataset enables machine learning model development to classify colorectal polyps and evaluate adenoma dysplasia, ultimately contributing to improving patient outcomes. The dataset's resources and associated information, including image annotations, are accessible through the UniToPatho website. This dataset can facilitate research in digital pathology, particularly for colorectal cancer and polyps with adenoma and dysplasia evaluations. Researchers can engage with the UniToPatho community for collaboration and support. The UniToPatho repository will remain online to make these research resources permanent and easily accessible. Data compression technology, known for reducing the amount of stored data, has an unexpected issue: some compressed files can easily be decompressed and reveal a significant amount of the original, uncensored data, thereby compromising user confidentiality. To address this problem of data leakage in compression, we need to develop new methods that minimize the amount of leaked information while achieving nearly lossless compression. From an information-theoretic perspective, this problem can be seen as a special case of source coding with zero error and data leakage constraints. We explore this new perspective and provide a mathematical framework for understanding data leakage in compression by using graph theory. Specifically, we examine the relationship between conditional entropy and graph topology, which allows us to establish a threshold for leakage in a compressed file. To illustrate our theoretical framework, we use an example of leakage in a binary tree code. This study provides a foundational understanding of the data-leakage-compression conflict and paves the way for further research on the quantitative analysis of data leakage. Moreover, we propose an approach to identify the optimal compression strategies that balance leakage and storage costs. To test our theoretical framework, we conducted an experiment on the leakage of binary files encoded using Huffman coding, which showed promising results. The developed approach can be used for various compression algorithms and source codes. Furthermore, we outline potential applications of our study in other fields, such as cryptography and graph theory, as well as the development of new compression schemes that take into account the costs associated with leakage and storage. Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variations persist as viable contenders for achieving near-optimal solutions to intricate combinatorial issues.  A crucial factor in QAOA's success lies in accurately selecting its operational angles ($\alpha$ and $\theta$), which, when optimized, lead to approximate solution quality enhancements.  We introduce a novel approach called Bayesian Maximization, which adapts the principle behind Bayesian Optimization to identify the optimal $\alpha$ and $\theta$ values with enhanced accuracy, even when only a limited number of measurements are taken on a quantum device.  This method is particularly useful on hardware platforms with restricted access to operations due to decoherence time constraints, allowing it to yield better results than traditional gradient-based approaches in such scenarios.  Our approach is further demonstrated through its successful application to solving both MaxCut and Platt's Phase Fidelity problems, yielding improved outcomes in comparison to previous QAOA optimization methods.  A comprehensive evaluation of its performance under different problem conditions is also provided.  Specifically, our analysis shows that applying Bayesian Maximization to the phase estimation problem in QAOA optimizations yields a 38\% improvement in solution quality over the best-known classical optimization methods studied in this research for a particular quantum problem instance, while achieving this improvement with an average $\pm 0.03$ error in target angle estimation, as opposed to a larger $\pm 0.1$ error associated with other methods.  This research presents strong evidence that BAM can significantly improve the outcome quality of near-term quantum hardware, while reducing the operational requirements of the device.  A related GitHub repository at https://github.com/qmbin/bam_qaoa can be accessed by the public to reproduce the study's results thanks to the team's efforts in developing a wide range of useful software tools to support QAOA optimizations with BAM.  The code in particular includes a Python script that runs the optimized protocol on real quantum hardware available in the public repository.  The team believes this resource will greatly aid in the reproduction of the research outcomes, while also facilitating the exploration of novel applications and extensions of the approach to other quantum algorithms with similar hardware implementation challenges.  Finally, the authors mention that the research presents a novel solution to a previously unstudied problem, namely the low-coherence issue that affects the performance of quantum machines, while showing great potential for the approach to be generalized and applied to a broader range of quantum algorithms with similar implementation issues.  This research could potentially have a great impact on the field by solving the low-coherence problem encountered

Vertebrae in the spine are a crucial area of focus for various medical and radiology tasks but their analysis via computer is hampered by time-consuming preparations required to accurately view and study them.  To address this, we have created a fully automated method for identifying and mapping vertebral bodies in chest and abdominal CT scans.  Our algorithm aligns the vertebral column with a standardized framework, then uses a non-convex optimization process to accurately place landmarks within.  To ensure accurate identification, we have incorporated anatomical constraints, including plausible acting, fitting, and relation constraints.  Evaluation of our method revealed accurate localization of vertebral bodies, with less than 0.5 mm and 0.7 degrees error in 3D-2D projection and shape similarity assessment.  Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our method outperforms a publicly available state-of-the-art deep learning platform in terms of precision and recall while also providing adjustable anatomical interpretation options for clinical use.  Overall, our method provides a reliable and accurate computer-based analysis of vertebral bodies, with potential applications in a variety of radiological fields. Additionally, the challenge dataset created for evaluation can be accessed via a GitHub repository at: https://github.com/pulmonary-sci/VertebralLandmarks. It contains the code and data needed to replicate our results and supports further research and development of anatomical structure localization and segmentation tasks.  The code has been reviewed and prepared for use by others with expertise in CNNs.  Future enhancements to our method could involve generating a full CNN model to automate the task even further.  Future work can also involve adjusting the optimization algorithm to include additional anatomical constraints, such as lumbar vertebrae variation trends, to further improve its accuracy.  Finally, we can apply our localization method to automatically generate vertebral centrelines, which can then be used to detect vertebral fractures and other diseases while greatly reducing the time needed for analysis. The accuracy of our localization has been confirmed, with potential clinical applications for radiological analysis soon to be confirmed. The anatomical interpretation provided by our method can also be used to improve the detection and analysis of various anatomical structures and diseases over large numbers of patients via automatic radiological analysis.  Precision and recall of our method were found to be 98% and 90% respectively, with potential applications in a variety of radiological fields due to its high accuracy in identifying vertebral bodies and projecting their shapes in a standardized manner. The discovery of atmospheric escape in hot Jupiters, particularly those with close proximity to their host stars, reveals the dynamic processes occurring in planetary atmospheres.  Kepler-2b, being one of the first discovered hot Jupiters with significant stellar irradiance, displays characteristics that set it apart from other similarly sized planets.  Notably, it orbits a G-dwarf star at a distance of 0.025 AU and has a mass comparable to that of Earth.  Recent studies of Kepler-2b's atmosphere, observed during its 0 phase, revealed signs of a scorching hot day-side atmosphere and a night-side atmosphere shrouded in a thick layer of dust.  A more recent study by McCullough et al. revealed the presence of a massive point source located near Kepler-2b's LBTI/PEPSI observing spot.  PEPSI data, exhibiting a signal-to-noise ratio of 135, failed to conclusively identify a spectral feature near the star's location.  Our analysis detects a star with a mass roughly 4 times that of Earth and properties distinct from its host star Kepler-2b.  A subsequent grazing impact event involving this object and the star appears to be the source of the anomalous S/N ratio data.  Our analysis of the PEPSI data, encompassing multiple passes, reveals a signal exceeding starlight in the red to near-infrared range, suggesting dust grains larger than typical atmospheric particles.  A theory proposing the planet's rapid spin could result in atmospheric non-uniformity, resulting in the observed dust signal, is ruled out.  Our findings indicate a mass loss rate for Kepler-2b that far exceeds that of other hot Jupiters, particularly those with orbits closer to their host stars, and place further pressure on the existing theoretical models.  Our analysis of the LBTI/PEPSI data also discloses evidence of the planet's non-axial rotation, revealed by the dust grain asymmetry, and uncovers a unique phenomenon in the near-infrared range resulting from Kepler-2b's close proximity to its host star.  Furthermore, our analysis indicates a hot zone near Kepler-2b's day-side atmosphere and a vast dust shroud enveloping its night-side atmosphere, and a sharp temperature drop occurring just beyond the carbon iionization radius, thereby invalidating thermodynamic equilibrium as a reliable model for the planet's atmosphere. Galileo's reliance on mathematics wasn't a pioneering effort, but rather a continuation of Ignorian achievements, speaking directly to the heart of the scientific revolution's dynamics. This revelation prompts a reexamination of the historical timeline, suggesting that the Ignorian influence on Galileo wasn't an anomaly, but rather a natural consequence of the scientific revolution's underlying characteristics. Furthermore, I argue that the Ignorian legacy survived long after the scientific revolution, influencing 20th-century physicists like Einstein. Through this analysis, I seek to reinterpret the relationship between mathematics and philosophy, revealing how the former often reflects the latter's dominant discursive practices. Ultimately, this study acknowledges the vast array of intellectual practices found in the scientific revolution and suggests that philosophy remained a vital force shaping the scientific enterprise. By reclaiming philosophy's historical influence, we can foster a more equitable present, acknowledging the diverse range of disciplines that contributed to the scientific revolution's development. Prior to the cosmic structure's formation, the ionization of photons resulting from the Big Bang's energy release played a pivotal role in determining the universe's state. Due to incompatibility with observed data, early universe models necessitate the introduction of an ionization variable to describe the universe's ionized state accurately. This, in turn, gives rise to a non-Gaussian distribution of photons, thereby affecting the cosmic structure's development through the photon-baryon fluid's anisotropic stress. The variable's impact, however, becomes more pronounced in the early universe due to its interaction with the fluid's anisotropic stress, thereby affecting the cosmic structure's development in a manner proportional to the universe's scale factor and the square of the photon ionization variable. The presence of anisotropic stresses also influences the gravitational field, thereby affecting the cosmic structure's development by means of perturbation growth. The consideration of anisotropic stresses thus yields growth rates differing significantly from the purely Gaussian photon distribution-based rates in the early universe. The impact of the anisotropic stresses eventually diminishes as the universe becomes ionized, thereby reducing the differential equation for perturbation growth by a factor proportional to the photon ionization variable. To study magnetic island reconnection in turbulent magnetic fields, a magnetohydrodynamic simulation with embedded particle-in-cell model was employed. These simulations revealed two types of island interactions: one-characteristic reconnection and multi-polar reconnection. A key finding shows that island merging can occur through one reconnection process only when the relative rotation speed between islands exceeds a certain threshold. Furthermore, a critical threshold for the magnetic field strength exists beyond which island interactions are hindered. Data indicates that island merging can occur at an angle other than 90 degrees and that magnetic island reconnection follows a universal scaling law. Additionally, certain characteristics of particle-in-cell reconnection were observed, particularly in relation to current per unit length, electron temperature, and an anisotropy measure, each exhibiting distinct stages across various reconnection processes. To validate these results, a second-order integration scheme was used to confirm the findings. Confirmation included matching previous research on magnetic island reconnection and also reproducing reconnection statistics across various parameters, confirming that island merging can occur at an angle other than 90 degrees. To extend the understanding of these reconnection processes, a summary of the embedded particle-in-cell simulation results was provided. It was demonstrated that reconnection can occur through multiple interactions but also through one reconnection process, each with distinct reconnection dynamics. Embodied PIC reconnection was found to be distinct from other reconnection processes, particularly mHD reconnection which was also simulated. Embodied PIC reconnection was characterized by multiple reconnection sites, non-local current, and other features, all of which are absent in mHD reconnection. Unlike mHD reconnection, embodied PIC reconnection can resemble multi-polar reconnection but also one-characteristic reconnection. Embodied PIC reconnection was found to be gradationally connected to mHD reconnection, meaning it shares some similarities with mHD reconnection. We present a novel technique in program analysis focused on identifying highly active contributors among multiple Git repositories. This strategy involves developing a vast language model from widely available open-source software, which we then use to create multiple descriptions of a new, unseen repository through brief summaries. A highly active contributor is predicted to leave behind traces - namely, partial code copies, similar commit patterns, and file naming conventions - within the new repository. By optimizing the description length and evaluating multiple model iterations, our approach excels in accurately identifying top contributors for numerous repositories, achieving superior results compared to established baselines. Furthermore, the accuracy of our predictions increases as the number of repository pairs grows, demonstrating valuable practical applications and showcasing the versatility of our method in analyzing complex software ecosystems. To facilitate comprehensive replication, the code, repository data, and pre-trained models used in this study are openly available on a dedicated GitHub platform. Additionally, a demonstration of this research is available on an interactive Colab environment. This work has been formally presented at the NeurIPS 2021 workshop on fair, transparent, and accountable NLP, boasting an impressive acceptance rate of 3.7%. Currently, a live, interactive visualization of this research can be found on the ContribAtlas platform, which has successfully identified contributors in over 20 new software projects since its initial release in 2021. The contributions of this research can be broadly categorized into three areas: identifying active contributors, refining software training datasets, and establishing effective software owner communications. The methodology employed in this study has also inspired the development of a novel evaluation metric, denoted as the Contriburator score, and a large collection of relevant papers, encompassing 554 scholarly works, which are openly available on a dedicated research database. The underlying software framework used in this research is freely available on GitHub, wherein it provides a functional, interactive environment for exploring the concepts presented in this research, collectively referred to as the Scribe method. This involves a multi-faceted system comprising: (i) a comprehensive repository taxonomy; (ii) a set of engaging, narrative descriptions; (ii) a sophisticated analysis module; and (iv) a suite of illustrative visualizations, all of which are openly available under a permissive, flexible license, facilitating seamless adoption into other software training datasets. The contributors of this research have also released a range of related educational resources, encompassing 14 scholarly works, which can be freely accessed through a dedicated repository.
